10.sign: Unilateral manual automatisms (ipsilateral fumbling, picking, patting)

12.sign: Late forced/tonic head version (>30s, sustained, contralateral)

13.sign: Early non-forced head turning (<30s, ipsilateral, exploratory)

14.sign: Figure-of-4 sign (extended arm + flexed arm asymmetric tonic)

25.sign: Ictal aphasia / speech arrest during seizure

28.sign: Simple auditory aura (tones, buzzing, hissing, roaring)

29.sign: Complex auditory hallucinations (formed music, songs, melodies)

31.sign: Auditory illusions (sounds distorted in quality, loudness, or distance)

35.sign: Formed semantic visual hallucinations (faces, people, scenes, objects)

44.sign: Bilateral asymmetric tonic posturing (fencing posture / BATS)

45.sign: M2E automatism (mouth-to-hand: ipsilateral hand moves to mouth)

46.sign: Chapeau de gendarme sign (bilateral forced lip-corner retraction)

47.sign: Ictal pout (perioral dystonic protrusion/pursing - distinct from chapeau)

49.sign: Speech arrest / ictal mutism (dominant SMA, inhibitory)

50.sign: Bilateral leg elevation with cycling/pedaling movements

51.sign: Nocturnal brief stereotyped seizures (rapid onset/offset, minimal postictal)

56.sign: Hypermotor agitated behavior (ACC-dominant type with emotional coloring)

61.sign: Ictal negative motor phenomenon (inhibitory arrest of contralateral limb)

62.sign: Somatosensory aura (tingling, numbness, paresthesia - contralateral, somatotopic)

63.sign: Somatosensory Jacksonian march (sensory spread through somatotopic map)

73.sign: Elementary visual phenomena (phosphenes, flickering lights, geometric forms, fortification spectra)

75.sign: Colored visual elementary hallucinations (yellow, red, blue, multicolored)

8.sign: Motionless stare / ictal behavioral arrest (hypomotor onset)

80.sign: Moving visual phenomena (motion-specific: moving dots, patterns, streams - without form)

81.sign: Geometric formed visual hallucinations (grids, kaleidoscope, checkerboards - without semantic content)

82.sign: Laryngeal / throat constriction (tightening, strangling, pressure sensation)

88.sign: Ictal autonomic cardiac arrhythmia (right insular predominance)

9.sign: Oral automatisms (lip smacking, chewing, swallowing, licking)

90.sign: Nocturnal hypermotor seizures from insular cortex (mimicking NFLE)

91.sign: Gelastic seizures (ictal mirthless laughter - pathognomonic for hypothalamic hamartoma)

92.sign: Dacrystic seizures (ictal crying - associated with hypothalamic hamartoma)

93.sign: Bilateral asymmetric tonic seizure (BATS) at secondary generalization

94.sign: Temporal seizure semiological sequence (orderly progression: aura->arrest->oral->manual->dystonia)

95.sign: Hypermotor vs. hypomotor distinction (primary semiological axis for lobe of origin)

96.sign: TIRDA (Temporal Intermittent Rhythmic Delta Activity) - scalp EEG interictal

99.sign: Axial tonic posturing (trunk extension or flexion)

sources.source_report_limitations: All 15 pages had present fresh text and represented PNG renderings. Figures 1–4 and Table 1 were visually inspected; pages 1, 5–10 contain the principal abstract, flow diagram, database heatmaps, table, and forest/OR plots. The article’s quantitative analysis uses normalized data points, multi-region encoding, heterogeneous ground truths, and author-defined topological labels. Figure 3/4 graphical cells are not converted into inferred exact values when the source does not print a number. Repeated abstract/discussion values are represented once with combined locators rather than duplicated as independent results. Cited-study restatements remain separate from the present primary analysis.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a primary systematic-review/database analysis, not a new prospective cohort. The authors report 11,230 localizing and 2,391 lateralizing data points from 4,643 patients across 309 articles. The analysis uses source-described semiologies, 103 hierarchical regions, mixed ground truths, patient-level normalization, 10,000 bootstrap samples for 95% CIs, and ORs from two-by-two contingency tables. Figure 3 and Figure 4 show plotted values, but exact point estimates for every plotted region/semiology cell are not tabulated in the source; only exact values stated in the prose or printed labels are entered as atomic findings below.
sources.source_report_summary: Alim-Marvasti et al., “Probabilistic landscape of seizure semiology localizing values,” Brain Communications 2022;4:fcac130, reports a PRISMA-guided systematic review and analysis of Semio2Brain v.1.2.2. The source links source-described semiologies to hierarchical localization categories using seizure-freedom, imaging/electrophysiology concordance, and invasive EEG/stimulation ground truths, while separating topological from non-topological studies to address temporal-lobe publication bias. Its primary results are conditional localization probabilities and intrinsic ORs for the 12 most common semiologies, with temporal subregions shown separately. Localization and lateralization are kept independent: the database contains lateralizing data points, but the main text does not provide a complete lateralizing-results table.

sources.source_report_limitations:
This is a small, selected lesional surgical series whose cingulate coverage by subdural electrodes was incomplete in all invasively evaluated patients. The source explicitly states that earliest EEG change may represent a spread-exit pattern rather than the actual onset zone and that scalp EEG was often misleading or nonlocalizing. The semiology/lateralization comparison uses only clinical signs with source-defined lateralizing value greater than 80%; available PET, interictal EEG, and ictal EEG denominators differ. Figure 3 is retained only for direct seizure signs, phase, and lesion-side observations; surgery, pathology, outcome, and demographic cells are not individual findings.

Owner question: Should the source’s 8/14 versus 8/9 versus 3/14 versus 6/13 lateralization comparison be integrated as a single analysis family with separate modality units, or retained as separate modality-specific estimates because the denominators and ascertainment differ?
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors retrospectively identified consecutive cases from Cleveland Clinic and University of Texas Southwestern databases, using MRI-defined lesions confined to the cingulate gyrus and source-defined follow-up/outcome criteria. Visual MRI analysis divided the cingulate into anterior and posterior portions using Talairach and Tournoux coordinates; invasive data were used when lesion overlap made localization uncertain. Fourteen cases were included, with 10 anterior and 4 posterior cingulate lesions; the report’s direct EEG/PET denominators are retained only where stated.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2013 original investigation reports lesional cingulate epilepsy in 14 surgically treated cases divided by source MRI anatomy into anterior and posterior cingulate groups, with typical and atypical anterior electroclinical subgroups. Direct findings retained here are cingulate anatomy, source-native seizure signs and auras, seizure evolution, EEG/PET localization and lateralization, seizure-duration comparisons, and directly linked cited-case restatements. Generic demographics, resection/outcome cells, and non-evidence table cells remain context only.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review and expert opinion, not an original empirical study, systematic review, or quantitative meta-analysis. Many cited-study claims are reported without endpoint numerators, denominators, confidence intervals, or exact site-level counts; study cohort size in Table 1 is not treated as an endpoint denominator. Cited studies are not independently reviewed here, and source-level attribution is preserved as reported. The body describes de Ribaupierre et al. (2012) speech arrest in three patients, while Table 1 lists eight subjects for that study; the source does not reconcile the narrative subset with the table total. The locked filename contains "2016," but the PDF title page and citation identify Aron et al. (2021), published 10 March 2021. The article concerns stimulation-evoked language responses and postoperative naming rather than spontaneous ictal seizure semiology, and its laterality statements are often task-, site-, or cohort-specific.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is not an original cohort or pooled analysis. The review discusses published sEEG/ECS, subdural ECS, intraoperative ECS, intracranial recording, fMRI, and surgical-outcome studies; Table 1 lists 16 reviewed depth-electrode studies with study-level subject counts ranging from 1 to 172, including pediatric and adult populations. The source does not define one aggregate analysis population, does not report a pooled estimate, and states that no proper comparison has been made between resections with and without extra-operative or intra-operative language mapping. Stimulation protocols and language-task choices are described as methodological context; findings below retain study-specific populations and units where the review reports them.
sources.source_report_summary: Aron, Jonas, Colnat-Coulbois, and Maillard, "Language Mapping Using Stereo Electroencephalography: A Review and Expert Opinion," Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 15:619521, published 10 March 2021. This narrative review and expert opinion evaluates electrical cortical stimulation (ECS) and related intracranial language mapping with stereo-electroencephalography (sEEG) in epilepsy surgery, distinguishing indispensable anterior/posterior language cortex from dispensable basal temporal language cortex. Its in-scope contribution is language localization, language-dominance lateralization, stimulation-evoked language responses, and postoperative naming outcomes.

sources.source_report_limitations:
This is a single-center, clinic-based retrospective surgical series with 18 patients and smaller EEG/MRI subsets. The source does not provide a complete independent denominator for every cited Table 1 percentage beyond the row patient count, and the underlying cited cohorts may overlap with one another or with the present cohort. The article states that semiology and scalp EEG may mislocalize parietal seizures; no performance estimate beyond the reported descriptive counts and percentages is available. Bibliography entries, generic methods, demographic cells, surgery/outcome counts, and non-evidence table cells were not made individual findings.

Owner question: Should the cited Table 1 EEG/semiology restatements be deduplicated against the primary cohorts before cross-source synthesis, given that the source does not resolve overlap?
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors reviewed patients with drug-resistant parietal lobe epilepsy evaluated for surgery at Jefferson Comprehensive Epilepsy Center from 1986 through 2015. The diagnosis was based on ictal semiology, MRI lesion, and EEG findings; presurgical evaluation included brain MRI and prolonged video-EEG, and all patients underwent resective surgery. Sufficient data were available for 18 patients in the present cohort; denominator-specific EEG and MRI analyses are represented only when source-explicit.
sources.source_report_summary: This original 2017 article reports a retrospective surgical cohort of drug-resistant parietal lobe epilepsy. Directly retained evidence concerns source-native aura and seizure terms, parietal and extra-parietal EEG localization, left/right or bilateral EEG findings, and MRI localization. Generic demographics, surgery counts, pathology totals, and postoperative outcome counts are retained only as compact context or omitted from findings under the bounded scope correction. Table 1 cited-study restatements are retained only for semiology and localization/lateralization results.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source is a retrospective, surgically selected cohort of patients evaluated with SEEG, not an unselected population with temporal or temporal-plus epilepsy. Only one typical seizure per patient entered the quantitative clinical analysis despite 607 SEEG-recorded seizures, and aura ascertainment could rely on event-time reports, post-ictal interview, or recent history. SEEG sampled targeted regions but did not explore most brain volume; the authors state that T+ subgroup assignment cannot be considered definitively error-free. The cohort excluded many patients with clear initial eloquent-cortex involvement, and the authors identify selection bias as a possible explanation for the reported seizure-lateralization difference. T+ subgroups were small. Table 2 percentages have no row-specific numerators or denominators, and the source does not provide confidence intervals or correction for multiple comparisons. Cluster analysis used 30 clusters from 72 non-zero events and is described by the authors as descriptive, with no well-established a-priori method for choosing the number of clusters. The rendered Table 1 lateralization cells (“4 L” and “20 L”) are not directionally concordant with the Results text's statement of left-side predominance in TL patients; this is retained as an unresolved source conflict rather than normalized. Cited-study statements remain unverified restatements and are not independent measurements of the present cohort.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The study was retrospective and included 80 of 212 consecutive patients with medically intractable seizures operated on after SEEG at Grenoble Hospital from 1990 to 1998. Eligibility required no detectable MRI lesion except hippocampal sclerosis, SEEG involvement of at least mesial and/or lateral temporal structures, SEEG-guided surgery, and at least 5 years of postoperative follow-up. The cohort comprised 42 females and 38 males; the reported mean age at SEEG was 29.3 ± 8.7 years, mean age at epilepsy onset 10.1 ± 7.9 years, mean epilepsy duration 19 ± 8 years, and mean seizure frequency 13.5 ± 17.5 per month. Sixty-six patients had unilateral hippocampal sclerosis; 14 had no clear MRI abnormality before surgery, with hamartoma or non-Taylor cortical dysplasia found in two of those at neuropathology. Long-term scalp video-EEG recorded 432 seizures in 79 patients; SEEG used 888 chronically implanted electrodes and recorded 607 seizures in 79 patients, with one patient not captured because the SEEG study was interrupted. The epileptogenic zone was defined by the first clear preclinical ictal SEEG change consisting of low-voltage fast activity or recruiting fast spikes and by the cortex considered for removal; 58 patients were classified TL and 22 T+, with T+ subgroups temporo-frontal (TF, n=9), temporo-sylvian (TS, n=7), and temporo-parieto-occipital (TPO, n=6). Clinical semiology was assessed on one typical seizure per patient, giving 80 analyzed seizures, because the number of recorded seizures per patient ranged from 1 to 44. The comparison used relative frequencies and contingency tables; Phi and Cramer V significance was set at P≤0.05. Scalp-EEG findings were classified by type, lateralization, and 10–20 localization; ictal onset included low-voltage fast activity, localized flattening, disappearance of localized interictal abnormalities, or rhythmic theta when the other patterns were absent. Tailored resections included at least the temporal pole and mesio-temporal structures; 18 of 22 T+ cases had extension outside the temporal lobe, and postoperative Engel classes were reported as context rather than as semiologic findings. The introduction also cites surgical outcome examples involving temporo-perisylvian, temporo-insular, temporo-parietal, and posterior basal temporal onsets; these cited reports are represented separately only where the outcome is inseparable from the localizing claim.
sources.source_report_summary: This is a retrospective primary empirical study of ictal clinical semiology and scalp-EEG findings differentiating SEEG-defined temporal lobe (TL) from temporal-plus (T+) epilepsies in 80 consecutive surgical patients. Its atlas relevance is the source-reported comparison of ictal auras, autonomic, motor, behavioural, post-ictal, interictal scalp-EEG, and ictal scalp-EEG features, including body-side and extra-temporal localization descriptors. The paper also reports cited-study restatements in its discussion; those are kept separate from the present cohort's results and are not verified against the cited sources here.

sources.source_report_limitations:
The review is secondary, heterogeneous, and based largely on small case reports and series. The source contains unresolved internal aggregate discrepancies: the abstract and several sections report 83 patients, whereas Study characteristics reports 86; the abstract reports 57% Engel I after one year, whereas the narrative and Table 2 report 87% (60/69) and the Table 1 rows contain heterogeneous denominators; the narrative reports 74% SEEG/intracranial and 83% operated, whereas Table 2 reports 64/83 (77%) SEEG and 71/83 (88%) operated; the narrative reports 55% adults and 76% MRI positive, whereas Table 2 reports 34/83 adults (40%) and 79/83 MRI positive (95%). The EZ-confidence totals also differ between narrative text and Table 2. Table 1 percentages and Table 3 percentages do not provide row denominators in the displayed table, and cited-study overlap cannot be resolved from the review alone. No anatomical or classification mapping beyond source-native terms is asserted.

Owner questions: Which review-level aggregate totals and outcome denominator should be retained for downstream synthesis when the abstract, narrative, and Table 2 conflict? Can the numbered Table 1 rows be linked to the cited studies and checked for cohort overlap from the source package alone, or should they remain separate review-table records?
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors state that the review followed PRISMA. Eligible peer-reviewed English, French, German, Spanish, or Italian papers had relevant video-EEG, semiology, stimulation, surgical, electrical-source-imaging, or anatomical data focused on basal temporal epilepsy; papers limited to stimulation were excluded. Two reviewers screened and extracted data, with a third resolving disagreements. Descriptive statistics summarized demographics, imaging, semiology, and outcomes. QUADAS-2-guided assessment addressed enrollment and symptom assessment. Epileptogenic-zone (EZ) confidence was graded very high, high, moderate, or low using MRI, intracerebral EEG, and postoperative outcome; selective/tailored surgery was considered for high evidence grading.
sources.source_report_summary: This is a 2025 systematic review of the clinical semiology and anatomical correlates of seizures attributed to the basal temporal region. The review searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through December 2023 and summarizes case reports, small series, SEEG/intracranial studies, imaging, and surgical outcomes. It is a review-authored synthesis; individual study results below are retained as cited-study restatements rather than independent primary observations.

findings.citation: [99] P. Kotagal et al., “Psychomotor seizures of temporal lobe onset: analysis of symptom clusters and sequences”
findings.claim: In an analysis of 31 Engel class 1 patients with complex partial seizures of temporal-lobe onset, 18 common symptoms formed four subclusters: epigastric aura with ictal emesis, alimentary and hand automatisms; behavioural arrest with complete loss of consciousness, staring and bilateral facial contraction; unilateral dystonic arm posturing with mimetic automatisms, complex gestures, ictal speech and partial loss of consciousness; and looking around with agitation, vocalizations and whole-body movements. sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review with heterogeneous cited populations, qualitative language, and no single source-wide denominator or reference standard. Several localizing or lateralizing statements are explicitly qualified as usual, typical, reported, suggested, or disputed; those qualifiers are retained. The review warns that scalp-inaccessible onset or propagation into eloquent cortex can produce false localization, so semiology may represent propagation rather than seizure origination. The cited articles were not inspected, and no outside source, public atlas, registry, prior review, sibling report, or handoff was used. Pages 7–10 contain only the article’s bibliography after the review text; bibliography entries were not treated as findings. No page was unreadable or blocked.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The document reports a narrative review and does not report a systematic-search method, single enrollment cohort, eligibility criteria, pooled analysis, or source-wide reference standard. Population descriptors are claim-specific and heterogeneous, including temporal-lobe, mesial-temporal, neocortical-temporal, frontal-versus-temporal, childhood, older-adult, benign mesial-temporal, and cited study cohorts. The review discusses 31 Engel class 1 patients in one cited symptom-cluster analysis and a 50-patient sample in one cited facial-asymmetry result; those cohort descriptors are retained only with the corresponding findings. It also reports lesion/etiologic context, including mesial temporal sclerosis or hippocampal sclerosis as a common cause of TLE and HS evidence in benign mTLE, but those context statements are not treated as stand-alone semiologic findings. No source-wide analysis unit, surgery-outcome analysis, or mortality-outcome analysis is reported. Cited-study restatements remain unverified against the cited articles under this review boundary.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2012 Review Article by Robert D. G. Blair, “Temporal Lobe Epilepsy Semiology,” is a narrative review of temporal-lobe seizure semiology and its localization or lateralization, including temporal-versus-frontal differential features, auras, automatisms, motor, autonomic, speech, age-related, childhood, sleep/wake, symptom-cluster, orgasmic-aura, and benign-mesial-temporal patterns. It is relevant as a source-authored synthesis and as a container for cited-study restatements; it is not a single primary cohort or pooled analysis.

findings.claim: Across all 374 recorded seizures, clinical signs began after SEEG ictal discharge; electrical onset to completion of clinical semiology was 1-12 s (median 4 s), and electrical-to-clinical onset was 0.5-10 s (median 3 s). Five patients had particularly long delays attributed to subtle or gradual clinical onset or slow discharge buildup. When discharge did not remain local, prefrontal or premotor onset propagated toward more caudal regions (premotor or precentral); caudal-to-rostral propagation was not observed.

findings.claim: The ordered sign-area matrix showed a diagonal posterior-to-anterior correlation pattern. Early clonic signs, contralateral versive signs, contralateral tonic posture, and somesthetic localized aura were associated with caudal regions including primary motor cortex and rolandic operculum, whereas staring, speech arrest, manipulation behavior, and fixed facial expression were associated with rostral or frontopolar regions. The diagonal pattern persisted for significant correlations at p < 0.05; early clonic signs and manipulation behavior were described as more specific to posterior and anterior regions respectively, while hyperkinetic movements and impaired consciousness were weaker, more distributed indicators.

findings.claim: Hierarchical clustering identified Group 1 (16 patients) with elementary motor signs including early clonic, contralateral tonic or versive, somesthetic localized aura, asymmetric tonic, and asymmetric facial signs, with gestural motor behavior and emotional features absent; rolandic BA4, low-BA4 rolandic operculum, parietal cortex, and other caudal or premotor regions were involved. Group 2 (23 patients) combined symmetric proximal or axial tonic posture or chapeau de gendarme with nonintegrated gestural motor behavior, often nonlocalized aura or vocalization, while integrated behavior, distal stereotypies, early clonic signs, and fixed facial expression were absent; premotor and lateral prefrontal regions were frequently co-involved, commonly with lateral-to-medial propagation. Group 3 (10 patients) showed integrated gestural behavior with distal stereotypies, fixed facial or positive emotional expression, proximal stereotypies, and speech production, with elementary motor signs absent; the early spread network involved rostral ventrolateral prefrontal BA47/12, BA10, BA11, BA46 and rostral cingulate BA32 or rostral BA24. Group 4 (5 patients) showed integrated fearful behavior, sometimes hyperkinetic, with fight or escape attempts, frightened expression, occasional screaming or swearing, and autonomic signs, with elementary motor signs absent; orbital or medial prefrontal BA14, BA32/24r, BA10 propagated to amygdala and anterior temporal regions but not lateral frontal cortex.
findings.evidence_text: The abstract names four semiologic-anatomic groups; Table 1 and the Results provide their group sizes, positive and negative semiologic features, and early spread networks.
findings.laterality_localization: Group 1 includes contralateral tonic and versive signs; Group 3 lists ipsilateral versive and contralateral tonic signs among negative v-test features; anatomic directions and regions are as stated in the claim, with no left/right hemisphere result
findings.limitations: Group-specific semiologic numerators, denominators, and exact region counts are not provided; the v-tests are standardized group-comparison measures rather than occurrence proportions.

findings.claim: The authors interpret the four clusters as bands within a continuum rather than rigid categories along a rostrocaudal axis: the most anterior prefrontal seizures showed the most integrated behavior, posterior prefrontal seizures progressively less integrated behavior, and still more posterior motor regions exclusively elementary motor signs. Hyperkinetic and normokinetic gestural behavior could occur within the same group and even in the same patient across seizures, so hyperkinetic character alone was not considered a useful localization indicator.
findings.evidence_text: The source states that the groups form “bands within a spectrum” and that integrated behavior increases with anterior seizure organization.
findings.laterality_localization: Rostral prefrontal or frontal-pole organization toward posterior prefrontal, premotor, and precentral regions; no left/right hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: This is the authors’ synthesis of the observed clusters and does not establish a rigid diagnostic rule or causal hierarchy.
findings.locators: PDF p.1, Summary; PDF p.10, Discussion; PDF p.11, Electroclinical spectrum following a rostrocaudal gradient
findings.population: Four clustered groups; 54 frontal lobe epilepsy patients
findings.source_term: Electroclinical spectrum; integrated behavior; rostrocaudal axis

findings.claim: In contrast to the anteroposterior organization, a similar mesiolateral organization was not observed during the early-spread interval. The paper reports lateral prefrontal discharge propagating to medial structures, notably anterior cingulate and pre-SMA, and SMA or pre-SMA discharge propagating to lateral areas 6 and 8; it therefore states that semiology cannot be attributed only to medial or lateral seizure origin and describes medial premotor and cingulate regions as a possible final common pathway for anterior frontal seizure organization.
findings.evidence_text: “A similar organization was not observed for the mesiolateral axis”; the source then gives lateral-to-medial and medial-to-lateral propagation examples.
findings.laterality_localization: Lateral prefrontal to medial anterior cingulate/pre-SMA and medial SMA/pre-SMA to lateral areas 6/8; no left/right hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: The source does not quantify the frequency of either propagation direction and does not report hemisphere-side laterality.
findings.locators: PDF p.12, Is medial versus lateral distinction a reliable indicator for localization?
findings.phase: Ictal early spread from electrical onset through completion of clinical semiology
findings.population: Frontal lobe epilepsy patients in the early-spread analysis
findings.source_term: Mesiolateral propagation and medial premotor/cingulate pathway

findings.claim: The source reports stereotypy subtype as an important semiologic distinction: distal stereotypies involving hands or feet were associated with the most anterior prefrontal localizations, whereas proximal stereotypies involving trunk or limbs occurred in more posterior prefrontal regions. Stereotypies were predominantly associated with seizures in which lateral prefrontal cortex was involved at onset and projected to anterior cingulate cortex or pre-SMA.
findings.evidence_text: The Summary contrasts distal stereotypies at the most anterior localizations with proximal stereotypies in more posterior prefrontal regions; the Discussion adds the lateral-onset projection pattern.
findings.laterality_localization: Most anterior versus more posterior prefrontal localization; lateral prefrontal onset with projection to anterior cingulate or pre-SMA; no left/right hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: “Associated” and “predominantly” are not accompanied by subtype-specific numerators, denominators, or effect estimates.

findings.population: Frontal lobe epilepsy cohort; group comparison across 54 patients

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a selected presurgical SEEG cohort with hypothesis-driven electrode placement and frontal-lobe EZ, so the findings do not directly generalize to unselected epilepsy or unsampled networks. The early spread network includes propagation during emergence of signs and is not identical to the EZ; the study is observational and correlational. The source describes 20 sampled cortical regions in one methods passage but 24 brain-area variables in the analysis matrices, without reconciliation. PCA variance is reported as 42.36% in the Results and 44.36% in the Supporting Information notice; the online supporting material is not included in the locked PDF. Whole-group percentage denominators and several group-specific feature denominators are not stated, and no left/right hemisphere lateralization accuracy is reported. Cited-study restatements in F009-F013 were not verified against their cited sources.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Consecutive presurgical SEEG series from Timone Hospital, Marseille, February 2000-November 2010: 54 patients in whom SEEG-defined EZ was within the frontal lobe, selected from 180 SEEG explorations; patients with inconclusive intracranial recording (n=1) or a nonpredominantly frontal EZ were excluded. All patients had noninvasive presurgical assessment and video-SEEG after complete or partial antiepileptic-drug withdrawal; 374 seizures were recorded and analyzed. The cohort included 22 male and 32 female patients, mean age 24.9 +/- 9.5 years, mean epilepsy duration 16.9 +/- 8 years, and 27/54 with normal MRI. Three epileptologists independently reviewed VEEG and electrical data; 31 ictal signs and 24 brain-area variables were scored 0-1-2 per patient, with rank-based PCA, hierarchical clustering, correlation matrices, and Kendall tests at p < 0.05. The source describes sampling 20 cortical regions in one methods passage and distinguishes the SEEG-defined EZ from the source-defined early spread network.
sources.source_report_summary: Bonini et al., “Frontal lobe seizures: From clinical semiology to localization” (Epilepsia 2014;55:264-277; DOI 10.1111/epi.12490), an original empirical SEEG study relating ictal semiology to anatomic early-spread networks in a selected frontal lobe epilepsy cohort.

findings.claim: In this 54-patient frontal-lobe epilepsy series, hierarchical analysis identified four semiologic groups associated with different early spread/anatomic patterns: Group 1 had elementary motor signs with precentral/premotor involvement; Group 2 had elementary motor plus nonintegrated gestural behavior with premotor/prefrontal involvement; Group 3 had integrated gestural behavior with distal stereotypies and anterior lateral/medial prefrontal involvement; and Group 4 had fearful behavior with ventromedial prefrontal/anterior temporal paralimbic involvement.
findings.evidence_text: “Four main groups of patients were identified” and correlated with specific anatomic seizure-localization patterns.
findings.laterality_localization: Rostrocaudal anatomical organization from precentral/premotor through premotor/prefrontal and anterior lateral/medial prefrontal to ventromedial prefrontal/anterior temporal regions; no left/right hemisphere direction reported
findings.limitations: The anatomical measure is the early spread network, which includes activity during clinical-sign production and is distinct from the EZ.

findings.claim: In all recorded seizures, clinical signs began after SEEG ictal discharge. Electrical onset to completion of clinical semiology ranged from 1 to 12 s (median 4 s), and the electrical-to-clinical-onset interval ranged from 0.5 to 10 s (median 3 s); shorter values usually occurred with motor/premotor onset, longer values with prefrontal onset, and five patients had particularly long delays. When discharge originating in prefrontal or premotor regions propagated, it tended toward caudal premotor/precentral regions; caudal-to-rostral propagation was not observed.

findings.limitations: Timing and propagation are observed within the early spread window and do not by themselves identify the EZ.

findings.claim: The sign-area correlation matrix showed a diagonal posterior-to-anterior pattern. Early clonic signs, contralateral versive signs, contralateral tonic posture, and somesthetic localized aura correlated with more caudal areas such as primary motor cortex and rolandic operculum, whereas staring, speech arrest, manipulation behavior, and fixed facial expression correlated with more rostral/frontopolar areas. Early clonic signs and manipulation behavior were relatively region-specific, while hyperkinetic movements and impairment of consciousness were weaker, more distributed associations involving caudal and rostral prefrontal regions; the diagonal pattern remained for significant correlations.

findings.laterality_localization: Posterior/caudal-to-anterior/rostral anatomical gradient; contralateral sign labels appear in the source examples, but no left/right hemisphere result is reported
findings.limitations: The reported associations concern areas involved during clinical-sign production; they do not establish that a sign uniquely identifies seizure onset.

findings.claim: Group 1 comprised 16 patients and was characterized by one or more elementary motor signs, including clonic signs, contralateral tonic posture, contralateral versive signs, asymmetric tonic posture, secondary generalization, or asymmetric facial contraction; somesthetic localized aura and tonic vocalization could also occur. Gestural motor behavior and emotional features were absent. Its early spread network showed significant involvement of rolandic cortex (BA 4), rolandic operculum (low BA 4), and parietal cortex, with other caudal and premotor regions also possible; discharge could begin in medial or lateral premotor regions or propagate lateromedially.
findings.evidence_text: “Group 1, composed of 16 patients,” was characterized by elementary motor signs.
findings.laterality_localization: Contralateral tonic and versive signs and asymmetric facial contraction are source-native labels; the reference side and left/right hemisphere pairing are not further specified. Early spread involved rolandic/caudal and premotor regions.
findings.limitations: The reported anatomic profile is an early spread-network association and includes possible propagation patterns, not a direct proof of EZ location.

findings.claim: Group 2 comprised 23 patients and was characterized by co-occurring elementary motor signs, typically symmetric axial tonic posture and facial contraction such as “chapeau de gendarme,” with nonintegrated gestural motor behavior. Nonlocalized aura and complex nonverbal vocalization were also frequent; integrated gestural behavior, distal stereotypies, early clonic signs, and fixed facial expression never occurred. Both premotor and lateral prefrontal regions were frequently co-involved; lateral-to-medial propagation was more frequent, although medial premotor onset could propagate laterally.
findings.evidence_text: “Group 2 (23 patients) was characterized by the co-occurrence of elementary motor signs ... and nonintegrated gestural motor behavior.”
findings.laterality_localization: Symmetric proximal/axial tonic posture and bilateral facial contraction are source-native descriptions; both medial and lateral premotor/prefrontal regions were involved, with lateral-to-medial propagation more frequent; no left/right hemisphere direction reported
findings.limitations: The group is described as heterogeneous, and its anatomic relation includes both onset and propagation patterns.

findings.limitations: Group features are associations with the early spread network and do not separate seizure-onset tissue from early propagation.

findings.claim: Figure 3 illustrates one Group 2 patient with nonintegrated gestural behavior and proximal stereotypies of the pelvis, trunk, and left upper limb, asymmetric bilateral facial contraction, tonic/dystonic posture of the right upper limb, and vocalization. SEEG showed low-voltage rapid discharge at electrical onset in ventrolateral prefrontal BA 45, BA 9/46V, and BA 44, followed at clinical onset by fast activity in BA 8V, BA 9, SMA, and lateral BA 6 and slower activity in the temporopolar region.
findings.evidence_text: Figure 3 labels “electrical onset” and “clinical onset” and shows the Group 2 semiologic and SEEG sequence.
findings.laterality_localization: Left upper-limb stereotypy and right upper-limb tonic/dystonic posture are source-native body-side observations; hemisphere correspondence is not stated. Electrical onset was ventrolateral prefrontal, followed by premotor/posterior lateral prefrontal and temporopolar involvement.
findings.limitations: This is one illustrative patient; the source does not state the hemisphere corresponding to the left/right limb observations.
findings.phase: Ictal; electrical onset and clinical-onset/early spread sequence
findings.population: One illustrative patient from Group 2

findings.claim: The authors interpret the four clusters as a continuum rather than rigid compartments: the most anterior prefrontal seizures showed the most integrated behavior, posterior prefrontal seizures progressively less integrated behavior, and still more posterior motor seizures exclusively elementary motor signs without a gestural component. Group 2 was described as a transition zone in which more anterior organization could show coordinated rocking and more posterior organization prominent tonic posturing that hindered gestural behavior.
findings.evidence_text: The groups were described as “forming a continuum along a rostrocaudal axis.”
findings.laterality_localization: Rostral prefrontal-to-posterior motor gradient; no left/right hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: This is an interpretive synthesis of clustered observations; the authors do not establish rigid anatomic boundaries.

findings.citation: Barbas & Pandya (1989); Bates & Goldman-Rakic (1993); Devinsky et al. (1995); Morecraft & Tanji (2009)
findings.claim: The authors conclude that a semiologic trait during the early-spread interval could not be attributed only to a lateral or medial discharge origin because propagation also mattered. They observed lateral prefrontal discharge tending to propagate to anterior cingulate and pre-SMA, and SMA/pre-SMA discharge tending to propagate to lateral areas 6 and 8; medial premotor and cingulate regions were proposed as a possible “final common pathway” for anterior frontal seizure organization.
findings.evidence_text: “A similar organization was not observed for the mesiolateral axis.”
findings.laterality_localization: Medial-versus-lateral anatomical axis and propagation; no left/right hemisphere lateralization
findings.limitations: The source explicitly cautions that propagation can produce the semiologic trait, limiting origin-only medial/lateral interpretation.

findings.claim: The authors interpret distal and proximal stereotypies within gestural behavior as an important distinction between anterior and posterior prefrontal involvement. In their series, stereotypies were predominantly associated with seizures involving lateral prefrontal cortex at onset and projecting to anterior cingulate cortex and/or pre-SMA.
findings.evidence_text: Stereotypy “allowed distinction between anterior and posterior prefrontal involvement.”
findings.laterality_localization: Distal/proximal stereotypy relation to anterior/posterior prefrontal involvement; lateral prefrontal onset with projection to anterior cingulate/pre-SMA; no left/right hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: The discussion links the observed pattern to proposed cortico-subcortical mechanisms; the current study establishes an association, not a mechanism.
findings.locators: PDF p.12, Stereotypies in frontal seizures; PDF p.1, Summary
findings.population: Frontal-lobe seizure series; patients with gestural motor behavior

findings.claim: Hyperkinetic and normokinetic gestural motor behavior could both occur within the same patient group and in the same patient from one seizure to another; the authors therefore judged hyperkinetic character per se not to be a useful indicator of seizure localization.
findings.evidence_text: Hyperkinetic character was described as “not a useful indicator of seizure localization.”
findings.laterality_localization: No reliable anatomical direction assigned to hyperkinetic character; no left/right hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: This conclusion is limited to the studied frontal-lobe SEEG population and the source's definitions of gestural behavior.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Electroclinical subgroups; PDF p.11, Electroclinical spectrum following a rostrocaudal gradient
findings.population: Groups 2–4 and individual patients in the frontal-lobe SEEG series

sources.source_report_limitations: The cohort is a single-center, presurgical SEEG-selected population: 54 frontal-lobe cases from 180 explorations, with electrode sampling and clinical ascertainment determined by presurgical hypotheses. The early spread network is not the EZ, and many reported associations include propagation during clinical-sign production. Group membership resulted from a chosen hierarchical-clustering cut, and the authors themselves characterize the groups as a continuum. Several percentage results lack numerators and use “patients” versus “cases” inconsistently. The main text reports three PCA components explaining 42.36% of variance, whereas the Supporting Information notice reports 44.36%; the same notice lists online Table S1 and Figures S1–S2, which are not included in this 14-page PDF. Methods text also describes 20 sampled cortical regions and later reports 24 brain-area variables. Contralateral/ipsilateral sign terminology appears in the source, but no dedicated left/right hemisphere lateralization analysis or side-specific diagnostic accuracy is reported.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This single-center presurgical series included 54 patients whose SEEG-defined epileptogenic zone (EZ) predominantly involved the frontal lobe, selected from 180 SEEG explorations performed from February 2000 through November 2010; one inconclusive exploration and nonpredominantly frontal cases were excluded. The cohort included 22 male and 32 female patients, mean age 24.9 ± 9.5 years, mean epilepsy duration 16.9 ± 8 years, and 27/54 with normal MRI. Three epileptologists independently reviewed all seizures and scored presence/absence of 31 ictal signs; each patient's sign was assigned 0, 1, or 2 according to reproducibility. The “early spread network” was the cortical tissue involved from electrical onset through completion of clinical semiology and was explicitly distinguished from the EZ. SEEG sampling is described as 20 frontal cortical regions, while the later matrices are described as containing 24 brain-area variables. Analyses used correlation matrices, Kendall tests with p < 0.05, PCA on rank-transformed sign scores, hierarchical clustering, and value-test ≥ 2 to identify characteristic variables.
sources.source_report_summary: Bonini et al., “Frontal lobe seizures: From clinical semiology to localization” (Epilepsia 55(2):264–277, 2014; doi: 10.1111/epi.12490), is a full-length original research report. It examines whether semiologic subgroups in frontal lobe seizures correlate with anatomic organization using SEEG-recorded ictal clinical and electrical data.

findings.claim: The source locates the supplementary motor area on the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus and subdivides it into rostral pre-SMA and caudal SMA-proper.
findings.evidence_text: The SMA is “located on the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus” and is subdivided into “the rostral pre-SMA and the caudal SMA-proper.”
findings.laterality_localization: SMA/pre-SMA localization is source-explicit; no hemisphere or Brodmann area is inferred.
findings.limitations: This is source anatomy and does not assert that a semiology uniquely identifies either subregion.
findings.population: SMA and pre-SMA anatomical/semiological literature
findings.source_term: supplementary motor area; pre-supplementary motor area

findings.claim: The source distinguishes “SMA seizures,” which may originate within the SMA or rapidly propagate to it from adjacent regions, from “SMA epilepsy,” in which the epileptogenic zone is confined to the SMA.
findings.evidence_text: “SMA seizures” may “either originate within the SMA or rapidly propagate to it from adjacent regions,” whereas “SMA epilepsy” refers to an epileptogenic zone “confined to the SMA.”
findings.laterality_localization: SMA/pre-SMA localization is source-explicit; no hemisphere or Brodmann area is inferred.
findings.limitations: The distinction is source-defined; it does not make propagation equivalent to onset.

sources.source_report_limitations: The narrowed report retains source-native SMA/pre-SMA terminology and only directly linked semiology, localization, seizure-phase, and atomic meta-analytic statistics. Search-flow, eligibility, reviewer-process, generic risk-of-bias, standalone imaging/surgery/outcome, and unlinked population rows are not treated as findings. Table 3 patient counts and pooled prevalences are separate records; heterogeneity I2 statistics and their p values are also separate records. The source does not provide a complete hemisphere-level lateralization result.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The review searched PubMed and Embase through December 2023, used adapted QUADAS-2 and GRADE assessments, and included primary adult/pediatric presurgical or surgical studies with explicit anatomo-electroclinical correlations. Fresh text from all 10 pages was read, and the abstract, PRISMA flow, individual-study table, aggregate table, symptom meta-analysis table, and discussion layouts were visually inspected. Table 1 cells are retained as cited-study restatements; Table 2 and Table 3 aggregate cells are retained as primary review results. Each count, percentage, subgroup component, confidence category, heterogeneity statistic, and p value is represented independently.
sources.source_report_summary: Buonocore et al., “Ictal semiology in supplementary motor area and pre-supplementary motor area epilepsy: A systematic review and meta-analysis,” Epileptic Disorders 2026;28:33–42, is a PRISMA-reported systematic review/meta-analysis of SMA and pre-SMA ictal semiology. It includes 20 articles with extractable data from 37 target patients, classifies 12 ictal symptoms, and reports pooled prevalence, heterogeneity, patient characteristics, surgical outcomes, and study-level confidence in epileptogenic-zone localization. The source repeatedly distinguishes SMA seizures from SMA epilepsy and cautions that rapid propagation can make semiology non-specific.

sources.source_report_limitations: All 18 pages had present fresh text and represented PNG renderings. Figure 2, Table 2, Figures 3–6, and Table 3 were visually inspected; Figure 6 pairwise OR cells are retained individually, while its printed bold significance indicator is recorded as a limitation because cell-level p values are not printed. Table 3 frequency estimates and displayed min–max ranges are separate records. The review includes heterogeneous terminology, incomplete chronology/awareness reporting, and mixed ACC/aMCC definitions. Interictal personality findings, search-flow counts, demographics, imaging, surgery, pathology, and generic methodological/risk-of-bias cells are kept out of findings unless directly linked to a seizure sign, phase, or localization result.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The review includes 23 studies and 93 patients, with ACC involvement defined through anatomical, invasive-electrophysiological, imaging, and clinical correlations. Study selection, demographic, imaging, surgery, pathology, confidence, and risk-of-bias details are retained as compact population/context here; they are not individual findings unless directly tied to an ictal sign, phase, or localization association. The review extracted aura type, vocalization/verbalization, laughter, autonomic and facial signs, automatisms, hypermotor behavior, dystonic/tonic-clonic signs, deviations, loss of consciousness, postictal confusion, timing, duration, sleep, and interictal behavior, then performed one-sided typicality tests and pairwise odds-ratio comparisons.
sources.source_report_summary: Chassoux et al., “Ictal semiology in anterior cingulate epilepsy: A systematic review,” Epileptic Disorders 2025;27:883–900, synthesizes ictal semiology and anatomo-clinical correlations for ACC seizures. The source preserves affective, autonomic, vocal, facial, motor, awareness, postictal, duration, and sleep-associated signs; it distinguishes onset from propagation timing and discusses ACC/aMCC and broader cingulate subdivisions. Localization and lateralization are independent: ACC, aMCC, mesial frontal, limbic, insular, and other network terms are retained as source-native anatomical references, with no hemisphere inferred.

findings.citation: Bancaud and Talairach 1965; McGonigal et al. 2007; Wendling et al. 2003
findings.claim: The review presents semiology as an evolving consequence of ictal electrical activity spreading through neural pathways in time and space: clinical signs appear after a variable lag and install more slowly in temporal than frontal seizures, and SEEG relates discharge timing and spread to clinical expression.
findings.evidence_text: Clinical signs evolve as discharge spreads in time and space; the review states that temporal seizures generally propagate more slowly than frontal seizures and that the onset lag may range from milliseconds to seconds.
findings.laterality_localization: Seizure-onset and propagation network; no fixed single-site assignment
findings.limitations: No unified cohort or pooled timing estimate
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract; PDF p.2, section 3
findings.phase: Electrical seizure onset through first clinical sign and full clinical expression
findings.population: Heterogeneous SEEG, stimulation, and clinical literature synthesized by the review; no single cohort
findings.source_term: seizure spread in time and space

findings.citation: Talairach and Bancaud 1966; Bonini et al. 2013; Penfield 1958
findings.claim: The structures involved in producing semiology form an early spread network tightly linked to the epileptogenic zone; its anatomical extent and the frequencies developed immediately after onset can produce different clinical features even when seizures arise from the same region, and fast immediate invasion of sensory or cognitive areas can abolish conscious perception.
findings.evidence_text: The review calls the early spread zone the organic link between the epileptogenic zone and emergence of semiology and states that immediate fast invasion may produce no conscious perception.
findings.laterality_localization: Epileptogenic zone versus the anatomically distributed early spread network; no fixed body-side direction
findings.limitations: Mechanistic attribution between frequency and spread rate remains unresolved in the source
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract; PDF p.4, section 5
findings.phase: Immediately after seizure onset and during early ictal spread
findings.population: Heterogeneous motor, sensory, and cognitive seizure observations synthesized by the review; no single cohort
findings.source_term: early spread network / early spread zone

findings.claim: Semiology is described as more elementary and directly sensory or motor when primary cortex is involved, whereas associative-cortex seizures produce more complex cognitive or behavioral signs through distributed cortical networks.
findings.evidence_text: The abstract contrasts direct primary-cortex relations producing visual or auditory hallucinations and elementary sensorimotor signs with associative-cortex involvement producing altered cognitive or behavioral signs.
findings.laterality_localization: Primary sensory or motor cortex versus distributed associative networks; no fixed side stated
findings.limitations: No quantitative boundary between primary and associative manifestations is reported
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract; PDF p.2, section 3
findings.population: Heterogeneous sensory, motor, cognitive, and behavioral seizure literature; no single cohort

findings.citation: Ikeda et al. 2000; Tassinari et al. 1998; Shibasaki et al. 1994
findings.claim: The review states that discharge frequency changes the peripheral expression of a seizure: fast gamma activity tends to deactivate normal function, whereas slower theta activity can mimic physiological function; in the same motor region, lower-frequency or phasic activity can produce a jerk while higher-frequency oscillation can produce arrest of posture or voluntary movement.
findings.evidence_text: The review links fast gamma activity with functional deactivation and slower theta activity with physiological mimicry, and contrasts a phasic discharge producing a myoclonic jerk with higher-frequency oscillation producing motor arrest.
findings.laterality_localization: Primary motor and other cortical regions; no fixed body-side direction
findings.limitations: No numeric frequency thresholds are reported
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract; PDF p.4, sections 4-5

findings.claim: The review concludes that clinical semiology can localize the epileptogenic phenomenon as a focal network rather than a single fixed-function area: frontopolar onset may recruit cingulate, amygdalar, temporopolar, and superior temporal regions to produce complex behavior, overlap with area 9 may add postural or tonic components, overlap with area 14 may add emotional or autonomic components, and full ictal-network mapping can support inference of the original determinant.
findings.evidence_text: The review states that a given network configuration may only be generated by a given area or group of areas and uses frontopolar area 10 and overlapping areas 9 or 14 as examples of different seizure compositions.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontopolar/area 10 with cingulate, amygdalar, temporopolar, superior temporal, area 9, and area 14 network relations; no fixed side
findings.limitations: Review-level inference; no independent validation statistic or pooled estimate is reported

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review rather than a single primary cohort or quantitative meta-analysis. Its scientific content mixes review-authored synthesis, cited-study restatements, and illustrative case or figure observations; cited sources remain unverified cited restatements under this review boundary. The review reports percentages of 80% and 41–55% for the auditory-stimulation comparison without numerator or denominator, and reports statistically significant synchronization differences without p values, intervals, or sample sizes. It provides no unified denominator, no pooled estimate, and no universal sign-to-lobe rule. Pages 9–10 are reference pages and were inspected but do not add source-reported scientific findings beyond the cited-source identities used for attribution.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a narrative review with no single study cohort, unified eligibility population, or common comparator. The evidence discussed spans heterogeneous SEEG recordings, cortical stimulation observations, clinical/video studies, ictal SPECT, and cited cases or series. Finding-specific populations and analysis units are retained below; where the review does not report a denominator, it is marked NOT_REPORTED rather than inferred.
sources.source_report_summary: Chauvel and McGonigal, “Emergence of semiology in epileptic seizures” (Epilepsy & Behavior 38, 2014), is a narrative review of seizure semiology using anatomo-electro-clinical correlations, SEEG, electrical stimulation, video/clinical observations, cited case and series reports, and network physiology. It is relevant to the atlas because it describes sensory, motor, cognitive, emotional, language, consciousness, localization, and laterality relationships as dynamic network phenomena. It does not present one new cohort or one unified quantitative dataset.

findings.claim: The review states that clinical signs evolve as seizures propagate and may be generated by slow activation of brain areas or faster disruption of connected networks; it contrasts an ictal wavefront of about 1 mm/s with a faster ictal discharge of about 300 mm/s detected by EEG, which does not necessarily mean the recruited cortex is firing.

findings.evidence_text: Table 2 lists abrupt, brief, rapidly evolving frontal seizures versus gradual, longer temporal seizures, with the stated differences in automatisms, complex motor features, vocalization, generalization, and postictal confusion.

findings.citation: Bonini F, McGonigal A, Trébuchon A, et al. Frontal lobe seizures: from clinical semiology to localization. Epilepsia 2014;55:264–77.; McGonigal A, Chauvel P. Prefrontal seizures manifesting as motor stereotypies. Mov Disord 2014;29:1181–5.
findings.claim: The review reports that intracranial stereo-EEG studies associate elementary clonic, tonic, and versive signs with precentral and premotor regions; more complex motor signs with more rostral frontal regions; non-integrated proximal stereotypies such as rocking and turning with premotor and posterior prefrontal regions; and integrated distal stereotypies such as manual automatisms with anterior prefrontal regions including orbitofrontal cortex, frontal pole, and anterior cingulate.
findings.evidence_text: Intracranial studies are summarized as linking elementary motor signs to precentral/premotor regions and complex or stereotyped behaviors to progressively more rostral frontal regions.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontal regional localization; no body-side direction
findings.limitations: The review states that rapid propagation can confound these distinctions in clinical practice.
findings.population: Patients in intracranial stereo-EEG studies; exact cohorts NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: elementary motor signs; complex motor signs; gestural behaviour

findings.citation: McGonigal A, Chauvel P. Frontal lobe epilepsy: seizure semiology and presurgical evaluation. Pract Neurol 2004;4:260–73.
findings.claim: Seizures from primary motor cortex comprise contralateral unilateral clonic, and sometimes tonic or myoclonic, activity that can spread to adjacent body parts in a Jacksonian march along the motor homunculus; the starting face, upper limb, or lower limb can distinguish lateral from medial precentral onset.
findings.evidence_text: Contralateral clonic activity may spread through the motor homunculus as a Jacksonian march.
findings.laterality_localization: Motor activity is contralateral to primary motor cortex onset; face, upper-limb, or lower-limb onset localizes along the precentral homunculus
findings.limitations: The source attributes the march to propagation through motor cortex, so the first observed sign and later spread are not interchangeable.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Primary motor cortex; PDF p.3, Figure 1
findings.population: NOT_REPORTED

findings.claim: In the review’s video case 1, a 50-year-old man with a cystic lesion in the right middle frontal gyrus had an aura followed by behavioural arrest, left-face clonic movements spreading over the left arm, then left-arm extension in a fencing posture before secondary generalisation; the semiology and ictal EEG pointed to right frontocentral/right hemispheric onset.
findings.evidence_text: The case had left-face clonus spreading to the left arm, followed by left-arm extension, with right frontocentral ictal EEG onset.
findings.laterality_localization: Left face/arm signs contralateral to right frontocentral onset; left-arm fencing posture indicating supplementary motor area involvement
findings.limitations: Single illustrative case; the reported lesion, EEG, and clinical semiology are concordant but do not establish general diagnostic accuracy.

findings.population: Single case: 50-year-old man with focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures and a right middle frontal gyrus lesion

findings.claim: The review associates orbitofrontal seizures with impaired awareness, automatisms, occasional olfactory aura, ictal tachycardia, and complex motor evolution; frontopolar seizures with impaired awareness followed by motor features; ventromedial prefrontal/anterior cingulate seizures with forced thinking, fear, and hypermotor features; contralateral dorsolateral frontal seizures involving frontal eye fields with early head and eye version; dominant frontal or Broca-region seizures with dysphasia; and frontal operculum seizures with unilateral face clonus, laryngeal symptoms, hypersalivation, and articulation difficulty.

findings.claim: Auras are less common in lateral temporal seizures and may be auditory or vertiginous; elementary sounds suggest primary auditory cortex, complex sounds or distortions auditory association areas, unilateral elementary auditory aura contralateral onset, and early ictal dysphasia dominant-hemisphere involvement. findings.laterality_localization: Anterior versus posterior cingulate localization; no hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: Most data are from case series of lesional cases, and posterior-cingulate signs depend on spread.

findings.evidence_text: The cited series is summarized as having two anterior-cingulate groups and temporal-like auras in all posterior-cingulate cases.
findings.laterality_localization: Anterior versus posterior cingulate; no hemisphere direction

findings.claim: Insular seizures are rare and heterogeneous, with viscerosensory, somatosensory, autonomic, language, complex auditory, automotor, hypermotor, tonic, or clonic manifestations; deep location and often non-localising scalp EEG can make them resemble temporal or frontal seizures and go unrecognized.

findings.citation: Jobst BC, Gonzalez-Martinez J, Isnard J, et al. The insula and its epilepsies. Epilepsy Curr 2019;19:11–21.
findings.claim: Viscerosensory symptoms such as abdominal aura and laryngeal constriction and autonomic signs such as nausea, hypersalivation, and sweating are suggested to arise from anterior insula, whereas painful burning, electric-shock, or tingling sensations are more likely posterior insular; insular sensory responses may involve a larger skin territory including perioral regions, be bilateral or ipsilateral, and more often evolve to complex motor phenomena than primary or secondary somatosensory responses.
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts anterior-insular visceral/autonomic symptoms with posterior-insular painful sensations and describes larger, sometimes bilateral or ipsilateral insular sensory territories.
findings.laterality_localization: Anterior versus posterior insula; responses can be bilateral or ipsilateral rather than strictly contralateral
findings.limitations: The review presents probabilistic associations and emphasizes heterogeneity rather than a definitive sign-to-region rule.
findings.population: Stimulation-study and review literature; exact cohorts NOT_REPORTED

findings.citation: Jobst BC, Gonzalez-Martinez J, Isnard J, et al. The insula and its epilepsies. Epilepsy Curr 2019;19:11–21.
findings.claim: The review states that seizures arising from hippocampus almost always propagate to the insula, so abdominal aura is also common in mesiotemporal seizures; nevertheless, the combination of complex visceral and somatosensory auras points toward insular onset.

findings.laterality_localization: Hippocampal-to-insular propagation; combined complex visceral and somatosensory aura points toward insular onset without a hemisphere direction
findings.limitations: Shared abdominal aura and rapid propagation make hippocampal, insular, temporal, and frontal localization difficult from aura alone.

findings.population: NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: hippocampal propagation to insula; complex visceral and somatosensory aura

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review rather than a single primary cohort or systematic quantitative synthesis. Cited studies, case series, and the seven illustrative cases have different populations, ascertainment methods, reference standards, phases, and analysis units; many percentages and probabilities have no endpoint denominator in the review. The source repeatedly cautions that symptomatogenic cortex may differ from seizure-onset or epileptogenic cortex, that propagation and network disruption can produce later signs, and that deep sources may have non-localising scalp EEG. Lesions may be incidental, and the review does not establish universal one-to-one sign-to-onset rules or a pooled effect estimate. All native pages 1-12 and their text/rendering representations were readable; no page was blocked.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Narrative review; the authors summarize literature on focal seizures and present illustrative cases from their centre using clinical history, videotelemetry, scalp or intracranial stereo-EEG, MRI/PET, and surgical outcome where stated. No single review cohort, systematic eligibility set, pooled analysis, or uniform endpoint denominator is reported. Populations, analysis units, and reference standards are therefore retained at finding level; source-reported reference standards include ictal EEG, imaging, lesion location, clinical semiology, and seizure freedom after resection.
sources.source_report_summary: Chowdhury FA, Silva R, Whatley B, and Walker MC, “Localisation in focal epilepsy: a practical guide,” Pract Neurol 2021;21:481-491, doi:10.1136/practneurol-2019-002341. This is a narrative review of focal-seizure semiology for localization and lateralization in presurgical evaluation, combining literature synthesis, two summary tables, a regional figure, and seven illustrative video cases. Cited-study restatements below are not independent primary observations.

findings.claim: The source states that seizure semiology reflects activation or dysfunction of brain areas in the symptomatogenic zone and can provide insight into the seizure-onset zone, while the symptomatogenic zone is usually but not always close to the epileptogenic zone that must be removed or disconnected for seizure freedom.
findings.evidence_text: The symptomatogenic zone is “where symptoms and clinical signs originate” and is “usually, but not always, close to the epileptogenic zone.”
findings.laterality_localization: Source distinguishes symptomatogenic, seizure-onset, and epileptogenic zones; no mandatory hemisphere or Brodmann level is asserted.
findings.limitations: This is a review-level conceptual distinction; no source cohort quantifies proximity or predictive accuracy.
findings.locators: PDF p.1, Abstract and Introduction; PDF p.2, Cortical zones table
findings.population: presurgical focal epilepsy assessment
findings.source_term: symptomatogenic zone; seizure onset zone; epileptogenic zone

findings.claim: Electrical stimulation studies and seizure observations are summarized as showing that most cortex is clinically silent and that clinical signs and symptoms appear when seizures spread enough to activate or disrupt cortical networks.
findings.evidence_text: “Most of cortex is clinically silent,” and signs occur only when seizure activity “spreads to activate or disrupt cortical networks.”
findings.laterality_localization: Source attributes semiology to activated or disrupted networks and does not equate every recruited cortical area with the symptomatogenic or onset zone.
findings.limitations: This is a narrative synthesis and does not quantify the proportion of clinically silent cortex.
findings.population: focal epilepsies; electrical-stimulation and seizure-observation literature

findings.citation: Liou J-Y, Smith EH, Bateman LM, et al. 2020 (ref. 4)
findings.claim: The review describes an ictal wavefront recruiting neurons into firing at approximately 1 mm/s, using the slow tangential recruitment of cortex as an example of the spread underlying a Jacksonian march.
findings.evidence_text: “There is an ictal wavefront moving at about 1 mm/s as neurones are slowly recruited into firing.”
findings.laterality_localization: Source relates the wavefront to tangential spread through cortex; no hemisphere is assigned by this propagation rate alone.
findings.limitations: The review does not report the source measurement method or a distribution around the approximate rate.
findings.population: focal seizure propagation literature

findings.limitations: This is a review restatement; no direct EEG or propagation measurement is presented in this document.

findings.claim: The source contrasts temporal lobe seizures, which depend mainly on activation of brain areas and evolve more slowly, with frontal lobe seizures, which may depend on disinhibition and propagate quickly.
findings.evidence_text: “Temporal lobe seizures ... evolve more slowly, whereas frontal lobe seizures ... propagate quickly.”
findings.laterality_localization: Temporal versus frontal lobe is the source’s localization contrast; no side is asserted.
findings.limitations: The comparison is qualitative and is qualified by multiple mechanisms of propagation.
findings.locators: PDF p.1, Introduction; PDF p.2, Frontal lobe seizures
findings.population: focal epilepsy literature
findings.source_term: temporal lobe seizure; frontal lobe seizure

findings.claim: The review describes focal motor seizures arising from contralateral primary motor cortex as highly specific or pathognomonic for that region, while automotor seizures are less localising because they can arise from different brain regions.
findings.evidence_text: Focal motor seizures from “contralateral primary motor cortex” are described as pathognomonic, whereas automotor seizures “can arise from different brain regions.”
findings.laterality_localization: Focal motor signs are source-described as contralateral to primary motor cortex; automotor seizures have non-unique localization.
findings.limitations: The review supplies no likelihood ratio or quantified specificity for this contrast.
findings.population: focal epilepsy literature

findings.claim: EEG maps ictal onset and spread but does not show the behaviour of the underlying cortex; scalp EEG may be absent or widespread for deep sources such as orbitofrontal cortex, movement artefact can obscure changes, and the epileptogenic zone may be adjacent to a lesion or the manifestations may reflect propagation, so clinical data must be integrated.
findings.evidence_text: Scalp EEG may show “no or widespread EEG changes” for deep orbitofrontal sources; clinicians must integrate “all the available data” to determine the epileptogenic zone.
findings.laterality_localization: Deep-source and propagation limitations can make scalp EEG non-localising; source requires integration of history, examination, imaging, neurophysiology, and neuropsychology.
findings.limitations: This is a practical warning, not a diagnostic-accuracy estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Introduction; PDF p.4, Other frontal regions
findings.population: presurgical focal epilepsy assessment

findings.claim: Frontal lobe seizures are described as typically brief, sometimes clustered, often occurring from sleep, with prominent vocalisation and motor phenomena including clonic movements, tonic posturing, eye deviation, cycling, rocking, and grimacing; bizarre bilateral motor phenomena can occur with retained awareness.
findings.evidence_text: Frontal lobe seizures are “typically brief,” may cluster, commonly occur from sleep, and can have bilateral motor phenomena with retained awareness.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontal lobe source context; bilateral motor manifestations do not by themselves establish bilateral cerebral onset.
findings.limitations: The review uses qualitative frequency terms and does not give a cohort denominator.
findings.population: frontal lobe epilepsy literature

findings.citation: Bonini F, McGonigal A, Trebuchon A, et al. 2014 (ref. 6); McGonigal A, Chauvel P. 2014 (ref. 7)
findings.claim: Intracranial stereo-EEG literature is summarized as placing elementary clonic, tonic, and versive signs in precentral and premotor regions; less-natural proximal stereotypies such as rocking and turning in premotor/posterior prefrontal regions; and more integrated natural gestural behaviour with distal stereotypies such as manual automatisms in more anterior prefrontal regions including orbitofrontal cortex, frontal pole, and anterior cingulate.
findings.evidence_text: Elementary signs arise from “precentral and premotor regions,” while more integrated gestural behaviour arises from “more anterior prefrontal regions.”
findings.laterality_localization: Source provides a regional frontal localization hierarchy without assigning a cerebral side.
findings.limitations: The review warns that rapid propagation can confound these distinctions in clinical practice.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Frontal lobe seizures; PDF p.3, Figure 1
findings.population: focal frontal epilepsy intracranial stereo-EEG literature
findings.source_term: elementary motor sign; complex motor sign; gestural behaviour

findings.claim: Seizures from primary motor cortex comprise contralateral unilateral clonic, and sometimes tonic or myoclonic, activity that can spread along the motor homunculus as a Jacksonian march; lateral versus medial precentral onset can be distinguished by initial face, upper-limb, or lower-limb involvement.
findings.evidence_text: Primary motor seizures comprise “contralateral unilateral clonic” activity and may spread along the homunculus as the “Jacksonian march.”
findings.laterality_localization: Symptoms are contralateral to the primary motor cortex onset; source distinguishes lateral from medial precentral onset by the initial body region.
findings.limitations: No cohort-level accuracy or distribution of body-region starts is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Primary motor cortex; PDF p.3, Figure 1
findings.population: focal motor epilepsy literature

findings.claim: In an illustrative 50-year-old man with a right middle frontal gyrus cystic lesion, a seizure evolved from an aura to behavioural arrest, left-face clonic movements spreading over the left arm, and left-arm extension in a fencing posture before secondary generalisation; the authors state that the semiology and ictal EEG supported right frontocentral onset.
findings.evidence_text: Clonic movements were visible in the “left face spreading ... over the left arm”; the semiology “pointed to right hemispheric onset.”
findings.laterality_localization: Left face/arm manifestations and fencing posture were interpreted as right hemispheric onset; ictal EEG onset was right frontocentral.
findings.limitations: This is a single illustrative case and cannot establish a general rule.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Video case 1 and Figure 1; PDF p.3, Figure 2 caption
findings.population: one illustrative case; seizure onset age 28; right middle frontal gyrus lesion
findings.source_term: aura; behavioural arrest; left-face clonic activity; fencing posture

findings.citation: Ikeda A, Sato T, Ohara S, et al. 2002 (ref. 9); Werhahn KJ, Noachtar S, Arnold S, et al. 2000 (ref. 10); Sitthinamsuwan B, Usui N, Tottori T, et al. 2016 (ref. 11)
findings.claim: Supplementary motor area seizures are characterized by asymmetric bilateral tonic posturing, with or without impaired awareness; the source describes contralateral upper-limb extension, ipsilateral upper-limb flexion as a fencing posture, and contralateral head and eye deviation, while noting that extrafrontal seizures can also produce asymmetric tonic posturing.
findings.evidence_text: SMA seizures show “asymmetric bilateral tonic posturing”; extrafrontal seizures “can have asymmetric tonic posturing.”
findings.laterality_localization: Contralateral limb extension and contralateral head/eye deviation are related to the hemisphere of onset; the source explicitly warns that the semiology is not exclusive to SMA onset.
findings.limitations: Rapid connectivity and propagation reduce the specificity of the observed posture for SMA onset.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Supplementary motor area; PDF p.4, Other frontal regions; PDF p.3, Figure 1
findings.population: supplementary motor area and extrafrontal epilepsy literature
findings.source_term: supplementary motor area seizure; fencing posture

findings.claim: The review relates early forced sustained extreme head and eye version to seizures involving the frontal eye fields in the contralateral dorsolateral frontal cortex; dominant-hemisphere or Broca-region seizures may cause dysphasia, while frontal opercular seizures may cause unilateral face clonic movements, laryngeal symptoms, hypersalivation, and articulation difficulty.
findings.evidence_text: Contralateral dorsolateral frontal seizures may show early head and eye version; dominant-hemisphere seizures near Broca’s area can cause dysphasia.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontal eye-field signs are contralateral to the described dorsolateral frontal cortex; dysphasia is linked to dominant hemisphere/Broca area; frontal operculum is source-localized without a side.
findings.limitations: The source notes overlap after spread to the insula and does not quantify specificity.

findings.claim: In an illustrative 24-year-old man with sleep-related hyperkinetic seizures, PET and stereo-EEG supported a right orbitofrontal source; seizures progressed to bilateral tonic seizures with loss of awareness, and the patient was seizure-free after right orbitofrontal resection.
