findings.claim: The source states that an asymmetric clonic ending of the generalised phase, with the last clonic jerk ipsilateral to seizure onset, and postictal Todd’s paresis contralateral to seizure onset are lateralising signs; these signs do not distinguish frontal from extrafrontal onset.
findings.evidence_text: The last clonic jerk is “ipsilateral to seizure onset,” while Todd’s paresis is “contralateral to seizure onset”; these features do not differentiate frontal from extrafrontal onset.
findings.laterality_localization: Last clonic jerk is ipsilateral and Todd’s paresis contralateral to seizure-onset hemisphere; lobe localization is not distinguished.
findings.limitations: No performance estimate is reported for either sign.
findings.population: focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure literature
findings.source_term: asymmetric clonic ending; postictal Todd’s paresis

findings.claim: Unilateral sensory aura is described as a contralateral sign.
findings.evidence_text: “Unilateral sensory aura is a contralateral sign.”
findings.laterality_localization: Sensory aura is contralateral to the cerebral hemisphere of seizure onset; source does not require a specific lobe.
findings.limitations: No frequency or accuracy is reported.
findings.population: focal seizure literature

findings.claim: Ictal or postictal dysphasia lateralises to the dominant hemisphere but has poor localising value; speech arrest is described as non-lateralising, whereas ictal speech consisting of formed nonsensical phrases is a non-dominant sign.
findings.evidence_text: Dysphasia “lateralises to dominant hemisphere but is of poor localising value”; speech arrest is “non-lateralising”; ictal speech is “a non-dominant sign.”
findings.laterality_localization: Dysphasia is linked to dominant hemisphere; ictal speech to non-dominant hemisphere; speech arrest is explicitly non-lateralising.
findings.limitations: The review supplies no accuracy or denominator and emphasizes the distinction between lateralization and localization.
findings.population: focal seizure literature
findings.source_term: ictal/postictal dysphasia; speech arrest; ictal speech

findings.citation: Blair RDG. 2012 (ref. 15); Lee GR, Arain A, Lim N, et al. 2006 (ref. 41)
findings.claim: Preserved awareness during ictal automatisms points to the non-dominant hemisphere; in temporal lobe epilepsy, rhythmic ictal non-clonic hand motions may be contralateral, while peri-ictal drinking, ictal spitting, ictal vomiting, and urge to urinate point to a non-dominant focus.
findings.evidence_text: “Preserved awareness during ictal automatism points to the non-dominant hemisphere”; peri-ictal drinking, spitting, vomiting, and urge to urinate point to a non-dominant focus.
findings.laterality_localization: Preserved awareness and autonomic/oral/urinary signs are linked to non-dominant hemisphere/focus; rhythmic hand motions are contralateral.
findings.limitations: The review gives qualitative directional associations without frequencies.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Lateralising signs; PDF p.5, Mesial temporal lobe including hippocampus
findings.population: temporal lobe seizure literature
findings.source_term: preserved awareness during ictal automatisms; temporal non-dominant signs

findings.citation: Lee GR, Arain A, Lim N, et al. 2006 (ref. 41)
findings.claim: Rhythmic ictal non-clonic hand motions may be a contralateral sign in temporal lobe epilepsy, and a simple unilateral auditory aura, described as rare, is also a contralateral sign.
findings.evidence_text: Rhythmic ictal non-clonic hand motions “may occur as a contralateral sign”; unilateral simple auditory aura “is a contralateral sign.”
findings.laterality_localization: Hand motion and unilateral simple auditory aura are contralateral to the seizure-onset hemisphere.
findings.limitations: The source calls unilateral auditory aura rare and gives no frequency or accuracy.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Lateralising signs; PDF p.6, Lateral/neocortical temporal lobe
findings.population: temporal lobe seizure literature
findings.source_term: rhythmic ictal non-clonic hand motion; unilateral elementary auditory aura

findings.citation: Salanova V, Andermann F, Olivier A, et al. 1992 (ref. 30); Benbadis SR, Kotagal P, Klem GH. 1996 (ref. 42); Lee S-U, Suh H-I, Choi JY, et al. 2014 (ref. 31)
findings.claim: Hemifield visual aura has good lateralising value to the contralateral occipital lobe; unilateral eye blinking lateralises to the hemisphere ipsilateral to the blinking eye; and in epileptic nystagmus the fast component is contralateral to the seizure-onset hemisphere.
findings.evidence_text: “Hemifield visual aura has good lateralising value to the contralateral occipital lobe”; unilateral eye blinking is ipsilateral to the blinking eye.
findings.laterality_localization: Hemifield visual aura is contralateral to occipital onset; eye blinking is ipsilateral to the blinking eye; nystagmus fast component is contralateral to onset.
findings.limitations: The review does not report sign-specific sensitivity, specificity, or denominators.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Lateralising signs; PDF p.8, Parieto-occipital junction
findings.population: occipital seizure literature
findings.source_term: hemifield visual aura; unilateral eye blinking; epileptic nystagmus

findings.claim: The conclusion states that careful history and analysis of video-EEG semiology can help localise seizures, but localization remains challenging because semiology may become apparent only after spread to eloquent cortex or engagement of networks; interpretation is enhanced when collated with ictal EEG, structural/functional imaging, and neuropsychometry.
findings.evidence_text: Semiological analysis can help localise seizures, but semiology may become apparent only after a seizure “has spread to an eloquent area” or engaged brain networks.
findings.laterality_localization: Source separates localizing and lateralising value and emphasizes that propagation/network engagement may obscure the onset relationship.
findings.limitations: The source provides practical guidance and cited literature, not a new prospective validation study.
findings.locators: PDF p.10, Conclusion; PDF p.11, Conclusion and Key points
findings.population: presurgical focal epilepsy assessment

sources.source_report_limitations: All 12 pages had present fresh text and represented PNG renderings; no page was blocked. Tables 1–3, Figure 1, the case-image pages, and the video-case layouts were visually inspected. The article is a narrative review with selected literature, illustrative cases, and source-authored tables rather than a systematic review or new cohort. Cited-study restatements retain the current article’s stated population, unit, denominator status, and citation identity; absent numerators, denominators, confidence intervals, and comparator values were not reconstructed. The many source-defined regional associations are often qualified by “tend to,” “may,” “suggests,” “probably,” “usually,” “rare,” or “highly localising,” and propagation can make symptomatogenic and onset regions diverge.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The article is labelled a Review and states that it summarizes current literature, focuses on common semiologies, and provides cases from the authors’ centre with online supplemental videos. No systematic search strategy, eligibility criteria, pooled analysis, or formal reference standard is reported. Cited-study populations remain those of the cited reports; the article also describes seven illustrative cases with patient ages, seizure histories, imaging, EEG, and outcomes. Patient consent for publication was obtained. The source integrates history, examination, neuroimaging, neurophysiology, and neuropsychology for presurgical interpretation and repeatedly cautions that semiology may reflect propagation rather than onset.
sources.source_report_summary: Chowdhury et al., “Localisation in focal epilepsy: a practical guide,” Practical Neurology 2021;21:481-492, is a narrative review with illustrative video and imaging cases. It summarizes semiological relationships to symptomatogenic and seizure-onset regions across frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital, cingulate, insular, and reflex epilepsies, and separately lists lateralising signs and aura-localization relationships. The paper is intended as a practical presurgical guide, not as a new cohort study or meta-analysis.

findings.claim: Among 114 AS with perceived-side data, AS were heard in the right ear in 33%, left ear in 26%, bilaterally in 31%, and inside the head in 10%; illusions were all bilateral, HD was mostly bilateral (70%), and other AS types showed no clear ear-side tendency.
findings.evidence_text: AS were more often perceived in the right (33%) than left (26%) ear, but were also bilateral (31%) or inside the head (10%).
findings.laterality_localization: Right ear, left ear, bilateral, or inside-head perception from the patient viewpoint
findings.limitations: The authors caution that inside-head and bilateral reports may not be separable and that many cases lacked perceived-side information.
findings.locators: PDF p.6, section 6.1; PDF p.7, Table 2; PDF p.9, Conclusion
findings.population: AS with reported perceived side in the review synthesis
findings.source_term: lateralization of the perceived auditory seizure (AS)

findings.evidence_text: When only one-ear AS were considered, 74% were contralateral to the SOZ; the authors state that unilateral AS are not always contralateral but are most often contralateral.
findings.laterality_localization: Patient-perceived ear/inside-head location relative to the probable SOZ hemisphere
findings.limitations: Bilateral and inside-head categories complicate interpretation; some cases were counted in multiple AS-type or SOZ-structure categories.

findings.claim: In temporal AS classifications, SH involved STG12/32 (38%) and HG3/32 (9%); CH and I tended toward STG and mesiotemporal structures; VH involved mesiotemporal structures in 20/43 (47%) temporal VH classifications versus 2/37 (5%) VH responses in the cortical-stimulation table; MH, PAL, and HD showed no clear temporal trends because precise sites were often unspecified.
findings.evidence_text: For SH, STG accounted for 38% and HG 9% of temporal SOZ localizations; almost half of temporal VH SOZ classifications were mesiotemporal.
findings.laterality_localization: Temporal STG, HG, mesiotemporal, and other temporal structures
findings.limitations: AS and stimulation populations are heterogeneous and not a direct controlled comparison; precise temporal sites were often unavailable.

sources.source_report_limitations: The review may have publication bias, and its proportions and comparisons are tentative because it narratively summarized heterogeneous literature without comparative statistical testing. AP subtype definitions varied across studies (CH sometimes included MH/VH and I sometimes included HD); cortical-stimulation brain-region labels and electrode localization varied, afterdischarges were often not reported, and stimulation may produce network-wide or remote effects. AS was not always the first ictal symptom, so some localized structures may reflect propagation rather than generation; Table 2 may count cases multiple times for multiple structures or AS types, and the authors sometimes interpreted SOZ localization across investigations. The paper refers readers to online supplementary data for exact type-specific counts, but no supplement was included in the authorized 12-page source package. The abstract reports right-hemisphere SOZ frequency as 38%, whereas Table 2 reports 77/200 (39%); the discrepancy is retained rather than resolved.
sources.source_report_methods_population: PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched without language or date restrictions through 11 December 2022. The review narratively summarized auditory-network anatomy and compiled encountered cortical-stimulation studies reporting auditory phenomena (AP) plus case reports/series with AS-like phenomena and enough information to determine seizure-onset-zone (SOZ) lateralization and/or localization; acute symptomatic seizures and cases without evident auditory semiology were excluded. Level A evidence comprised seizure freedom after surgery with more than 1 year follow-up, seizures demonstrated from a SOZ on intracranial EEG, a concordant structural MRI lesion, or a concordant MEG cluster of at least 6 spike sources within 1 cm; Level B used MEG scatters, scalp EEG, PET/SPECT, and/or other clinical features. Localization and lateralization were analyzed for Level A, but only lateralization for Level B; data were tabulated as count (frequency), missing data were pairwise-deleted, and no comparative statistical tests were performed.
sources.source_report_summary: Perspective and narrative literature review of the localizing and lateralizing value of auditory phenomena in focal seizures, combining cortical-stimulation reports with case reports and series of auditory seizures (AS).

sources.source_report_limitations: All 8 pages had present fresh text and represented PNG renderings. Pages 2, 4, 6, and 7 were visually inspected for Table 1, Figure 1, Figure 2, and Table 2 layout and values. The review contains repeated estimates from detailed subgroup paragraphs, figures, and summary statements; repeated same-source values are retained only when the source presents a distinct group, endpoint, analysis unit, or cited-study restatement. The restricted-group sleep estimate is reported as 46.1% in the detailed analysis and 63% in the later profile comparison; the source does not reconcile their availability denominators, so both remain explicit and unresolved. No hemisphere-level lateralization result is reported.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a narrative/systematic literature review with 21 included studies selected from 171 considered studies. The source reports 87 confidently included cases involving OFC onset, of which 26 were analyzed as OFC-restricted and 33 as OFC-extended based on resection evidence; extended cases were grouped by frontal, insular, or temporal accessory resection. The review applies the proposed ILAE seizure-description framework and a published EZN confidence grading score. Search counts, study-list cells, standalone resection/imaging/surgery/outcome counts, and generic method/risk-of-bias statements remain context here rather than individual findings.
sources.source_report_summary: Despins et al., “Semiology of Seizures Involving the OFC: A Narrative Review About a Silent Epilepsy,” J Clin Neurophysiol 2025;42:592–599, reviews 87 reported cases with seizure onset involving the orbitofrontal cortex. The review separates EZN restricted to the OFC from EZN extending beyond it and compares source-native semiological profiles, including hyperkinetic behavior, auras, vocal/oro-alimentary/gestural/mimic automatisms, sleep association, consciousness, sensory, autonomic, affective, tonic, and versive phenomena. It treats localization and lateralization independently: OFC compartments and propagation targets are reported, but no hemisphere-level result is asserted unless source-explicit.

sources.source_report_limitations: The review's central limitation is anatomical and cohort heterogeneity: included studies did not exclusively analyze strict lateral temporal epilepsy, and individual studies often did not distinguish seizure onset from propagation. The source states that the overall evidence for anatomic localization is very low, with wide confidence intervals and potential confounding by other neocortical temporal cases. Table 3 prevalence values are study-level minimum-to-maximum percentages, not pooled estimates. Table 4 odds estimates, Table 5 lateral-versus-mesial percentage ranges, and Table 6 diagnostic metrics remain separate analyses with their own denominators and heterogeneity tests. The source explicitly states that auditory aura is highly specific but rare, and that absence of epigastric or olfactory/gustatory aura has high sensitivity but low-to-moderate specificity.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The review used a PRISMA-based systematic search of PubMed and EMBASE and included six studies with 94 patients; the source states that only an estimated 56–69 patients had unambiguous lateral temporal epilepsy because other neocortical temporal structures were included. The review used random-effects meta-analysis for sign odds and diagnostic accuracy, with sensitivity analysis for studies in which more than half of patients unequivocally had lateral seizure onset. Search/duplicate/exclusion counts, reviewer details, eligibility thresholds, Table 1/2 imaging and surgery cells, and standalone population/outcome facts are retained as compact context here rather than individual findings.
sources.source_report_summary: Doerrfuss et al., “Ictal semiology in lateral temporal epilepsy: A systematic review and meta-analysis” (Epileptic Disorders 2026;28:678–689), synthesizes six studies and 94 patients with neocortical temporal epileptogenic-zone involvement. The review retains source heterogeneity between strict lateral temporal, other neocortical, temporo-basal, and temporal-polar definitions. It reports sign-level prevalence ranges, odds estimates, lateral-versus-mesial prevalence comparisons, and diagnostic sensitivity/specificity estimates. Auditory aura is the source's most specific lateral-temporal sign, but it is uncommon; absence of epigastric or olfactory/gustatory aura is more sensitive for lateral-versus-mesial differentiation.

findings.claim: The index patient was a 24-year-old right-handed woman with a ruptured left temporal cavernous malformation causing subarachnoid and intraparenchymal haemorrhage over the left Heschl's gyrus and Wernicke area; after aphasia improved, she heard recently heard words and sounds in her right ear.

sources.source_report_limitations: The report is a single case plus a heterogeneous review of case reports, with no controlled comparator and no seizure captured during the index palinacousis. The index EEG was obtained after symptoms ceased, and intraoperative stimulation occurred after phenytoin. Several review percentages and subset summaries lack explicit denominators. Table 2's printed lesion-aetiology counts sum to 37 although the review states 36 cases; the printed tumour-subtype counts also do not reconcile with the Table 2 tumour total. The source refers to online supplemental table E1 and figure E1, but those materials are not part of this five-page locked package and were not used.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The index report concerns one 24-year-old Caucasian right-handed woman with a ruptured left temporal cavernous malformation. The review searched PubMed for the word “palinacousis,” found 26 reports including 3 reviews, cross-referenced all publications, excluded reports without perseveration of previously heard sounds or words and all review articles, and retained 22 articles with 35 cases; the authors added their own case. No year or primary-language exclusions were applied. The source does not state a diagnostic reference standard or provide complete denominators for several review percentages; the index EEG was performed after symptoms had ceased.
sources.source_report_summary: Veilleux C, El-Hage G, L'Ecuyer N, Bojanowski MW, “Palinacousis: an eloquent symptom of temporal lobe lesion,” BMJ Case Reports 2021;14:e236615. This is a case report of palinacousis after a left temporal cavernous-malformation haemorrhage plus a systematic review of 22 articles reporting 35 cases, to which the index case was added for a total of 36 cases. It addresses auditory perseveration, structural localization, ear/lesion laterality, and the unresolved ictal, postictal, or non-ictal mechanism.

findings.laterality_localization: Lateralization to the side of ictal onset or epileptogenic zone; MRI was localizing but non-lateralizing in the two bilateral hippocampal-sclerosis cases noted by the source.
findings.limitations: EEG, MRI, and PET were not subjected to the same inter-observer analysis as semiology; MRI PPV uses the source’s lesional-case framing, and Figure 1 labels are not reconciled with Table 2.
findings.phase: Aggregate seizure semiology versus interictal or ictal presurgical tests.
findings.population: The 73-patient cohort; MRI values are reported for lesional cases and PET is not part of Table 4.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source is retrospective and restricted to a highly selected group rendered completely seizure free and aura free after resection confined to one anatomical lobe; it states that applicability to patients rejected for surgery or with non-intractable epilepsy is unknown. Parietal and occipital subgroups were small, sublobar analysis was limited, and PET was available only in 40/73 clinically selected patients; ictal SPECT was performed in 20/73. The study did not correlate semiology with intracranial EEG because of electrode-placement bias and lack of stereo-EEG before 2008, and EEG/MRI/PET were not subjected to the same inter-observer analysis as semiology. The article reports unresolved internal numerical discrepancies, including 20/27 versus 21/27 for frontal lateralization and localization, 54/73 in text/Table 2 versus the Figure 1 semiology-lateralization label of 53, and differing displayed Figure 1 counts versus Table 4 values. Cited-study restatements in F025–F032 are claims made by the current article and were not independently verified against the cited sources. No page was blocked; page 6 contains the reference list and no additional primary result beyond the cited targets named in the report.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The cohort comprised consecutive patients operated between 1999 and 2007: temporal lobe epilepsy (30 patients, 63 seizures), frontal lobe epilepsy (27 patients, 51 seizures), parietal lobe epilepsy (8 patients, 14 seizures), and occipital lobe epilepsy (8 patients, 18 seizures). Patients were at least 12 years old, had one focal resection without hemispherectomy or multilobar resection, and had Engel class Ia outcome for at least 1 year; the study population was 73 patients and 145 seizures. Three investigators independently reviewed one or two best video examples of each seizure type while blinded to clinical details, with charted auras supplied by an unblinded investigator. A positive result required agreement of at least two of three raters; the same rule defined presence of a sign, correct lateralization, and correct lobar or sublobar localization. The surgical resection and lasting seizure freedom were used as the reference for the epileptogenic zone. Free Marginal Kappa and positive predictive value were calculated. Noninvasive EEG, MRI, and PET had been reviewed in the presurgical conference; PET was available for 40/73 patients and ictal SPECT for 20/73.
sources.source_report_summary: Elwan, Alexopoulos, Silveira, and Kotagal report a retrospective original empirical study of the lateralizing and lobar-localizing value of seizure semiology in 73 patients rendered Engel class Ia seizure free after focal resective epilepsy surgery. Three blinded investigators reviewed seizure videos and charted auras, then compared semiology with scalp interictal and ictal EEG, MRI, and clinically indicated PET.

sources.source_report_limitations:
This is a seven-patient, selected invasive-monitoring series. Electrode coverage and the number of recorded seizures varied by patient; Case 7 had no recorded seizure and was not evaluated with SEEG. Cingulate coverage was incomplete in all invasive evaluations, and the authors state that earliest EEG change may reflect a spread-exit pattern rather than the actual onset zone. CCEP responses were not necessarily consistent with seizure spread, especially in Case 1, and medication effects may have influenced CCEP results. Table 1 and figures were used for direct semiology/localization context only; surgery and outcome cells were not made individual findings.

Owner question: Should CCEP connectivity findings be integrated as a separate network-evidence layer from ictal spread, given the source’s explicit statement that the two were not necessarily consistent?
sources.source_report_methods_population: The study enrolled seven consecutive PCE patients; six had SEEG-identified posterior cingulate ictal onset and one had an MRI-identified postcingulate tumour. Four patients underwent CCEP. SEEG and scalp EEG were retrospectively analyzed with video-documented ictal semiology; the source used the Lüders seizure-classification scheme. The posterior cingulate was operationally defined caudal to the vertical posterior commissure line.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2014 primary study characterizes posterior cingulate epilepsy in seven intractable patients using scalp EEG, SEEG, and CCEP. Direct findings retained here include motor versus dialeptic/automotor semiology, case-level ictal spread, source-native scalp EEG categories, posterior-cingulate network connectivity, and localization/lateralization limitations. Generic demographic, electrode-count, surgery, and outcome cells are retained only as compact context.

sources.source_report_summary: This source is a 3-page scanned institutional Epilepsy Fellow Handbook excerpt, with the UTHealth and McGovern Medical School identity visible on the title page. PDF p.1 is a title page; PDF pp.2-3 are tables headed "Lateralizing signs" and "Localization". The tables provide qualitative seizure-semiology side, hemisphere, and anatomical localization pairings and do not report primary-study methods or quantitative results.

sources.source_report_limitations: The study is a retrospective review of medical charts, videotapes, and EEG recordings. The patient count was relatively small despite the larger number of seizure events; participants were selected surgical candidates with precise localization, and patients with unclear localization were excluded. Speech arrest, aphasia, and rapid return to baseline required specific testing that was not performed universally, particularly for seizures occurring at night. The source reports unequal seizure counts and a mixture of patient- and seizure-level wording in discussion paragraphs; this report preserves the stated units and does not calculate conversions. Table 5 states that percentages are relative to automatisms involving extremities for the relevant subrows, but does not provide every row-specific denominator. There is also an unresolved internal PET description: the prose says PET scans were abnormal in all patients except 2 with RTLE, while Tables 3-4 display missing PET entries for LTL patients 8-9 and RTL patient 19 and a normal PET entry for RTL patient 10. Cited-study restatements above were not independently verified against their cited targets.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Patients were admitted to an epilepsy unit over 30 months and underwent 5-14 days of scalp and sphenoidal EEG-CCTV monitoring with antiepileptic-drug discontinuation; all had head MRI, 16 had PET, 18 had neuropsychological testing, 16 had Wada testing, and 6 had repeat monitoring with implanted subdural grids. The 19 patients were divided by unilateral temporal onset using interictal discharges, ictal EEG onset, MRI lesions including mesiotemporal sclerosis, PET hypometabolism, neuropsychological testing, Wada testing, preoperative evaluation, and surgical outcome; 10 patients had RTL onset and 9 had LTL onset, yielding 54 and 73 recorded seizures, respectively. Only complex partial seizures (CPS) and secondarily generalized or partial-evolving-to-generalized (PE) seizures were analyzed. Clinical features were compared with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests.
sources.source_report_summary: This original empirical study retrospectively reviewed EEG/closed-circuit-TV-recorded seizures in 19 consecutive patients with medically intractable temporal lobe epilepsy undergoing preoperative evaluation, comparing clinical features of left temporal lobe (LTL/LTLE) and right temporal lobe (RTL/RTLE) seizure onset. Its purpose was to assess seizure semiology with potential lateralizing value, especially auras, automatisms, motor signs, ictal language, and postictal manifestations.

sources.source_report_limitations: The chapter is a scanned educational source with no usable fresh page text; all 16 pages were reviewed from the authorized page images. Page 16 is an upside-down continuation of the reference list and contains no additional semiology or localization claim. Pages 14-16 contain references and case material; the cited papers themselves were not reviewed, so reference markers in the chapter are retained as attribution rather than treated as independently verified evidence. The chapter mixes review-synthesized series with illustrative cases and reports heterogeneous units (patients, seizures, cases, and source-defined observations). Many percentages lack numerators, denominators, confidence limits, or a fully specified cohort, and silence is not interpreted as a negative finding. Illustrative EEG figures were not promoted to separate findings when the surrounding text did not add a distinct semiology, localization, or lateralization claim.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is an educational chapter rather than a single primary cohort. The general text synthesizes source-cited series involving focal epilepsy, temporal/mesial temporal epilepsy, and frontal, parietal, or occipital epilepsy, and separately presents three illustrative case observations. The source uses patients, cases, seizures, and source-defined observations as analysis units; no common cohort, eligibility rule, comparator, reference standard, or chapter-wide denominator is reported. The report retains the source's unit and missingness for each finding and does not infer denominators from percentages.
sources.source_report_summary: Scanned educational chapter 34, "Focal Epilepsy and Surgical Evaluation," by Nancy Foldvary, DO. The chapter discusses clinical semiology and EEG correlates of focal epilepsy involving temporal, frontal, parietal, and occipital regions, with implications for localization and lateralization during surgical evaluation; it also includes three illustrative cases.

findings.citation: Lesser RP, Lüders H, Klem G, Dinner DS, Morris HH, Hahn J. Cortical afterdischarge and functional response thresholds: results of extraoperative testing. Epilepsia 1984;25:615–21 [2]; Kellinghaus C, Lüders HO. The symptomatogenic zone: general principles. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 425–31 [3]
findings.claim: The review states that seizure symptomatology reflects activation of specific brain regions by ictal discharge; the symptomatogenic zone is generally near, though not necessarily immediately near, the epileptogenic zone, and sequential signs can reveal propagation patterns. Multiple symptomatogenic zones may be activated simultaneously and obscure one another, while different onset regions can evolve to a common symptomatogenic zone such as the SSMA.
findings.evidence_text: The review links sequential ictal signs to propagation and cautions that simultaneous activation or convergent pathways can produce variable or misleading semiology.
findings.laterality_localization: localization to the symptomatogenic network and relationship to the epileptogenic zone; no fixed laterality
findings.limitations: The review notes that the sign itself may not identify the onset site when propagation or network convergence dominates.
findings.locators: PDF p.1, section 2 General principles of ictal symptomatology; PDF p.1, abstract
findings.population: focal epilepsy and presurgical evaluation

findings.citation: Sperling MR, O'Connor MJ. Auras and subclinical seizures: characteristics and prognostic significance. Ann Neurol 1990;28:320–8 [4]; Palmini A, Gloor P. The localizing value of auras in partial seizures: a prospective and retrospective study. Neurology 1992;42:801–8 [5]
findings.claim: As first ictal symptoms, auras provide important localizing and lateralizing information about the relationship between the symptomatogenic and epileptogenic zones. They are reported by most patients with temporal and parieto-occipital epilepsies, are associated with favorable outcome after temporal lobectomy, and were reported to localize the most likely lobe of origin as well as EEG and imaging.
findings.evidence_text: The review calls auras important first ictal symptoms and compares their lobe-of-origin value with EEG and imaging.
findings.laterality_localization: most likely lobe of seizure origin and relationship between symptomatogenic and epileptogenic zones
findings.limitations: The review does not provide a common cohort size or denominator for these cross-study statements.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with temporal or parieto-occipital epilepsy and temporal-lobectomy candidates

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Somatosensory auras arising from SI involve discrete body parts contralateral to the ictal discharge; SII produces similar symptoms that may be bilateral or ipsilateral to the seizure focus; and SSMA symptoms are poorly localized and primarily involve contralateral proximal body parts. The source table likewise lists SI and SSMA as mainly contralateral and SII as ipsilateral when unilateral.
findings.evidence_text: The text distinguishes discrete contralateral SI symptoms from bilateral or ipsilateral SII symptoms and poorly localized SSMA symptoms.
findings.laterality_localization: SI contralateral to ictal discharge; SII bilateral or ipsilateral to focus; SSMA primarily contralateral proximal body parts
findings.limitations: Electrical-stimulation findings and clinical seizure observations are presented together without a single common analysis unit.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy; electrical-stimulation and semiology observations

findings.citation: Manford M, Fish DR, Shorvon SD. An analysis of clinical seizure patterns and their localizing value in frontal and temporal lobe epilepsies. Brain 1996;119:17–40 [6]
findings.claim: Well-localized somatosensory auras that evolve to motor features are usually associated with a perirolandic epileptogenic zone close to the symptomatogenic zone, whereas illusions of swelling, shrinking, or movement of body parts are often elicited by activation of the nondominant inferior parietal lobe or TPO junction.
findings.evidence_text: Motor evolution is linked to perirolandic localization, while body-part illusions are linked to nondominant inferior parietal or TPO activation.
findings.laterality_localization: perirolandic region; nondominant inferior parietal lobe or TPO junction
findings.limitations: The review does not state denominators for either association.
findings.phase: aura with evolution to motor features; ictal sensory illusion
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations
findings.source_term: well-localized somatosensory auras and somatosensory illusions

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Simple visual auras with static, flashing, or moving lights suggest activation of the primary visual cortex and contiguous visual association areas, whereas complex visual auras involving people, scenes, objects, or illusions suggest the temporo-occipital junction or basal temporal cortex.
findings.evidence_text: The review contrasts elementary lights with complex scenes and objects as clues to different visual regions.
findings.laterality_localization: primary visual cortex and contiguous visual association areas for simple visual auras; temporo-occipital junction or basal temporal cortex for complex visual auras
findings.limitations: The review does not state a common cohort or denominator.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Visual phenomena lateralized to one hemi-field as an early ictal manifestation are highly suggestive of onset in the contralateral occipital lobe. Symptoms restricted to the lower or upper quadrant are reported to localize to the contralateral supra- or infracalcarine fissure, respectively.
findings.evidence_text: An early hemi-field symptom is linked to contralateral occipital onset, with lower and upper quadrant symptoms assigned to opposite supra- and infracalcarine regions.
findings.laterality_localization: one hemi-field or quadrant is interpreted relative to the contralateral occipital lobe and supra- or infracalcarine fissure
findings.limitations: No frequency or denominator is reported.
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy
findings.source_term: lateralized visual phenomena and visual field auras

findings.citation: Richer F, Martinez M, Cohen H, Saint-Hilaire JM. Visual motion perception from stimulation of the human medial parieto-occipital cortex. Exp Brain Res 1991;87:649–52 [7]
findings.claim: Stimulation of the precuneus, posterior cingulum, or mesial parieto-occipital region produces blurry vision or visual motions, and visual distortions such as micropsia, macropsia, metamorphopsia, and palinopsia suggest activation near the geniculostriate radiation.
findings.evidence_text: The review links blurry or moving vision to posterior medial regions and distortions to the geniculostriate-radiation vicinity.
findings.laterality_localization: precuneus, posterior cingulum, mesial parieto-occipital region, or tissue near the geniculostriate radiation
findings.limitations: The source combines stimulation findings with a localization inference and gives no frequency.
findings.population: electrical-stimulation observations in patients with epilepsy
findings.source_term: visual motion, blurry vision, and visual distortions

findings.citation: Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. In: Lüders HO, editor. Textbook of epilepsy surgery. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Simple auditory auras such as ringing or buzzing are associated with the primary auditory cortex, while complex voices, music, hallucinations, or illusions are associated with auditory association areas in the temporo-occipital cortex. Although auditory information has bilateral innervation, the contralateral ear is better represented in auditory cortex.
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts simple ringing or buzzing with complex voices or music and notes the stronger contralateral-ear representation.
findings.laterality_localization: primary auditory cortex for simple symptoms; temporo-occipital auditory association cortex for complex symptoms; contralateral ear has better cortical representation
findings.limitations: No frequency, denominator, or laterality performance estimate is reported.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations

findings.citation: Kahane P, Hoffmann D, Minotti L, Berthoz A. Reappraisal of the human vestibular cortex by cortical electrical stimulation study. Ann Neurol 2003;54:615–24 [8]
findings.claim: Vertiginous auras with sensations of rotation or movement are usually associated with visual or auditory symptoms and a symptomatogenic zone near the visual and auditory association areas at the temporoparietal junction. Electrical stimulation readily elicits vestibular or rotatory sensations from a lateral temporoparietal region spanning the Sylvian fissure, including the parietal operculum and middle and posterior superior and middle temporal gyri.
findings.evidence_text: The review places vertiginous symptomatology near visual and auditory association cortex and describes a stimulation-defined lateral temporoparietal region.
findings.laterality_localization: temporoparietal junction and lateral temporoparietal cortex above and below the Sylvian fissure
findings.limitations: The review does not provide a common clinical denominator.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations

findings.citation: Bancaud J, Talairach J. Clinical semiology of frontal lobe seizures. Adv Neurol 1992;57:3–58 [9]; Hausser-Hauw C, Bancaud J. Gustatory hallucinations in epileptic seizures: electrophysiological, clinical and anatomical correlates. Brain 1987;110:339–59 [10]; Rona S. Auras: localizing and lateralizing value. 2008. p. 432–42 [61]
findings.claim: Olfactory auras are typically unpleasant and often associated with gustatory phenomena; stimulation of the amygdala, olfactory bulb, insula, or posterior orbitofrontal region can produce olfactory sensations or illusions. Gustatory auras can be difficult to distinguish from olfactory disturbances, and stimulation of the parietal operculum or mesiobasal temporal regions can produce gustatory hallucinations.
findings.evidence_text: The text identifies several stimulated olfactory and gustatory regions and says the two symptom types may be hard to separate clinically.
findings.laterality_localization: amygdala, olfactory bulb, insula, posterior orbitofrontal region, parietal operculum, or mesiobasal temporal region; table classifies these auras as generally nonlateralizing
findings.limitations: The table's NonLAT label is a source summary and is not accompanied by a performance estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations

findings.citation: Fish DR, Gloor P, Quesney FL, Olivier A. Clinical responses to electrical brain stimulation of the temporal and frontal lobes in patients with epilepsy: pathophysiological implications. Brain 1993;116:397–414 [11]
findings.claim: Autonomic auras include cardiorespiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and cutaneous sensations and are attributed to activation of the insular cortex, anterior cingulum, SSMA, or amygdala; the source notes that these areas share a subcortical relay station with the hypothalamus.
findings.evidence_text: The review groups several visceral and cutaneous sensations under autonomic auras and identifies four cortical regions.
findings.laterality_localization: insular cortex, anterior cingulum, SSMA, or amygdala; source table classifies autonomic auras as nonlateralizing
findings.limitations: The source does not provide a single autonomic-aura cohort or frequency estimate.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.3, section 3.1 Auras; PDF p.2, Table 1
findings.population: patients with focal epilepsy and electrical-stimulation observations

findings.citation: Henkel A, Noachtar S, Pfander M, Lüders HO. The localizing value of the abdominal aura and its evolution: a study in focal epilepsies. Neurology 2002;58:271–6 [12]; Kotagal P, Lüders HO, Williams G, Nichols TR, McPherson J. Psychomotor seizures of temporal lobe onset: analysis of symptom clusters and sequences. Epilepsy Res 1995;20:49–67 [13]
findings.claim: Abdominal auras are described as the most common autonomic aura and are localized to the anterior insula, frontal operculum, mesial temporal structures, and SSMA. In isolation they carry a reported 74% probability of TLE, rising to 98% when they evolve into an automotor component; when combined with vomiting they suggest an epileptogenic zone in the nondominant temporal lobe.
findings.evidence_text: The review gives 74% for isolated abdominal auras and 98% when an automotor component develops, and links vomiting to nondominant temporal onset.
findings.laterality_localization: anterior insula, frontal operculum, mesial temporal structures, and SSMA; vomiting-associated abdominal aura suggests nondominant temporal onset
findings.limitations: The source does not report the numerators, denominators, or analysis unit underlying the probabilities.

findings.claim: Psychic auras include emotional symptoms and familiarity distortions; the symptomatogenic zone is generally temporal neocortex or mesial temporal structures, except that forced thoughts are generally observed in FLE. Fear is associated with amygdala, hippocampal, mesial frontal, or temporal-neocortical activation, and Table 1 lists fear as nonlateralizing.

findings.claim: Pure insular epilepsy has a typical sequence beginning with laryngeal discomfort and thoraco-abdominal constriction or dyspnea, followed by unpleasant perioral or large-area paresthesias or warmth, dysarthria or dysphonia, and focal motor manifestations. Consciousness is not impaired in seizures restricted to the insula, and unilateral sensory symptoms and focal motor activity are usually contralateral to the epileptogenic zone.

findings.claim: Temporal-plus epilepsy involves the temporal lobe and a connected network including orbitofrontal region, insula, frontal or parietal operculum, and TPO junction. Hippocampal sclerosis on MRI cannot reliably differentiate pure TLE from temporal-plus epilepsy, whereas semiology distinguishes them: pure TLE more often has abdominal auras evolving to automatisms and postictal amnesia, while temporal-plus epilepsy is associated with gustatory, auditory, or vertiginous auras, version, piloerection, ipsilateral tonic signs, and postictal dysphoria.
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts the semiology of pure TLE with temporal-plus epilepsy and cautions against relying on hippocampal sclerosis alone.
findings.laterality_localization: Temporal-plus network; ipsilateral tonic signs in temporal-plus epilepsy
findings.limitations: No quantitative diagnostic performance is reported.

sources.source_report_limitations: This review is a narrative synthesis with heterogeneous cited populations, phases, reference standards, and analysis units rather than a single original dataset. Many numerical statements are given only as percentages or ranges without numerators, denominators, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, and the review does not report a common denominator across its cited studies. The source explicitly cautions that clinical history depends on patient and observer factors, video/EEG depends on reproducible signs and technical quality, and electrical stimulation may activate distant areas. Several claims are explicitly limited to one series, isolated cases, or pediatric populations. Table 1 is modified from Rona [61] and Table 2 from Bianchin and Sakamoto [62]; cited-source restatements were not independently verified against the cited papers in this review.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a narrative review rather than a single original cohort or systematic quantitative synthesis. The discussed populations include patients with focal epilepsy, temporal lobe epilepsy, mesial and neocortical temporal lobe epilepsy, extratemporal and posterior-cortex epilepsy, children and infants, and presurgical epilepsy-surgery candidates. The review draws on clinical history, video/EEG and electrical-stimulation observations and on cited case series and cohorts; a single review-wide analysis population, eligibility rule, reference standard, and common denominator are not reported.
sources.source_report_summary: Foldvary-Schaefer and Unnwongse's narrative review from the American Epilepsy Society 2009 Annual Course surveys the localizing and lateralizing value of auras, ictal and postictal motor signs, autonomic manifestations, speech and language findings, and semiology that distinguishes temporal from extratemporal epilepsies. It emphasizes that semiology estimates the symptomatogenic zone and its relationship to the epileptogenic zone, but must be interpreted with clinical history, video/EEG, electrical stimulation, and the other components of presurgical evaluation. The review contains two source-modified summary tables and restates findings from cited studies.

sources.source_report_limitations: This chapter is a broad narrative review with heterogeneous cited populations, evidence roles, and reference standards. It does not provide a single systematic search, unified cohort, pooled denominator, or pooled diagnostic estimate. Many percentages are reported without numerators, denominators, confidence intervals, or the exact study population in the chapter. Several localization statements are explicitly qualified by propagation, network connectivity, pathology, timing, or uncertainty between early regional involvement and true seizure onset. Pages 21–30 are bibliography and were inspected for complete page coverage but do not add separate source-native semiology or localization claims beyond the cited attributions already retained above. No PDF page, figure, or table was blocked; figure-bearing pages were visually checked for layout-dependent MRI, EEG, PET, and SPECT content.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This source is a narrative review chapter and does not state a unified search strategy, eligibility set, enrollment cohort, or pooled analysis population. It draws on heterogeneous cited patient cohorts, seizure/event observations, imaging and EEG studies, and case reports, with emphasis on drug-resistant and presurgical temporal lobe epilepsy. Denominators, reference standards, and analysis units therefore remain study-specific; no chapter-level aggregate estimate is established.
sources.source_report_summary: Chapter 27, “Semiology, EEG, and neuroimaging findings in temporal lobe epilepsies,” by Valerio Frazzini, Louis Cousyn, and Vincent Navarro, is a narrative educational/review chapter in the 2022 Handbook of Clinical Neurology volume The Temporal Lobe. It synthesizes clinical semiology, scalp and intracranial EEG, and interictal/ictal metabolic imaging relevant to temporal seizure-onset localization and lateralization. It is not a single primary cohort or a pooled quantitative analysis; claims attributed to individual cited studies are retained as cited-study restatements.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a selected surgical cohort of patients with intractable temporal-lobe epilepsy who underwent temporal lobectomy; patients with bihemispheric speech representation were excluded. Seizures were limited to good-quality video recordings, up to four per patient, and speech testing was constrained by consciousness and seizure duration. Several findings are based on small subgroups, and the source notes limited ability to perform thorough ictal aphasia testing for isolated paraphasia. Dominant/nondominant origin and speech dominance are retained as the source’s viewpoints; no left/right equivalence is inferred. Cited-study restatements are reported as such and were not verified against the cited originals.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Thirty-five patients aged 12-39 years (mean 24.6) were selected from an epilepsy-surgery population; all had intractable temporal-lobe epilepsy and subsequently underwent temporal lobectomy. The investigators reviewed up to four good-quality videotaped seizures per patient until 100 seizures were reached; 94 were spontaneous, 3 hyperventilation-induced, and 3 Metrazol-activated. The cohort comprised 80 complex partial seizures and 20 complex partial seizures with secondary generalization; 48 seizures arose from the dominant temporal lobe in 16 patients and 52 from the nondominant temporal lobe in 19 patients. Simultaneous scalp and chronically implanted subdural EEG-video monitoring was used, speech dominance was determined by intracarotid amobarbital testing, and patients with bihemispheric speech representation were excluded. One author reviewed the videotapes without knowledge of EEG localization or eventual surgical management.
sources.source_report_summary: Gabr M, Lüders H, Dinner D, Morris H, and Wyllie E, “Speech manifestations in lateralization of temporal lobe seizures,” Annals of Neurology 1989;25:82-87. This primary empirical study evaluates the incidence, ictal/postictal timing, and dominant-versus-nondominant temporal-lobe lateralizing value of speech manifestations in 100 seizures from 35 patients with intractable temporal-lobe epilepsy.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a retrospective, single-center surgical series of drug-resistant SHE and therefore has referral and surgical-selection constraints; the source specifically notes that the high FCD type II proportion reflects surgical bias and that applicability to drug-sensitive SHE and autosomal dominant NFLE remains uncertain. The semiology analysis excluded 20 patients with unclear or widespread SOZ, and the extrafrontal subgroups were small. SOZ-overlap and incomplete-resection handling are described in Methods, but no independent general-population estimate is established. Most findings have no hemisphere or body-side direction. Figure 3 explicitly displays all SOZs on the left hemisphere for clarity, so that rendering cannot support left-sided lateralization. Table 2 and the narrative differ on autonomic manifestations in the operculoinsular subgroup; the discrepancy is retained in F006 without converting an absent table entry to zero. The article announces online supporting information, but no supporting file is part of this 11-page source package and no claim from it is used. Cited-study restatements in F012, F013, F015, F019, and F020 remain unverified against their cited sources.
sources.source_report_methods_population:
The study retrospectively identified 155 patients with drug-resistant sleep-related epilepsy from 1433 consecutive epilepsy-surgery patients treated from October 1997 through July 2015; sleep-related epilepsy required more than 90% of seizures during sleep. After exclusion of 20 patients with nocturnal temporal lobe epilepsy who did not meet confirmed SHE criteria, 135 patients comprised the SHE series. SOZ location was assigned from presurgical anatomo-electroclinical data, including stereo-EEG when performed, postoperative MRI, and postoperative Engel outcome. Six patients with overlapping frontal and extrafrontal SOZs were assigned to the principal SOZ location; seven patients with incomplete resection but confidently localized SOZs were retained using stereo-EEG; 20 patients with unclear or widespread SOZs were excluded from the semiology analysis. The semiology analysis therefore included 115 patients: 74 frontal and 41 extrafrontal, comprising 14 temporal, 18 operculoinsular, and 9 posterior cases.

Clinical descriptions came from patients and family members, and the earliest nonmotor manifestation was selected when more than one was reported. All patients had at least one typical sleep-related event captured during video-EEG and stereo-EEG monitoring when performed. Five epileptologists reviewed captured events; two independently categorized the four video-documented semiology patterns, and four reviewed discordant assignments. One semiology pattern was assigned per patient because seizures were considered stereotyped, with early motor semiology weighted more heavily than late semiology. Seventeen patients (15%) required consensus review for discordant categorization. Postictal confusion was assessed from the clinical assessment during ictal recordings. Welch-corrected unpaired t tests, two-tailed Fisher exact tests, and kappa statistics were used; significance was retained at P < 0.05.

Context reported by the source: mean seizure-onset age was 5.8 +/- 4.4 years, mean disease duration was 17.9 +/- 10.3 years, 64% had at least one seizure per night, and 90% had at least one seizure per week. An MRI-identifiable lesion was present in 88/135 patients (65%); probable focal cortical dysplasia was the most common MRI diagnosis (52%). The most common postoperative histopathologic diagnosis was FCD type II (67%). At least 2 years of postoperative outcome data were available for 127/135 patients (94%); Engel I outcome occurred in 104/127 (82%) and Engel class Ia in 86/127 (68%). Mortality outcomes were NOT_REPORTED.
sources.source_report_summary: Source role: full-length original empirical research report and retrospective single-center case series, published in Epilepsia in 2019. The article reviews 135 surgically treated, drug-resistant patients with video-EEG documented sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) and examines whether ictal semiology patterns and early nonmotor manifestations differ by seizure-onset zone (SOZ) and can help localize seizure onset. It compares frontal SHE with temporal, operculoinsular, and posterior SHE.

sources.source_report_limitations: The evidence is based on 21 patients from heterogeneous case reports and small series, with incomplete semiology reporting and no quantitative meta-analysis. The source contains direct internal discrepancies that are preserved: the narrative reports impaired consciousness in 3 patients (35%) versus 8/21 (38%) in Table 2; narrative vocalization/grunts in 2 patients (12%) versus 2/21 (10%) in Table 2; narrative negative motor signs in 2 patients (12%) versus 2/21 (10%) in Table 2; and the discussion reports two laughter patients versus 3/21 (14%) in Table 2. The source also states that anarthria alone cannot designate hemispheric lateralization. Cited pure-insular comparisons are retained as restatements, not pooled with the fronto-opercular cohort.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a systematic review of non-idiopathic focal fronto-opercular epilepsy. The included population is 21 patients from 16 studies, including case series and case reports; the source reports 13 adults and 8 children in its population context. The review used anatomical and electroclinical evidence to define the EZ and divided the cohort into 12 prefrontal-operculum and 9 precentral Rolandic-operculum patients. Study-selection counts, Table 1 demographic/exploration cells, publication details, and risk-of-bias statements are retained here as context rather than individual findings. The source states that quantitative meta-analysis was not possible because of heterogeneity and low patient numbers; Fisher's exact tests compared semiological variables between the two EZ groups.
sources.source_report_summary: Gokce-Samar et al., “Ictal semiology in fronto-opercular epilepsy: A systematic review” (Epileptic Disorders 2026), reviews 21 patients from 16 studies. The source separates prefrontal operculum from precentral Rolandic operculum and reports aura, somatosensory, motor, speech, respiratory, autonomic, laughter, consciousness, and focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic findings with onset/propagation timing. It also compares fronto-opercular and pure-insular patterns. Source-native anatomy and semiology are preserved without forced hemisphere, Brodmann, Lüders, or ILAE mapping.

sources.source_report_limitations: All 16 native pages were reviewed from the fresh per-page text, and the page renderings were checked for the title and definitions, Table 1, Figures 1-26, Tables 2-3, references, and translated summaries; no page was blocked, and no rotation, clipping, table-layout, figure, or missing-text issue changed interpretation. The source describes a predominantly white, middle-class Rochester population and a 50-year record-based cohort in which diagnostic terminology was not constant. Classification was based primarily on historical documentation and the study neurologist's diagnostic impression; EEG was not used to modify seizure-type assignment. The authors note that some sources of medical care in the first 15 years were absent from the project index, that case ascertainment and medical-care use could have changed over time, and that potential underenumeration may affect time-trend interpretation. General methods and definitions are referred to a companion paper, and cited comparison studies were not separately reviewed under this source authorization. The seizure-type incidence distributions, epidemiologic definitions, tables, and age/gender/etiology/time plots were not converted into V30 findings because they do not constitute source-reported semiology-localization or lateralization claims; the document reports no body-side, reference-side, anatomical-localization, or laterality result for a semiologic phenomenon.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The Rochester Project diagnostic record system was screened for residents with records of seizures, convulsions, or epilepsy, including broad rubrics such as syncope and loss of consciousness; a neurologist reviewed potential cases, and residency was verified. Epilepsy incidence used residents at the date of epilepsy diagnosis and recurrent unprovoked seizures, whereas FUS included residents with one or more unprovoked seizures at first medical contact and used age at first seizure; a cluster within one 24-hour interval was treated as one seizure episode. Denominators were projected age- and gender-specific resident populations derived from census data and modified for Rochester epidemiology exclusions; rates were age-adjusted by the direct method to the 1970 total United States population. The study identified 880 individuals with a new diagnosis of epilepsy (418 male and 462 female) and 1,208 individuals with one or more unprovoked seizures who received medical attention while Rochester residents (584 male and 624 female). Seizure type was classified from the history using the 1981 ILAE criteria, based on the predominant type at diagnosis and the study neurologist's review of available histories; interictal EEG was not used to modify classification.
sources.source_report_summary: This is a population-based incidence study of epilepsy and unprovoked seizures among residents of Rochester, Minnesota, during 1935-1984, using the Rochester Project medical-record linkage system. It reports age-, gender-, seizure-type-, etiology-, and time-specific incidence and cumulative incidence, including comparisons between epilepsy and a first medical diagnosis of an unprovoked seizure (FUS). The paper is epidemiologic and does not report a source-specific semiologic sign, a semiology-to-localization relationship, or a lateralizing direction that meets the V30 finding definition.

findings.citation: Rauschecker, J. P. (ref. 18); Scott, S. K. (ref. 19); Scott, S. K. & Johnsrude, I. S. (ref. 20); Warren, J. E., Wise, R. J. & Warren, J. D. (ref. 21); Wise, R. J. S. et al. (ref. 22)
findings.claim: The authors propose that a ventral stream involving superior and middle temporal structures processes speech signals for comprehension or recognition, whereas a dorsal stream involving posterior frontal, posterior dorsal temporal, and parietal-opercular structures translates acoustic speech into frontal articulatory representations; speech-perception tasks rely more on dorsal circuitry and speech-recognition tasks more on ventral circuitry with shared tissue in the left STG. They further propose bilateral ventral organization with computational differences between hemispheres and strong left dominance of the dorsal stream.

(ref. 112)
findings.claim: The review states that portions of the STS are important for phonological representation or processing, are activated during speech perception, speech production, and active maintenance of phonemic information, and can respond preferentially to phonemic acoustic signals relative to complex non-speech signals. It reports that STS activity is modulated by phonological-neighborhood density, with middle-to-posterior STS activation in both hemispheres greater for high- than low-density words, and proposes a crucial phonological STS region extending from the most anterolateral Heschl’s gyrus to the posterior-most Sylvian fissure, with bilateral organization and a mild leftward bias.
findings.evidence_text: The review identifies the STS as a bilateral, mildly left-biased site for phonological-level processes and states that high-neighborhood-density words produce greater middle-to-posterior STS activation than low-density words.
findings.laterality_localization: Middle-to-posterior STS bilaterally with a mild leftward bias; proposed anterior boundary at the most anterolateral Heschl’s gyrus and posterior boundary at the posterior-most Sylvian fissure
findings.limitations: Review synthesis; the source does not provide a single cohort, denominator, or pooled quantitative estimate for this convergence.

findings.claim: The review reports strong evidence that posterior middle temporal regions participate in lexical and semantic access from auditory input. It states that damage particularly along the middle temporal gyrus has long been associated with auditory-comprehension deficits, an effect confirmed in a cited large-scale study involving 101 patients; direct cortical stimulation implicates the middle temporal gyrus but also a broader network including most of the superior temporal lobe, anterior portions, and inferior frontal lobe. The review says most evidence indicates left-dominant organization, while the right hemisphere can comprehend words reasonably well, implying bilateral capability with computational differences.
findings.evidence_text: The review links posterior middle temporal damage to auditory-comprehension deficits, reports confirmation in a study involving 101 patients, and states that most evidence is left-dominant while right-hemisphere word comprehension remains possible.
findings.laterality_localization: Posterior middle temporal gyrus and broader superior temporal/inferior frontal network; mostly left-dominant, with some right-hemisphere comprehension capability
findings.limitations: Cited restatement; the 101-patient cohort size is not treated as a finding denominator, and the underlying study is not verified here.

findings.population: Patients with posterior temporal damage, a cited study involving 101 patients, direct-stimulation participants, and functional-imaging participants; finding denominator NOT_REPORTED

findings.claim: The authors propose that the auditory dorsal stream interfaces with the motor system, serves speech development and continues to function in adults, and provides basic mechanisms for phonological short-term memory. They distinguish segment-level auditory-motor processes for acquisition and maintenance of articulatory phonetic skills from segment-sequence processes for new vocabulary and online guidance of speech sequences.

findings.claim: The review reports that damage to the left dorsal STG or temporoparietal junction is associated with conduction aphasia, characterized by good comprehension but frequent phonemic errors in speech production. It states that errors are more likely for longer, lower-frequency words and verbal repetition of strings with little semantic constraint, and that current evidence favors cortical dysfunction rather than a simple arcuate-fasciculus disconnection account.

findings.laterality_localization: Left dorsal STG or temporoparietal junction; comprehension relatively preserved while production contains frequent phonemic errors

findings.citation: Hickok, G. & Poeppel, D. (ref. 6); Goodglass, H. (ref. 85); Anderson, J. M. et al. (ref. 86); Hickok, G. et al. (ref. 87); Wilshire, C. E. & McCarthy, R. A. (ref. 89); Hickok, G. (ref. 90)
findings.claim: The authors interpret conduction aphasia as disruption of an auditory-motor interface, particularly at the segment-sequence level. They propose that comprehension is preserved because ventral pathways are spared and/or right-hemisphere speech systems compensate for left-hemisphere disruption, while phonological errors arise because sensory speech representations cannot provide online guidance for speech-sound sequencing.
findings.evidence_text: The authors state that conduction aphasia reflects auditory-motor interface disruption and that preserved comprehension may reflect spared ventral pathways or right-hemisphere compensation.
findings.laterality_localization: Left auditory-motor interface or left-hemisphere speech-perception system; ventral pathways and right-hemisphere speech systems proposed as compensatory or spared
findings.limitations: Review-level interpretation; no direct seizure or stimulation evidence is presented for this mechanism in the document.

findings.claim: The review reports that cited functional-imaging studies asked individuals to listen to pseudowords and then subvocally reproduce them, identifying a network active during both perceptual and motor-related phases. The network included posterior STS bilaterally, a left-dominant site in the Sylvian fissure at the parietotemporal boundary called area Spt, and left posterior frontal regions; the authors propose that posterior STS supports sensory speech coding and Spt translates sensory codes to the motor system.

findings.claim: The review reports that Spt was activated during perception and reproduction of tonal sequences and during reproduction of spoken or written words, indicating that access to the network is not restricted to speech or the auditory modality. It also reports a skilled-pianist observation in which Spt was more active during humming than imagined keyboard playing despite the greater difficulty of the playing condition, and the authors infer that Spt may be more tightly coupled to the vocal-tract effector than to a specific sensory system.

findings.citation: Griffiths, T. D. & Warren, J. D. (ref. 95); Galaburda, A. & Sanides, F. (ref. 96)
findings.claim: The review cautions that the PT should not be treated as one speech-specific module: it reports PT activation for tone sequences, music, spatial signals, visual speech, sign language, and visual motion, and notes four cytoarchitectonic fields in the region. It contrasts the authors’ sensorimotor-integration account with an alternative computational-hub account involving segregation and spectrotemporal pattern matching, allows that sensorimotor and spatial-hearing functions could coexist, and limits the proposed strongly left-dominant dorsal circuit to only part of the PT rather than general cortical auditory or PT function.
findings.evidence_text: The review notes that PT activity is not restricted to speech, that four cytoarchitectonic fields have been observed, and that the proposed left-dominant Spt circuit occupies only part of PT.
findings.laterality_localization: Area Spt is within PT and the proposed dorsal circuit is strongly left-dominant; PT as a whole is not assigned one function or laterality
findings.limitations: Review-level interpretive constraint; no seizure or epilepsy evidence is reported.

findings.phase: Speech, tonal, musical, spatial, and non-acoustic sensory or sensorimotor tasks
findings.population: Functional-imaging and cytoarchitectonic evidence reviewed by the authors; exact cohorts NOT_REPORTED
findings.source_term: planum temporale (PT) heterogeneity and competing functions

sources.source_report_limitations: The document is an opinion/review rather than a primary seizure or epilepsy study and contains no ictal, postictal, seizure-frequency, or semiology cohort. Its lesion, aphasia, functional-imaging, direct-stimulation, Wada, split-brain, and unpublished-observation statements are reported at the level supplied by the review; cited sources were not independently consulted. Many claims lack study-level denominators, numerators, effect sizes, or statistical uncertainty. The model’s within-stream organization, task dependence, hemispheric differences, compensatory mechanisms, and PT/Spt parcellation are presented as hypotheses or unresolved questions in parts of the article. No individual table-cell coordinates were promoted to findings, and no inference or normalization was performed.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Narrative opinion/review; no single study cohort, eligibility rule, comparator set, or reference standard is reported for the document as a whole. The review discusses aphasia and lesion evidence, functional MRI, direct cortical stimulation, Wada and split-brain evidence, and normal speech perception, recognition, production, and auditory-motor tasks. Cited-study sample sizes, finding denominators, and effect sizes are generally not reported in this document.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2007 Nature Reviews Neuroscience OPINION by Gregory Hickok and David Poeppel is a narrative review and proposed dual-stream model of cortical speech processing. It synthesizes lesion, neuropsychological, functional-imaging, direct-stimulation, Wada/split-brain, and speech-task evidence to distinguish speech perception, speech recognition, and speech production. Its relevance to the atlas is indirect: it provides speech-related localization and lateralization constraints, but it reports no seizure or epilepsy cohort and no seizure semiology.

sources.source_report_limitations: The document is a narrative review and does not present a unified cohort, prespecified search methods, pooled estimates, or a uniform reference standard. It repeatedly summarizes cited case reports, retrospective cohorts, EMU series, stimulation studies, and functional-imaging studies with heterogeneous definitions and ascertainment. Several percentages lack exact numerators or subgroup denominators; approximate language such as “nearly,” “about,” “most,” and “or fewer” is retained rather than converted. The review explicitly notes that scalp EEG, selective invasive coverage, propagation, and method-dependent sampling can make symptom-related network involvement difficult to distinguish from seizure onset. PDF p.7 is the reference list and publisher note; no additional source-reported semiology, localization, or lateralization claim was extracted from bibliography metadata alone.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Narrative literature review; no original study population or independent patient-level analysis is reported. The review summarizes retrospective cohorts, EMU series, case series, individual cases, electrical-stimulation and functional-neuroimaging studies, and prior reviews. Populations therefore vary by finding and include patients with epilepsy, focal or temporal/occipital epilepsy, EMU admissions, painful somatosensory seizures, abdominal epilepsy, and cited literature case collections. Exact ascertainment, subgroup denominators, and reference standards are retained only where the source reports them.
sources.source_report_summary: Hwang, Goodman, and Stevens present a narrative review of epileptic ictal pain, covering cephalic, somatosensory, and abdominal presentations, their reported frequency and semiology, associated EEG and anatomic localization, pain-network evidence, and selected treatment observations. The document is a review of cited studies and case reports rather than a new patient cohort.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a single case report without a comparator or cohort-level estimate. The source reports 12 recorded seizures but does not provide a population-level diagnostic or localization accuracy measure, formal language-dominance testing, or an independent reference standard. The abstract calls the lesion a low-grade glioma, whereas Results report an IDH-R132H-negative infiltrating III grade glioma; this terminology is preserved without reconciliation. Literature claims are cited restatements or qualitative synthesis, and cited sources were not reviewed under this source-only scope. The authors explicitly state that the available literature is insufficient to establish ictal paraphasia as a strong localizing element and call for further reliable techniques.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Single case assessed by clinical history, examination, brain MRI, video-EEG, and pathology; 12 typical seizures were recorded; no comparator or formal independent reference standard was reported, and the authors used an anatomo-electro-clinical correlation.
sources.source_report_summary: 2022 Neurocase single-patient case report describing ictal semantic/verbal and phonemic paraphasias in a 73-year-old right-handed woman with a left temporal lesion and discussing the possible lateralizing value of ictal paraphasia.

findings.claim: The authors propose that speech automatism may occur when pathological excitation does not spread to speech areas during a confusional state, and that it may arise from regions other than the temporal lobe, including occasionally leftward regions distant from the temporal lobe.
findings.evidence_text: The discussion presents failure of spread to speech areas and possible non-temporal or distant leftward origins as explanations for speech automatism.
findings.laterality_localization: Speech areas and possible non-temporal or leftward regions distant from the temporal lobe
findings.limitations: This is an untested discussion hypothesis, not a quantified localization result.
findings.locators: PDF p.5, Discussion paragraphs beginning “Speech automatism seem” and “The question of why”
findings.population: Current authors’ discussion of speech automatism; NOT_REPORTED

sources.source_report_limitations: PDF p.1 is a repository metadata cover; the scientific article occupies PDF pp.2-6 (printed pp.40-44). Seven initially collected cases were excluded for independent foci, absent laterality, or normal findings, and two left-handed patients were excluded from statistical testing. Statistical reporting is limited to P thresholds without test statistics, confidence intervals, or effect sizes. The article uses interictal EEG/lesion criteria for side and focus and does not report a separate functional language-dominance reference standard. The aphasic-fit plus speech-arrest combination was unresolved. Cited-study claims were not independently verified because those sources were outside scope.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors collected about 43 cases with ictal speech disturbances over 8 years. Interictal EEG was examined at least twice per case; laterality was defined by a spike or sharp-wave focus, unilateral dominant spike or sharp wave, or unilateral slow wave corresponding to same-region brain damage or tumor. Laterality was confirmed in 36 cases; 7 cases with independent foci, no laterality, or normal findings were excluded. The statistical report concerns 34 right-handed epileptics because 2 left-handed patients could not be tested statistically. A control pool comprised 243 right-handed patients with unilateral abnormal EEG findings, 136 left and 117 right, and was assessed by t test.
sources.source_report_summary: Kawai and Ohashi, “Ictal Speech Disturbance and Cerebral Dominance,” Studia Phonologica IX (1975), pp. 40-44; an original empirical case series examining aphasic fit, speech arrest, and speech automatism in relation to interictal-EEG laterality and localization.
