sources.source_report_limitations: The source is primarily a consensus guideline and expert review rather than a single primary patient-level study; most recommendations therefore lack a reported cohort denominator, comparator cohort, effect estimate, confidence interval, or diagnostic-accuracy statistic. The source explicitly identifies sampling bias as the main SEEG limitation and difficulty precisely localizing functional areas, particularly language areas, as another limitation. Several recommendations are labeled non-consensual, and the detailed topic chapters referenced throughout the guideline are not included in this 9-page PDF, so their supporting literature and subgroup detail were not reviewed. No source-reported left/right semiology direction, sign-level frequency table, or validated sign-specific localization/lateralization estimate is provided in this document.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The document reports a French expert workgroup drawn from centers performing more than 10 SEEG explorations per year for at least 5 years; six subgroups of 4–6 experts developed topics, and the complete workgroup graded recommendations by the RAND/UCLA 1–9 method through four rounds, with at most one deviating grade discarded. Scores of 1–3, 4–6, and 7–9 represented disagreement, unresolved, and agreement areas; overlap produced weak status, and items without consensus were labeled “non-consensual agreement.” The subgroup literature searches covered French- and English-language medical articles in PubMed and Web of Science through June 2017, with topic-specific keywords. The intended population is adults and children with drug-resistant focal epilepsy being considered for invasive presurgical SEEG, with recommendations addressing temporal, frontal, posterior, perisylvian, lesional, focal cortical dysplasia, polymicrogyria, and hypothalamic-hamartoma contexts. The guideline does not report one analyzed patient cohort, a single reference standard, or patient-level denominators for its recommendations; where relevant, non-invasive anatomo-electroclinical data, subdural exploration, conventional surgery, and the epileptogenic zone are the source's comparators or decision references.
sources.source_report_summary: This source is a French expert guideline and comprehensive review on stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) for drug-resistant focal epilepsy, presenting consensus recommendations on indications, planning, recording, interpretation, and SEEG-guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation; it is intended as a practical framework for centers using or beginning SEEG practice.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source package represented all 11 native pages with present text and renderings, and no page was unreadable or blocked. Although seizure semiology was abstracted from medical records, the article does not provide a systematic cohort-level table of individual clinical seizure manifestations; detailed semiologic and localization examples are concentrated in the figure captions. The 23-of-34 ictal-onset-zone extension result is limited to IVEEG patients with available ictal data. F001 is a cited-study restatement and remains unverified against the cited papers. The source reports no mortality outcome. MRI-detection rates, lesion distribution, histology, procedure type or extent, and seizure-outcome results were not promoted to findings because they are outside the requested semiology/localization boundary.
sources.source_report_methods_population:
The study included consecutive children with focal epilepsy and MRI-defined BOSD evaluated at The Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto between January 2007 and July 2019; patients with less than 1 year of postsurgical follow-up were excluded. Forty-one children were included. Medical-record data included seizure semiology, seizure frequency, age at seizure onset, antiseizure medications, and comorbidities. Mean age at surgery was 9.7 years (SD 4.5), 29 patients were male (70.7%), and mean age at seizure onset was 4.7 years (SD 3.5). Table 1 reported daily seizures in 30 of 41 patients (73.2%), weekly seizures in 9 (22.0%), monthly seizures in 1 (2.4%), yearly seizures in 1 (2.4%), and a history of focal status epilepticus requiring hospitalization in 8 (19.5%); these are cohort descriptors, not separate findings here.

Presurgical evaluation included scalp video EEG, MEG, FDG-PET, and invasive video EEG when indicated. Thirty-seven patients underwent IVEEG, and 34 had available ictal data. Forty patients underwent MEG. MRI context included left-sided lesions in 23 of 41 patients (56.1%) and right-sided lesions in 18 (43.9%); lesion distributions were frontal 21 (51.2%), parietal 6 (14.6%), temporal 2 (4.9%), insular 4 (9.8%), and pre- or postcentral 8 (19.5%). These lesion-distribution and treatment details are contextual only and are not findings in this report.
sources.source_report_summary: Jain et al., “Surgical outcomes in children with bottom-of-sulcus dysplasia and drug-resistant epilepsy: a retrospective cohort study,” is an original retrospective cohort study of children with radiologically defined BOSD and focal epilepsy undergoing epilepsy-surgery evaluation and treatment. The source is primarily a surgery/outcome study; the findings below retain only source-reported seizure manifestations and direct electrophysiological localization or laterality claims. The cohort context included 32 of 41 children seizure free after a mean 4.3 years of follow-up; this outcome is not treated as a finding below. No mortality outcome is reported.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review; cited cohorts, stimulation series, case reports, and figure data are not one harmonized population. Several source statements are qualitative (“most,” “common,” “suggestive,” or “poorly”) and have no denominator. Some cited percentages lack numerators or denominators. Insular, operculo-insular, insulo-opercular, and extrainsular spread are source-distinct terms and are not collapsed. Figure 8 contains a single-case presurgery/postsurgery interictal HRV table (NNM, SDNN, RMSSD, SDSD, HF, LF, and LF/HF means, standard deviations, and comparison p values); those standalone table cells are retained only as compact context and are not individual atlas findings or statistic entries. The source’s generic anatomy organization counts (7 subdivisions, 5 gyri, 4 functional areas) are likewise retained only in Source terminology and not as a standalone seizure finding. Directly sign-attached autonomic observations, stimulation responses, seizure-localization/lateralization results, and propagation findings remain in the Findings list. No source-native claim is mapped to a Lüders or ILAE category, and no anatomy synonym or Brodmann equivalence is inferred.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a multi-author narrative review with educational sections and cited-study restatements rather than a single primary cohort. Denominators therefore belong to the cited series named in each finding. The review includes insular stimulation series, noninvasive-test series, SEEG observations, and case reports. Source-native distinctions between insular, operculo-insular, insulo-opercular, extrainsular, temporal-like, and frontal-like are preserved.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2019 Epilepsy Currents review discusses insular and operculo-insular epilepsy, including source-native semiology, propagation patterns, electrical-stimulation responses, noninvasive test performance, SEEG localization, and selected autonomic/SUDEP case observations. Findings below retain only direct seizure-sign, seizure-phase, localization, lateralization, source-definition, or directly linked statistic evidence. General surgical treatment, complication, demographic, publication, and review-method statements are not individual findings.

sources.source_report_limitations: The study is retrospective and from a single tertiary hospital in the UK, so semiology details could not be probed and the cohort may not represent people who did not proceed to surgery. Seizure chronology was not analyzed beyond initial versus subsequent manifestations because the literature underpinning SVT lacked chronological sequence. The final resection site was used as a surrogate for the seizure-onset zone/EZ; the source notes that a symptomatogenic network may be distant from seizure onset. SVT predictions spanning many gyri could favor larger resection volumes, and combined orbitofrontal, frontomedial, dorsolateral, and precentral resections reduce analysis granularity. Lesional and non-lesional cases were considered together, age-dependent semiology was not investigated in this adult service, and all seizure outcomes were self-reported and susceptible to reporting bias. The seven-page package contains the main PDF only; the article refers to Supplementary Tables 1-4, including chronological sequences, individual-semiology details, and feature-specific SVT results, but those supplementary tables were not represented in the supplied package. The cited-study restatements above were not verified against their cited targets.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Electronic records were reviewed for all individuals who underwent frontal lobe epilepsy surgery at the National Hospital for Neurology & Neurosurgery, London, UK, between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2020; 61 individuals were included after excluding operations performed primarily for reasons other than epilepsy. All had presurgical multidisciplinary review after scalp video-EEG telemetry, neuropsychology and neuropsychiatry assessment, MRI, and, in selected cases, FDG-PET, ictal SPECT, or intracranial EEG. Ictal semiology and its evolution came from video-EEG telemetry reports and multidisciplinary-team summaries, were documented in a predetermined format, and were independently categorized by two investigators with discrepancies resolved by discussion. Surgical records and postoperative MRI identified resection site and extent; the final resection site was the presumed EZ surrogate, and only the first resection was retained for the one individual with more than one procedure. At 12 months, outcomes came from a prospective epilepsy-surgery database and were classified with the ILAE surgery outcome scale. The cohort had median age at surgery 33.9 years (IQR 28.1-43.1) and median epilepsy duration 21.9 years (IQR 21.3-25.1); 43/61 (70%) had abnormal MRI, including 35 (57%) focal and 8 (13%) diffuse abnormalities, while 18 had normal MRI; 41/61 (67%) underwent intracranial EEG. Operations included 52/61 (85%) cortical resections and 9/61 (15%) lesionectomies; resections were left-sided in 32/61 (53%) and right-sided in 29/61 (47%), with orbitofrontal, frontomedial, dorsolateral, frontocentral, and combined extensive resections reported in Table 1. Twenty-three individuals (38%) had anterior cingulate extension and one had insular extension.
sources.source_report_summary: Original retrospective cohort study evaluating how initial and combined ictal seizure semiology, processed through a Semiology Visualisation Tool (SVT), corresponded with the presumed epileptogenic zone represented by the final resection site in adults who underwent frontal lobe epilepsy surgery at a London tertiary centre from 2011 through 2020. The source also reports 12-month postsurgical seizure outcomes and discusses the limits of semiology-only localization and lateralization.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review, not an original cohort or systematic quantitative synthesis. Most atlas-relevant rows are review syntheses, reproduced/adapted tables, or cited-study restatements; cited sources were not separately authorized or reviewed here and remain unverified cited restatements. The review often reports qualitative terms such as “strong”, “great”, “most commonly”, “almost always”, or “poor” without denominators or uncertainty intervals. Several table rows provide symptomatogenic zones and laterality without a population, phase-specific sample, comparator, or quantitative estimate. The source notes that the duration of postictal dysphasia is unclear and that there is no specific consensus guidance for ictal testing in suspected PNES. No page was unreadable, and no required source claim was blocked from representation.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors report a PubMed literature review using the search terms “seizure”, “ictal”, “postictal”, “testing”, “examination”, and “interview”, followed by selection of relevant literature and references for a narrative review. The intended setting is an epilepsy long-term monitoring unit with video-EEG and ictal/postictal bedside testing. The source contains no single original cohort, unified analysis population, or uniform reference standard; cited populations and analysis units vary and are retained at the finding level when reported. Cited evidence includes video-EEG seizure series, temporal-lobe cohorts, stereo-EEG language observations, electrical cortical stimulation studies, and PNES diagnostic studies. Cohort demographics, lesion prevalence, etiology, surgery outcomes, and mortality outcomes are not reported as a unified study dataset. The review reports contextual testing metrics, including 27% of seizures assessed within 30 seconds and 50% unassessed in one UK study, and describes PNES comorbidity and induction literature; these are not treated as atlas findings.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2019 article by Michael Owen Kinney, Stjepana Kovac, and Beate Diehl is a narrative review and practical guide to the proposed International League Against Epilepsy-European Epilepsy Monitoring Unit Association structured ictal-postictal testing battery during video-EEG long-term monitoring. It addresses consciousness, language, motor, sensory, visual, and psychogenic nonepileptic seizure (PNES) assessment, with the stated aim of improving diagnostic, localization, and lateralization yield. The article is a review rather than a single original patient cohort; its atlas-relevant claims include review-authored synthesis, reproduced/adapted summary tables, and restatements of cited studies.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source is fully represented and readable, with no blocked pages. It reports two aggregate laterality values that do not reconcile: the summary gives 35/39, while the printed subgroup values are 10/12, 7/8, and 17/18. Table 1 also prints Group II joint version/ATLP categories whose numerators sum to 31 despite a denominator of 26, and prints 2/26 (7.6%) for Group II patients with ATLP in every GTC seizure; these values are retained without correction. Six seizures and two patients were excluded for poor video quality. The paper includes small anecdotal observations, cited-study restatements, and an explicitly unconfirmed focal-origin hypothesis; cited sources were not separately reviewed. The source does not always identify whether timing/duration analyses use patients or seizures.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Group I comprised 54 patients with partial epilepsy successfully treated by temporal-lobe resection (n=34) or extratemporal resection (n=20: 14 frontal, 3 parietal, 3 occipital); 238 seizures were recorded, including 59 secondarily generalized seizures from 31 patients. Surgical success was complete seizure freedom or >90% seizure reduction at 1 year. Group II comprised 28 prospectively collected patients with 70 GTC or generalized clonic seizures over 7 months; 6 seizures and 2 patients were excluded for inadequate video visualization of both upper limbs, leaving 64 seizures from 26 patients, including 23 with focal epilepsy and 3 with symptomatic generalized epilepsy. Three observers reviewed seizures independently while blinded to ictal EEG side and other clinical data. Version was defined as forced, sustained, unnatural eye and/or head deviation to one side; ATLP was assessed against version using interobserver kappa, and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests compared ATLP timing and duration between temporal-lobe epilepsy (TLE) and extratemporal epilepsy (XTLE).
sources.source_report_summary: Original empirical clinical research paper: Kotagal et al., “Lateralizing Value of Asymmetric Tonic Limb Posturing Observed in Secondarily Generalized Tonic-Clonic Seizures,” Epilepsia 41(4):457-462, 2000. It evaluates asymmetric tonic limb posturing (ATLP, also called the “Figure 4 Sign”) as a lateralizing sign in secondarily generalized tonic-clonic (GTC) seizures, compares it with head/eye version, describes associated seizure evolution, and reports a small number of anecdotal observations.

sources.source_report_limitations:
The source has restricted spatial sampling because electrode locations were selected for clinical care and the surgical hypothesis; sampled and unsampled regions may be simultaneously involved during propagation. The quantitative high-gamma analysis is limited to the 20-patient/39-ICA-seizure subset with all listed regions sampled, and the smaller EZ subgroup produces wide confidence intervals. The source does not report a general hemispheric laterality result; right- and left-sided localization appears only in the two illustrative figure cases.

The source references supplementary material on PDF page 10, but no supplementary file is present in the locked 23-page package; no supplementary claims were extracted. Table 2 does not consistently disclose the analysis unit for its EZ denominators or for the timing means, and the 30/30 and 28/30 mesial-temporal involvement denominators do not match the 35/81 mesial-temporal ICA prevalence without an explanation. Figure 3 does not print denominators and its EZ distribution is not directly reconcilable with the Table 2 region-specific counts. The source prints an apparent percentage inconsistency for the Engel class I EZ distribution (5/30 reported as 1.7% for occipital) and uses z >= 4 in the Methods/Results but z > 4 in the Figure 4 caption; neither was silently corrected. These ambiguities remain source-faithful and do not authorize recalculation.
sources.source_report_methods_population:
The investigators prospectively enrolled 85 consecutive adult persons with epilepsy undergoing standard-of-care SEEG evaluation in an epilepsy monitoring unit from June 2016 through April 2023. They prospectively collected 220 seizures; 39 seizures in 13 patients were excluded because breathing signals were unreliable or artifactual. The analyzed population was 179 seizures in 72 patients with reliable artifact-free respiratory signals. Real-time SEEG, video, thoracic and abdominal respiratory inductance plethysmography, oxygen saturation, heart rate, and four-channel EKG were obtained simultaneously. The analyzed cohort included 1,196 intracranial depth electrodes (mean 16.6 +/- 3.0 per patient); 55 seizures in 23 patients had ICA.

All seizures were classified by seizure onset zone (SOZ), defined by the source as the cortical area from which seizures start. The source separately defined the epileptogenic zone (EZ) as the region resected to produce seizure freedom; only patients who underwent resective surgery or laser interstitial thermal therapy and had Engel class I outcome with at least six months of follow-up were classified for EZ determination. Of 31 Engel class I patients, 30 had at least six months of follow-up (mean 22.8 months +/- SD 13.1, range 6-50) and one did not. The source reports separate SOZ and EZ analyses and does not authorize conversion between their patient- and seizure-level denominators. A high-gamma analysis used a subset of 20 patients with 39 ICA seizures whose SEEG implantation sampled all regions of breathing interest; the early-onset subgroup contained 27 seizures in 13 patients and the late-onset subgroup 12 seizures in seven patients.

Predictive associations were assessed with separate simple logistic-regression models; statistically significant semiologic signs were also entered as one additional predictor with ICA in multiple logistic regression. Fisher's exact test assessed ICA presence and mesial temporal sclerosis (MTS). The source used two-sided p < 0.05 for statistical significance, made no multiple-comparison correction because the study was exploratory, and treated z >= 4 as significant for the quantitative gamma analysis.
sources.source_report_summary: Primary empirical intracranial study published in Annals of Neurology in 2024 (95(5):998-1008; doi:10.1002/ana.26888), assessing the semiologic and localizational value of ictal central apnea (ICA) in medically refractory focal epilepsy during prospective stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) evaluation with simultaneous multimodal cardiorespiratory monitoring. The report combines seizure-level qualitative and logistic-regression analyses with a quantitatively analyzed high-gamma SEEG subset. Native pages 1-2 are repository front matter for the same source; the manuscript begins on page 3 and includes figures and tables through page 23.

sources.source_report_limitations: All native pages 1–93 were reviewed; the package reported 60 pages without extractable text, and each of those rendered PNGs was inspected. Text-bearing pages were read from the locked per-page text files, with visual inspection used for figures, tables, screenshots, diagrams, layout, and extraction uncertainty. No page was blocked. The deck contains repeated educational diagrams and article screenshots with heterogeneous citation detail; figures without a source-native caption or interpretable claim were not promoted to findings. Quantitative values remain tied to their displayed study, subgroup, procedure, patient, or contact denominator; missing denominators, unresolved table cells, and presenter thresholds were not reconstructed or promoted into repository rules.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Document type: educational slide deck. No source-wide cohort, prospective protocol, sampling frame, or unified analysis population is reported. The deck combines heterogeneous cited studies, article screenshots, modality tables, conceptual diagrams, and individual cases. Study-specific populations, analysis units, denominators, comparators, and follow-up intervals are retained only where stated on the relevant slide; no source-wide denominator is inferred.
sources.source_report_summary: This is a 93-page educational slide deck titled “Stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG)” by Pramote Laoprasert, M.D. It presents SEEG as an anatomo-electro-clinical method for testing individualized hypotheses and examining seizure onset and propagation, with definitions, cited literature summaries, MRI-negative epilepsy material, and selected electroclinical/SEEG examples. It is not a unified presenter primary-cohort report; study-specific results, presenter synthesis, educational statements, and case observations are kept distinct below.

findings.claim: The authors propose classifying epilepsy with five independent dimensions—epileptogenic-zone localization, seizure semiology, etiology, seizure frequency, and related medical conditions—so that patients can be classified at an initial encounter and the working hypothesis can become more precise as additional clinical information becomes available.
findings.evidence_text: The source states that the five dimensions are localization of the epileptogenic zone, seizure semiology, etiology, seizure frequency, and related medical conditions, and that clinical-test information is translated into a working hypothesis that can be refined.
findings.laterality_localization: Dimension 1 records epileptogenic-zone localization; the proposal does not state a laterality direction in this general framework claim
findings.limitations: The proposal is conceptual and does not report empirical performance, diagnostic accuracy, or outcome validation for the five-dimensional format.
findings.locators: PDF p.1, Abstract; PDF p.2, Patient-oriented epilepsy classification and Table 1; PDF p.7, Independence of dimensions and Independence from contemporary diagnostic tools; PDF p.8, Applicable to all patients and Conclusion
findings.phase: Initial clinical classification with later refinement as information accrues
findings.population: Patients with epilepsy; framework-level proposal with no analyzed cohort

findings.citation: Rosenow and Luders 2001 (definition of the epileptogenic zone)
findings.claim: The source defines focal localization as an EZ within one cerebral lobe, multilobar localization as one EZ involving two or more contiguous unilateral lobes, hemispheric localization as an EZ covering most or all of one hemisphere, multifocal localization as more than one independent non-adjacent EZ, and generalized localization as diffusely epileptogenic cortex; all terms except generalized can be assigned to the side of the EZ, such as left or right.
findings.evidence_text: The source describes focal, multilobar, hemispheric, multifocal, and generalized EZ categories and states that all terms except generalized can be attributed to the side of the EZ, for example left or right.
findings.laterality_localization: Anatomical extent categories are focal within one lobe, multilobar across contiguous unilateral lobes, hemispheric across most or all of one hemisphere, multifocal across independent non-adjacent EZs, or generalized diffuse cortex; source permits left/right assignment except for generalized
findings.limitations: The source emphasizes that the EZ is a time-specific working hypothesis influenced by available clinical information, diagnostic techniques, and physician experience; it does not establish a validated localization rule from semiology alone.

findings.phase: Diagnostic classification and subsequent refinement with additional information
findings.population: Patients with epilepsy to whom the localization dimension is applied; no cohort
findings.source_term: epileptogenic zone (EZ); focal, multilobar, hemispheric, multifocal, generalized

sources.source_report_limitations: The article is a proposal, not a primary semiology or localization study. It reports no cohort-level denominators, diagnostic accuracy, confidence intervals, sensitivity/specificity, or statistical tests for the proposed dimensions or the illustrative signs. The source describes the EZ as a time-specific working hypothesis: the resection-plus-seizure-freedom standard is not applicable to most patients at diagnosis, and available tests and clinician experience affect precision. The authors state that the approach is oriented toward focal epilepsy and may be less practical for generalized and childhood epilepsies, where a syndrome approach may be useful in selected cases. The page images are the authoritative representation because all fresh page-text files are empty; no page was unreadable.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a proposal and narrative synthesis, not a primary empirical study. The authors review prior classification approaches, define the five dimensions, provide tables and conceptual figures, and demonstrate the proposed format with illustrative profiles. The framework is stated to apply to patients with epilepsy, defined here as at least two spontaneous epileptic seizures; for patients with unclear epileptic or nonepileptic events, the source recommends the term paroxysmal event. Clinical history, seizure semiology, EEG, MRI, other diagnostic studies, and etiologic information are translated into a best available working classification that can be refined as information accrues. No formal study cohort, sampling method, reference standard, comparator cohort, or statistical analysis is reported.
sources.source_report_summary: Conceptual proposal article presenting a five-dimensional, patient-oriented epilepsy classification as an alternative to a syndrome-oriented approach. Its atlas-relevant contribution is a source-defined separation of epileptogenic-zone localization, seizure semiology, etiology, seizure frequency, and related medical information, plus illustrative longitudinal and profile-level examples. It contains no primary cohort analysis of semiology, localization, or lateralization; the patient examples are educational illustrations, and the prevalence percentages are restatements attributed to cited studies.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a subjective, non-exhaustive narrative review rather than a systematic review or pooled analysis. The cited evidence is heterogeneous and often consists of small retrospective series, selected surgical cohorts, or case reports with mixed reference standards; several percentages lack underlying counts, language dominance is not uniformly tested, and some signs may reflect seizure propagation rather than onset. No semiological sign is presented as 100% certain because the symptomatogenic and epileptogenic zones may differ. The authors further warn about atypical functional representation with large lesions, focal-appearing signs in generalized epilepsy, observer-training effects, and bias when multiple signs coexist; pages 14-17 are bibliography only.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a narrative review with a subjective selection of semiological features. The summarized populations vary across epilepsy monitoring units, focal epilepsy and temporal/frontal/occipital lobe epilepsy cohorts, infants, surgical series, case reports, and stimulation or lesion studies. Reference standards include video/EEG, EEG, MRI, CT, PET, SPECT, Wada testing, presurgical evaluation, seizure freedom or seizure reduction after surgery, and combinations of these; the source frequently states when the standard was incomplete or unavailable.
sources.source_report_summary: Loddenkemper and Kotagal, Epilepsy & Behavior 7 (2005) 1-17, is a narrative review of semiological signs and symptoms that may lateralize or localize focal epileptic seizures for presurgical evaluation. It summarizes prior case series, observational studies, case reports, literature reviews, surgical outcomes, electrophysiology, imaging, cortical stimulation, and language testing; it does not present one common cohort or a pooled analysis.

sources.source_report_limitations: All 8 pages had present fresh text and represented PNG renderings; no page was blocked. This methods/classification article supplies source-native definitions, classification rules, examples, and qualitative localization/lateralization relationships, but no empirical cohort, denominator, diagnostic-performance analysis, formal validation statistics, or quantitative prevalence estimates. The localizing statements are explicitly qualified in places by “suggests,” “probably,” “most probably,” or “usually.” The reference list was treated as bibliography, not as independent source evidence, and no cited study was re-reviewed under this report.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a classification/methods article rather than a cohort study. The proposed classification is based on semiology reported by the patient or observers or observed during video monitoring; the article gives definitions, examples, and clinical-application rationale. No study cohort, eligibility criteria, analysis population, reference standard, diagnostic accuracy analysis, or comparative denominator is reported. The authors state that the system had been tested in selected epilepsy centers for more than 10 years, without presenting a validation cohort or performance estimates in this report.
sources.source_report_summary: Luders et al., “Semiological Seizure Classification,” Epilepsia 1998;39:1006-1013, is a special-article proposal for a seizure classification based exclusively on ictal semiology. It separates seizure semiology from electroclinical syndrome classification, preserves source-native seizure components and their evolution, and introduces somatotopic and hemispheric modifiers for more precise description. The article reports that the present version or variants had been used in daily practice for more than 10 years at selected epilepsy centers, but it is not an empirical outcome study.

findings.claim: The authors organize ictal symptoms into four spheres—sensorial, consciousness, autonomic, and motor—and state that a seizure involving more than one sphere is classified according to its predominant clinical manifestation.
findings.evidence_text: Ictal symptoms can arise from four “spheres”; loss of awareness with slight eye blinking is classified as dialeptic rather than motor because consciousness predominates.

findings.claim: Auras consist exclusively of subjective ictal symptoms, usually occur at the beginning of a seizure, are generally brief, and may occur in isolation; their epileptic nature can be documented objectively when they consistently evolve into a dialeptic or motor seizure or when EEG monitoring shows an EEG seizure pattern during the aura.
findings.evidence_text: Auras are exclusively subjective symptoms and are generally brief; objective epileptic documentation is linked to evolution or an EEG seizure pattern.
findings.laterality_localization: NOT_APPLICABLE
findings.limitations: No frequency, cohort, or duration distribution is reported

findings.population: NOT_REPORTED

findings.claim: Somatosensory auras are abnormal somatosensory sensations or paresthesias limited to a clearly defined somatosensory region of the body; poorly localized or vague sensations are classified only as unclassifiable auras.
findings.evidence_text: Somatosensory sensations are classified as this aura type only when limited to a clearly defined somatosensory region.

findings.claim: Isolated visual hallucinations or illusions are visual auras; when visual phenomena occur with complex perceptual distortions they remain visual only if clearly predominant for a significant part of the aura, otherwise they are psychic auras, while poorly defined blurry vision is unclassifiable.

findings.claim: Dialeptic seizure is the authors’ term for a seizure whose predominant manifestation is altered consciousness, defined for this purpose as unresponsiveness or decreased responsiveness not caused by motor alterations; complete or partial amnesia for the episode is necessary, and the concept is independent of associated ictal or interictal EEG changes.

findings.claim: Bilateral asymmetric denotes bilateral symptoms with significant asymmetry and suggests focal epilepsy; generalized denotes widespread manifestations with approximately equal involvement of both sides and distal and proximal segments; axial denotes predominant trunk and proximal-extremity involvement, and the source cautions that focal epilepsies may have axial or generalized seizures and generalized epilepsies may have focal elements.

findings.claim: The authors distinguish classification of seizure semiology from classification of the epileptic syndrome: the syndrome requires semiological type plus interictal and ictal EEG, functional and anatomic neuroimaging, seizure evolution, neurological examination, and other clinical information; because many syndromes may share the same semiological seizure types, a dialeptic seizure alone does not distinguish generalized absence epilepsy from a focal syndrome with different treatment implications.
findings.evidence_text: Establishing a dialeptic seizure does not by itself identify generalized absence epilepsy versus a focal epileptic syndrome.
findings.laterality_localization: Source examples include left mesial temporal and right frontal syndromes; no general side rule beyond the separate hemispheric modifier
findings.limitations: Source-authored conceptual and illustrative statement; cited editorial and treatment implications were not independently reviewed

sources.source_report_limitations: This Special Article is a source-authored classification proposal and explanation rather than a defined empirical study. It reports no cohort size, denominators, numerators, inferential statistics, confidence intervals, or diagnostic-performance estimates. Qualifiers such as “usually,” “frequently,” “most probably,” “strongly suggests,” “only a few,” and “in most patients” are preserved as source-native uncertainty but are not quantified. Localization and lateralization statements are conceptual rules, proposed anatomical relations, or conditional examples; they do not establish accuracy or generalizability. The cited-study restatement in F002 and the cited editorial context in F040 were not independently verified because they are outside the authorized source package.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors describe a classification based exclusively on ictal seizure semiology as reported by patients or observers or analyzed during video monitoring. EEG and other test results do not influence the semiological classification, although EEG may be used to distinguish epileptic from nonepileptic paroxysmal events. The authors state that the classification had been tested for more than 10 years in selected epilepsy centers and that the present version or variants had been used in daily practice for more than 10 years, without reporting a defined cohort, eligibility criteria, sample size, or evaluation design.
sources.source_report_summary: Lüders et al., “Semiological Seizure Classification,” Epilepsia 1998;39:1006-1013, is a Special Article proposing and explaining a semiology-only semiological seizure classification (SSC), its source-native seizure categories, somatotopic and hemispheric modifiers, and seizure-sequence notation. It is not an empirical cohort report: no defined study population, sample size, numerator/denominator, or inferential statistical analysis is reported.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a retrospective study of a selected, medically intractable unilateral TLE population undergoing SEEG, not an unselected seizure cohort. The source states that many patients with clear left lateral temporal epilepsy in the language-dominant hemisphere did not proceed to SEEG, whereas right lateral temporal cases were selected, limiting interpretation of side distributions. SEEG sampling carries a theoretical risk of sampling error, although the authors state that the protocol systematically explored relevant temporal structures and that the discharge preceded the first clinical sign. Some prose percentages or p values conflict with displayed tables and are retained in the affected findings: left-L temporal epilepsy is 46.2% in prose versus 42.6% in Table 1; early ML upper-limb elementary automatisms are 36.9% in prose versus 38.9% in Table 4; and early verbal automatisms have p=0.004 in prose versus p=0.028 in Table 4. Several side-specific prose percentages lack counts or denominators. The source’s cited-study restatements were not verified against the cited publications. No unreported counts, denominators, statistics, or sign mappings were inferred.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The study retrospectively evaluated 55 patients with medically intractable unilateral temporal lobe epilepsy selected from 132 consecutive surgical-evaluation patients seen in Rennes (1994–1997) and Marseille (1997–2001). A total of 187 SEEG-recorded seizures were analyzed, with a reported mean of 3.4 seizures per patient. Clinical variables included initial ictal subjective symptoms, early and late ictal signs, loss of contact, seizure duration, and postictal deficits. Clinical data were acquired during video-SEEG testing and retrospectively reviewed by two independent investigators; seizure onset and termination were determined from the earliest and latest ictal SEEG changes. Group comparisons used Pearson’s chi-square or Fisher’s exact test, with two-sided p<0.05 considered significant. The tabulated percentages use patient subgroup sizes M=24, ML=18, and L=13 unless otherwise stated.
sources.source_report_summary: Maillard et al. (2004), “Semiologic and Electrophysiologic Correlations in Temporal Lobe Seizure Subtypes,” is an original retrospective empirical study of stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG)-recorded temporal lobe seizures. It examines whether ictal semiology differs according to the anatomic distribution of the initial fast tonic discharge in medial, lateral, and medial-lateral temporal structures. The source contributes patient-level semiologic comparisons, phase-specific findings, and selected laterality/localization observations relevant to temporal lobe seizure interpretation.

findings.claim: The source excluded figure of 4 and hand dystonia (ictal dystonia) from sequence analysis because their PPVs were below the source-defined reliability threshold, retained 38 of the 47 representative seizures with at least two reliable motor signs, and identified version, unilateral tonic posturing, M2e, unilateral clonic seizure, asymmetric clonic ending, and Todd's paralysis as reliable signs.
findings.evidence_text: The Summary says sequences with PPV ≥80% were analyzed, whereas Methods defines reliable signs as PPV >80% and says PPV ≤80% signs were excluded; Results states that 9 seizures were excluded and 38 remained.
findings.laterality_localization: reliable signs were selected for their ability to predict the EZ side; source-defined reliable directions are sign-specific and primarily contralateral, with asymmetric clonic ending directed ipsilaterally
findings.limitations: The threshold wording is retained exactly as a source ambiguity and is not converted into a general review rule.

findings.claim: Among the 38 sequence seizures, version was the first motor sign in 29/38; among those 29 version-first seizures, M2e followed in 15/29 and tonic posturing in 7/29, which the authors combine as version followed by a tonic seizure in 22/29 because they treat M2e as a special tonic form. One seizure had simultaneous version and tonic posturing as the first sign followed by secondary generalization and asymmetric clonic ending; three of the remaining non-version-first seizures showed version plus tonic activity in a different order; in total 33/38 showed version plus tonic activity in variable order. Version was absent in 5/38, four seizures started with tonic activity and ended with asymmetric clonic ending, three of those lateralized the EZ correctly, and one M2e-to-clonic sequence lateralized the EZ correctly.
findings.evidence_text: Version was the most common initial sign, usually followed by M2e and/or tonic posturing; the manuscript reports 29/38 version-first seizures and 22/29 version-to-tonic progressions when M2e is included as tonic.
findings.laterality_localization: sequence order and sign combinations are described relative to the EZ side; the correctly lateralized examples follow the source-defined sign directions
findings.limitations: The manuscript reports both seizure-based and patient-based labels for this subset and does not resolve the 3/9 versus 4/9 non-version-first description.

findings.claim: Of the 38 seizures with at least two reliable signs, 32 had signs consistently lateralizing the EZ, six had a mixture of signs pointing to either hemisphere, five of those six still had at least two consistent signs and only one contradictory sign, and one seizure had two contradictory signs. In all 37 seizures with at least two consistent signs, a combination of two or more of version, clonic, tonic, M2e, asymmetric clonic, or Todd's signs, when in agreement, had a PPV of 100% and lateralized the EZ to the contralateral hemisphere.
findings.evidence_text: The source states that all 37 seizures with two or more consistent signs had a 100% PPV for contralateral EZ lateralization.
findings.laterality_localization: agreeing combinations predicted the EZ in the contralateral hemisphere
findings.limitations: The source reports no confidence interval or independent validation set for the 100% PPV statement.

findings.citation: Wyllie E, Lüders HO, Morris HH et al. The lateralizing significance of versive head and eye movements during epileptic seizures. Neurology 1986;36:606–11 (ref. 6); Kernan JC, Devinsky O, Luciano DJ et al. Lateralizing significance of head and eye deviation in secondary generalized tonic clonic seizures. Neurology 1993 Jul;43(7):1308–10 (ref. 19); Chee MW, Kotagal P, Van Ness PC et al. Lateralizing signs in intractable partial epilepsy: blinded multiple-observer analysis. Neurology 1993 Dec;43(12):2519–25 (ref. 20)
findings.claim: The current paper reports that defined versive head and eye deviation lateralized the EZ to the contralateral hemisphere, describes a value above 90% when version occurred within 10 seconds or less before motor generalization, and reports 100% contralateral lateralization under the cited conditions of neck extension and late ipsiversion after the end of a generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
findings.evidence_text: The source attributes a contralateral value above 90% to version within 10 seconds of generalization and reports a 100% value for the cited neck-extension and late-ipsiversion conditions.
findings.laterality_localization: Contralateral hemisphere relative to the EZ
findings.limitations: This is a restatement by the current paper and was not verified against the cited studies in this review; denominators are not supplied.
findings.locators: PDF p.7, Version definition and cited value; PDF p.13, discussion of version; PDF p.14, discussion of cited version conditions
findings.phase: Version within 10 seconds before motor generalization; late ipsiversion after generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the cited condition
findings.population: Cited-study populations as summarized in the current paper; NOT_REPORTED

findings.citation: Ajmone-Marsan C, Ralston BL. The Epileptic Seizure. A Clinical –electrographic Analysis of Metrazol Attacks. Charles Thomas. Publisher, 1957 (ref. 22)
findings.claim: The current paper attributes an excellent or very strong contralateral lateralizing value for M2e to the definition described by Ajmone-Marsan, in which one arm is elevated with no or late involvement of the opposite arm.
findings.evidence_text: The paper states that, according to Ajmone Marsan, M2e had an excellent lateralizing value pointing to the contralateral hemisphere.

findings.limitations: This is a cited-study restatement not independently verified here, and the current source does not provide the cited denominator.

findings.citation: Kotagal P, Bleasel A, Geller E et al. Lateralizing value in asymmetric tonic limb posturing observed in secondarily generalized tonic clonic seizures. Epilepsia 41:457–462, 2000 (ref. 7)
findings.claim: The current paper reports that figure of 4 has been described as having approximately 90% contralateral lateralizing value and attributes to the original Kotagal report the rule that the initial tonic arm extension is the component to use because a later figure of 4 may appear on the opposite side.
findings.evidence_text: The source says the initial figure of 4 is the component that lateralizes the EZ correctly because a later posture may appear on the opposite side.

findings.limitations: This is a restatement of the cited Kotagal report; the current source notes that strict use of the definition in subsequent studies is unclear.

findings.claim: The current paper reports that ictal dystonia, as described in the cited literature, almost always lateralizes to the contralateral hemisphere in temporal lobe epilepsy, and that Rusu et al. described the earliest and/or most marked dystonic posturing as contralateral to the epileptogenic focus, mainly involving the hand.
findings.evidence_text: The source contrasts the cited near-contralateral dystonia literature with its own lower PPV and notes that its broader pre-generalization definition may explain the difference.

findings.population: Temporal lobe epilepsy populations in the cited reports as summarized in the current paper; exact cited denominators NOT_REPORTED

sources.source_report_limitations:
This was a retrospective presurgical EMU study in a selected cohort with an expert-panel EZ reference standard based on concordant presurgical investigations; all included patients had reached evaluation for possible surgery. Most participants were adults, the youngest was 12 years old, and the authors state that results may not apply to neonates and toddlers. One representative seizure per patient was selected rather than analyzing every captured seizure, and the selection sought to reflect habitual seizure components.

Face tonic and clonic signs were excluded from sequence analysis because of camera angle, resolution, and face-position limitations. Figure of 4 had a modest inter-rater Kappa and difficult lateralization; ictal dystonia had the lowest inter-rater reliability. Todd's paralysis was often identified retrospectively from video or an apparent inability to move one side rather than by an active postictal strength examination, so short or mild cases could be missed and a wrong-sided assessment could be included. The manuscript also states that postictal coma can delay detection.

The source alternates PPV ≥80% and PPV >80% as the reliability threshold and reports both PPV ≤80% exclusion and >80% inclusion language; this report does not choose between them. Results describe three non-version-first seizures with version plus tonic activity in a different order, whereas the Discussion describes version as second in 4/9 non-version-first seizures. Table 3 visually prints a one-patient V→M2e+C→T row with temporal and extra-temporal cells both 0; the displayed cells therefore do not fully reconcile to the stated 30-patient cohort. These source ambiguities are retained without imputation or methodological reinterpretation.
sources.source_report_methods_population:
The authors screened 1,970 patients admitted to adult and pediatric epilepsy monitoring units at University Hospitals of Case Medical Center, Cleveland, Ohio, from 2009 through 2014; 236 had a documented secondarily generalized motor seizure. Inclusion required focal epilepsy, a video-captured seizure manifesting at least two defined motor signs, and evolution to a generalized motor seizure. Exclusions were more than one or an ill-defined EZ, focal motor signs in generalized epilepsy, or no secondary generalization during EMU monitoring. The final cohort was 47 patients: 26 with temporal lobe epilepsy, 13 with frontal lobe epilepsy, and 8 with other epilepsy types (1 parietal, 2 parieto-occipital, 3 hemispheric, 1 fronto-temporal, and 1 central).

One representative seizure per patient was selected from the available video and history to reflect the patient's habitual seizure components; the face, trunk, and all limbs were visible in the selected recordings. Three investigators independently reviewed the videos while blinded to all clinical and electrographic data; a motor component was accepted when at least two readers agreed, and Fleiss Kappa quantified inter-observer agreement. The study's sign and sequence analyses therefore use one representative seizure per patient, although the manuscript alternates “patients” and “seizures” for some subset descriptions.

EZ localization and lateralization were based on extensive presurgical evaluation including surface and/or invasive EEG, available MRI, PET, and SPECT, followed by presentation at a weekly patient-management conference where an expert panel agreed on each EZ using concordance across modalities; the authors call this their gold standard. The analysis was restricted to simple motor seizures and excluded complex motor seizures such as automatisms. Sequence analysis retained signs meeting the source's “reliable” PPV criterion and required at least two reliable signs; the source uses both PPV ≥80% and PPV >80% wording, documented below without resolving the discrepancy.
sources.source_report_summary: This accepted author manuscript is a full-length original retrospective study, accepted 23-Dec-2015, titled “Ictal Motor Sequences: Lateralization and Localization Values” (doi: 10.1111/EPI.13322). It studies individual ictal motor signs and their sequences in focal epilepsy ending with a secondarily generalized motor seizure, with outcomes for epileptogenic-zone (EZ) lateralization and temporal versus extratemporal localization.

findings.claim: Vestibular responses included translation illusions in 14/41 (34.1%) and rotation illusions in 9/41 (21.9%); translation included levitation/flying (5/14), rising (3/14), or falling (6/14), and fall direction was unrelated to stimulation side. Yaw-plane rotation was most common (7/9), with source-reported clockwise 5/7 and counterclockwise 2/5 responses; clockwise responses followed right-sided stimulation in 3/5 and left-sided stimulation in 2/5, roll-plane illusions numbered 2, and 18/41 (43.9%) responses could not be precisely classified.
findings.evidence_text: "The side of falling sensation was not related to the side of insular stimulation"; 18/41 responses were not precisely classifiable.
findings.laterality_localization: fall direction relative to stimulated side; clockwise response by right versus left insular stimulation; yaw versus roll plane
findings.limitations: The source's reported denominators are not uniform across the nested vestibular descriptions, and no recalculation is performed.

findings.source_term: bipolar organization of major insular functions

findings.citation: Mazzola L, Isnard J, Mauguiere F. Somatosensory and pain responses to stimulation of the second somatosensory area (SII) in humans. A comparison with SI and insular responses. Cereb Cortex 2006;16:960-968 (ref. 11)
findings.claim: Restating its cited comparison study, the source says insular somato-sensory responses involve larger skin territories than SI/SII responses, can be bilateral or ipsilateral rather than the SI pattern of strict contralaterality except for poorly lateralized perioral sensations, and that pain occurs after both SII and insular stimulation at about 10% with similar 4-9/10 intensity and stimulus threshold; SII responses were bilateral in 36% versus 30% for insular responses, and strictly ipsilateral responses were exclusive to insular stimulation.
findings.evidence_text: "Some features distinguish insular somato-sensory responses (SSR)" from SI, while the SII-insular distinction is "less straightforward."
findings.laterality_localization: SI strict contralateral pattern except perioral; insular bilateral or ipsilateral patterns; SII versus insular bilateral percentages
findings.limitations: Cited-study restatement only; the cited source was not reviewed in this bounded report and the current PDF does not supply its underlying denominators.

findings.citation: Montavont A, Mauguiere F, Mazzola L, et al. On the origin of painful somatosensory seizures. Neurology 2015;84:594-601 (ref. 27)
findings.claim: Restating a cited SEEG study, the source reports that ictal pain in patients with painful seizures could be reproduced by insular or SII stimulation and that both the insula and SII were systematically involved at seizure onset.
findings.evidence_text: "ictal pain can be reproduced by insular or SII stimulation, and the insula and SII regions are systematically involved at onset of seizures."
findings.laterality_localization: insular cortex and secondary somatosensory area (SII) involved at onset
findings.limitations: Cited-study restatement only; the cited source was not reviewed and no cited-study denominators are given here.
findings.population: Patients with painful seizures explored by SEEG in the cited study
findings.source_term: ictal pain and insular/SII seizure-onset involvement

findings.citation: Penfield W, Faulk ME Jr. The insula; further observations on its function. Brain 1955;78:445-470 (ref. 5)
findings.claim: Restating observations attributed to Penfield and Faulk, the source reports a high frequency of visceral responses from the antero-inferior insular quadrant exposed after temporal-operculum removal, with patients describing those symptoms as identical to their ictal aura during surgery for temporal-lobe epilepsy.
findings.evidence_text: Penfield and Faulk "noted the high frequency of visceral responses" in the antero-inferior quadrant; patients reported symptoms as identical to their ictal aura.
findings.laterality_localization: antero-inferior insular quadrant
findings.limitations: Cited-study restatement only; the cited source and its surgical sampling were not reviewed here.
findings.phase: stimulation-evoked visceral response compared with ictal aura
findings.population: Patients undergoing temporal-operculum surgery for temporal-lobe epilepsy in the cited observations
findings.source_term: visceral responses and temporal-lobe seizure aura

findings.citation: Isnard J, Guenot M, Ostrowsky K, Sindou M, Mauguiere F. The role of the insular cortex in temporal lobe epilepsy. Ann Neurol 2000;48:614-2330 (ref. 29)
findings.claim: The authors state from their temporo-insular SEEG experience that hippocampal discharges almost always spread into the insular cortex, which they consider probably responsible for the genesis of the associated ictal symptoms, often with anxiety.
findings.evidence_text: "hippocampal discharges almost always spread into the insular cortex," which is "probably responsible" for these ictal symptoms.
findings.laterality_localization: hippocampus to insular cortex spread; anxiety association
findings.limitations: Cited-study restatement and author experience statement; the cited study was not reviewed and no underlying denominator is reported.
findings.phase: ictal discharge spread and associated ictal symptoms
findings.population: Temporo-insular SEEG explorations described by the source
findings.source_term: hippocampal discharge spread into the insula

findings.claim: The source concludes that no major or minor symptom evoked by insular stimulation is absolutely specific to an insular origin and that any one symptom in isolation is not specific of an insular discharge; pain can also follow SII stimulation and speech or auditory responses can follow frontal or temporal opercular stimulation, whereas a sequence combining several major or minor symptoms, especially laryngeal constriction, strongly suggests insular seizure origin.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source is an invited narrative review that combines a retrospective stimulation series with review-authored synthesis and restatements of cited studies; cited-study claims above were not independently verified against those sources. The stimulation paradigm excluded sites in or around lesions and sites producing after-discharges, and direct stimulation responses are not identical to spontaneous seizures. The source states that anterior insular implantation was scarcer because of Sylvian vessels, so viscero-sensitive responses may be underestimated. It also states that no systematic precise cardiac-rhythm analysis was performed, and several vestibular explanations are explicitly speculative. Some percentages lack subgroup denominators, Table 1 lacks group sample sizes, and the source does not resolve whether all response counts represent unique patients. No page or representation was blocked.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors reviewed stimulation data from 222 patients (107 women, 114 men; mean age 35.5 years, range 20-59) explored for atypical temporal or perisylvian epilepsy between March 1997 and April 2015; 669 insular sites were stimulated through transopercular electrodes orthogonal to the midsagittal plane using bipolar 50-Hz stimulation, 0.5-ms pulses, 5-second trains, and 0.2-3.5-mA intensity. Subjective reports and clinical observations were collected immediately after stimulation, with EEG and video reviewed retrospectively; stimulations in or around lesions or inducing an after-discharge were excluded, and multivariate logistic regression compared coordinates of contacts evoking each sensation with all other stimulated contacts, including non-eloquent contacts.
sources.source_report_summary: Invited narrative review of direct electrical stimulation of the human insula, including the authors' retrospective review of insular stimulation responses obtained during presurgical SEEG exploration, with relevance to the semiology and localizing or lateralizing interpretation of insular seizures.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review and not a unified primary cohort or systematic quantitative synthesis. Most localization relationships are qualitative restatements or review syntheses; the document does not provide a common denominator, numerator, confidence interval, or statistical test for the cited comparisons. The around 40%, around 20%, and around 10% emotional values are attributed to Singh et al. in preparation, with only the series size of 42 patients reported and no separate numerators or denominators. The review repeatedly emphasizes heterogeneity, rapid propagation, dense frontal and extra-frontal connectivity, and group-level rather than deterministic inference. No left/right hemispheric lateralization result is reported; lateral/mesial terminology in the motor-network discussion refers to anatomical surfaces, not hemispheric laterality. All cited-study restatements remain unverified against the cited sources under this review boundary.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This document is a review/Neurological Update and reports or synthesizes observations from multiple SEEG, intracerebral-recording, and other cited series rather than a single study population. It specifically describes a cited SEEG series of 54 patients with FLE and a cited series of 42 patients with prefrontal seizures for emotional prevalence; other cited cohort sizes, ascertainment details, reference standards, and region-specific denominators are not reported in the document. The review frames its electroclinical correlations as group-level aids for presurgical sublobar hypotheses. It states that both seizure onset and propagation contribute to semiological expression and distinguishes elementary motor signs from complex motor behavior.
sources.source_report_summary: McGonigal's 2022 Journal of Neurology Neurological Update is a narrative review of frontal lobe seizures, with emphasis on SEEG-based motor and emotional semiology, anatomical electroclinical correlations, genetic context, and surgical outcome. For the atlas, it contributes review-level localization patterns and constraints on the specificity of individual signs; it does not present a unified new cohort or a hemispheric lateralization analysis.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a critical review/commentary, not a primary cohort or systematic quantitative synthesis, and it does not report a search strategy, study-selection flow, pooled estimates, or a unified denominator across cited studies. The source explicitly identifies narrative semiology as prone to inaccuracy compared with recorded seizures; recording conditions, insufficient ictal testing, camera coverage, lighting, resolution, observer bias, observer experience, inter-observer agreement, ambiguous terms such as “automatism” and “hyperkinetic seizure,” nonspecificity for localization, and difficulty quantifying emotional signs or altered consciousness can affect interpretation. SEEG findings are limited by hypothesis-dependent spatial sampling, the missing-electrode problem, vascular constraints, relatively limited subcortical exploration, choice of analysis period, and signal-analysis method. The review notes that many SEEG series contain around 20-50 subjects or fewer. Table 1 and Table 2 are cited-study restatements: study totals are retained, but exact subgroup counts, finding-specific denominators, p-values, confidence intervals, and other uncertainty are frequently not reported in this document. No native page was blocked; fresh text and page renderings covered all 17 pages, and visual inspection found no table, figure, clipping, rotation, or missing-text defect that changed the evidence.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The article reports a narrative critical overview rather than a systematic search, primary cohort, or pooled quantitative analysis; search and study-selection methods are not reported. Its emphasis is on spontaneous seizures in patients with intractable focal epilepsy undergoing presurgical evaluation, with additional discussion of SEEG stimulation studies, functional imaging, and broader epilepsy classification. The cited-study summaries in Tables 1 and 2 report study-level numbers of subjects and, where available, seizures; exact subgroup denominators and statistical uncertainty are often not provided in this document.
sources.source_report_summary: On seizure semiology is a 2021 Epilepsia critical review and invited commentary by Aileen McGonigal, Fabrice Bartolomei, and Patrick Chauvel (62:2019-2035; DOI 10.1111/epi.16994). It reviews seizure semiology as a data source, with emphasis on focal epilepsy, neural correlates, presurgical evaluation, seizure classification, and network-based interpretations. The document is a review/commentary rather than a primary cohort report; Tables 1 and 2 restate selected cited SEEG studies, and Table 3 consolidates methodological challenges.

findings.claim: The authors state that neural mechanisms underlying seizure semiology, especially complex ictal behaviors, remain poorly known and propose that semiology is dynamically produced by interconnected structures in which rhythmic interactions, rather than anatomical localization alone, contribute to clinical expression.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a critical review and invited commentary rather than a systematic review or primary cohort report; it reports no search strategy, unified eligibility set, pooled estimate, common reference standard, confidence intervals, or unified denominator. Tables 1 and 2 are cited-study restatements, and their analysis units, sampling strategies, comparators, and uncertainty reporting remain study-specific; many qualitative associations have no finding-specific numerator, denominator, p value, or interval. The source emphasizes observer and categorization ambiguity, hypothesis-dependent SEEG implantation, missing-electrode and subcortical-sampling limitations, and generally small SEEG series. No page was blocked; pages 14-17 contain acknowledgments, conflicts, ORCID information, and references/how-to-cite material rather than additional original semiologic results. The review does not establish a unified side-specific lateralization rule.
sources.source_report_methods_population: No systematic-search method or unified study cohort is reported. The review focuses mainly on spontaneous focal seizures in patients undergoing presurgical evaluation for intractable focal epilepsy and discusses SEEG recordings, signal analysis, cortical stimulation, and complementary imaging. Tables 1 and 2 retain the study-specific numbers of subjects and seizures, controls or comparators, brain regions, and analysis approaches; the review does not pool their results.
sources.source_report_summary: McGonigal, Bartolomei, and Chauvel, “On seizure semiology,” Epilepsia 2021;62:2019-2035, is a critical review and invited commentary. It reviews seizure semiology as a data source, with emphasis on focal epilepsy and SEEG, compares network and focus/symptomatogenic-zone models, summarizes cited electroclinical studies, describes methodological challenges, and discusses future research and therapeutic implications.

sources.source_report_limitations: The study is observational and did not standardize postictal testing or systematically assess awareness. Only five focal seizures with tonic-clonic evolution were recorded, none in patients with ICA/PICA, so associations with postconvulsive apnea or SUDEP risk cannot be evaluated. No intracranial EEG was recorded, respiratory-muscle EMG was not directly measured, and the MRI groups were small and require replication. The source also contains an awareness-wording ambiguity (“in any seizures, the patient was aware” conflicts with the surrounding no-awareness account) and two unresolved denominator ambiguities: the Table 2 vigilance row displays 22 PICA wake/sleep observations despite 24 PICA seizures, and the awareness paragraph describes 15 actively interrogated plus 8 untested PICA seizures while stating 24 total.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Consecutive patients older than 13 years admitted to the Epilepsy Monitoring Unit at Baggiovara Civil Hospital, Modena Academic Hospital, Italy, from April 2020 through December 2023 were studied with long-term video-EEG and cardiorespiratory polygraphy; 71 met inclusion, 2 were discarded for technical artifact, 5 focal seizures with bilateral tonic-clonic evolution were excluded, and the final analysis comprised 69 patients and 406 focal-onset seizures. MRI analyses included 22 patients with ICA/PICA, 31 patients without seizure-related breathing disorders, and 30 healthy controls; analyses adjusted for age, sex, and intracranial volume and used false-discovery-rate correction.
sources.source_report_summary: Original prospective observational research article evaluating the incidence and features of postictal central apnea (PICA) in focal-onset seizures without secondary bilateral tonic-clonic evolution and comparing subcortical MRI morphometry, with particular attention to the amygdala and seizure-onset localization.

findings.claim: Frontal auras are less common and less specific than temporal auras; abdominal sensations can arise from orbitofrontal or cingulate regions; forced thinking suggests dorsolateral frontal involvement; preserved-awareness clonic activity is most localizing to primary motor cortex, with lower-extremity signs suggesting mesial frontal and facial signs suggesting inferior frontal involvement; supplementary sensorimotor seizures tend to be brief, clustered, nocturnal, asymmetrical tonic or postural events with proximal predominance, and may include vocalization, startle precipitation, or bilateral symptoms without loss of consciousness.

findings.claim: A parietal sensory march suggests postcentral primary sensory cortex involvement contralateral to the ictal discharge, while a sensory aura without march may arise from the second sensory area or parietal operculum; focal weakness may represent a parietal inhibitory motor seizure. Occipital seizures are suggested by elementary visual aura or a contralateral visual-field deficit, complex scenes by occipitotemporal involvement, and variable spread to temporal or frontal regions by oroalimentary or asymmetric tonic manifestations.

findings.claim: Typical generalized absence seizures are abrupt, usually lack an aura, commonly last less than 15 seconds, terminate abruptly without a postictal state, and are associated with generalized 2.5-4 Hz spike-and-wave activity; arrest, simple or perseverative automatisms, blinking, subtle myoclonus, eye or neck movements, atonic slumping, and autonomic signs may occur. sources.source_report_limitations: This is a heterogeneous educational atlas with review synthesis, cited restatements, EEG teaching figures, and individual cases rather than one primary dataset. Denominators, ascertainment methods, and diagnostic reference standards vary across the cited material and are often not reproduced in the atlas text. Semiology and scalp EEG are affected by timing, propagation, montage, electrode field, artifact, sleep or age state, and deep-generator sampling. Quantitative values above remain source-native and are not recalculated or harmonized. No external links, public repository, master ledger, website, integration, promotion, or deployment artifact was accessed or changed.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The complete native PDF page set 1-473 was reviewed as one source. Per-page text was read in coherent sections with targeted consolidation of repeated headers, references, medication material, and non-in-scope management content. Renderings were additionally inspected for the vision-required pages and for selected semiology diagrams, EEG traces, montages, tables, captions, and case figures where visual field, waveform evolution, or extraction uncertainty carried scientific meaning. Populations are heterogeneous and source-native: educational descriptions, selected cited-study restatements, and distinct illustrated patient cases are kept separate below. Quantitative values are reported only when the source states them.
sources.source_report_summary: This is the complete native 473-page third edition of Atlas of EEG, Seizure Semiology, and Management (Misulis, Sonmezturk, Ess, and Abou-Khalil; Oxford University Press, 2022). It is an educational atlas and review synthesis, not a single primary cohort. The in-scope review covered seizure semiology, seizure classification, clinical and ictal EEG interpretation, localization/lateralization, ictal propagation, selected electroclinical status criteria, pediatric electroclinical syndromes, and source-native teaching cases. The 12 package pages marked NONE_REQUIRES_VISION were inspected as renderings; they were blank, section-only, or cover material and none was blocked.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a single-patient case report without a control group, population estimate, or independent reference standard. The cited background literature is reported as restatement or discussion synthesis rather than independently verified source evidence here. The authors identify intrinsic SEEG anatomical sampling as a limitation and do not exclude adjacent regions; stimulation-trial counts and most comparative statistics are not reported. All five pages and all three figures were readable; no tables or blocked page regions were present.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The report concerns one 35-year-old right-handed man with drug-resistant partial epilepsy. Long-term video-EEG captured 6 electroclinical seizures; SEEG recorded 5 stereotyped spontaneous electroclinical seizures using 11 right-hemisphere electrodes and 1 left-amygdala electrode. The report also describes high-frequency stimulation of the right amygdala and right precentral operculum. No control group or independent reference standard is reported.
sources.source_report_summary: Original single-patient case report in Epileptic Disorders (2005) describing recurrent ictal speech with altered prosody in a right-handed man with drug-resistant right mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, using video-EEG, multimodal imaging, SEEG, and intracranial stimulation to examine non-dominant frontal-opercular involvement.

sources.source_report_limitations:
This is a heterogeneous systematic review dominated by descriptive studies and case reports. The review states that semiologic definitions vary and that onset versus propagation is unclear in many cases. Study-level cohort overlap was assessed by the review authors, but the underlying articles are not part of this source package. Aggregate review context retained in the summary and methods includes 27 articles and 71 patients; search-flow counts, generic risk-of-bias counts, demographics, and standalone imaging/surgery/outcome/table-population cells were pruned as out of scope. EZ confidence records and cited-study sign/localization records were retained because they directly bear on localization or the seizure sign. No non-source anatomy, classification, or hemisphere inference was added.

Owner questions: Should the source’s region percentages and confidence distributions be integrated as review-level localization evidence despite incomplete denominators and substantial onset-versus-propagation uncertainty? Should the Table 1 sign-case rows be retained as separate cited-study records if downstream deduplication cannot link their underlying cohorts?
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors registered the review in PROSPERO (CRD42024519156) and report PRISMA methods. PubMed, EMBASE, and Scopus were searched through December 1, 2024. Original peer-reviewed studies with individual-level spontaneous ictal descriptions and invasive EEG, surgery/outcome, or imaging data were eligible; case reports were included. EZ confidence was graded as very high, high, moderate, or low using MRI, invasive EEG, and postsurgical outcome, and GRADE was used for overall evidence. Descriptive statistics and Pearson chi-squared tests with Holm-corrected pairwise proportion tests were reported.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2025 systematic review examines the “chapeau de gendarme” sign, also called ictal pouting, in focal epilepsy. It includes 27 articles and a 71-patient review cohort, combining cohort studies and single-case reports. The review presents source-native semiologic descriptions, brain-region localization, imaging and electrophysiology findings, surgery and outcome statistics, and an assessment of bias. It concludes that the sign is most strongly associated with mesial frontal localization, with moderate evidence for insulo-opercular involvement, but states that no apparent lateralizing value has been attributed to the semiology.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source is heterogeneous, with many small case reports/series and sign-selected cohorts. The paper reports a moderate overall evidence reliability and cautions that network propagation does not necessarily equal the epileptogenic zone. Cluster coefficients measure co-occurrence similarity rather than diagnostic accuracy. A genuine internal discrepancy remains for the fronto-temporal subgroup association between elementary motor signs and multilobar resection: the abstract reports p=.0012, whereas the body text reports p=.12. The source also includes a temporo-frontal subgroup count of 67 while propagation-site counts in the same narrative may overlap and sum beyond that count; these are retained as source-reported, non-mutually-exclusive localization descriptions. No standalone surgery, pathology, or seizure-outcome counts are treated as findings.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The review included English-language case series and selected case reports of drug-resistant temporal or frontal epilepsy with electroclinical or imaging evidence of temporo-frontal/fronto-temporal network involvement. The reviewed population is 40 articles and 109 patients; the source divides them into a temporo-frontal subgroup (temporal seizure-onset zone with frontal extension) and a fronto-temporal subgroup (frontal onset with temporal involvement). Search counts, duplicate resolution, reviewer roles, eligibility/risk-of-bias details, Table 1 per-study MRI/SEEG/surgery/outcome cells, and standalone surgery/outcome counts are retained only as compact context here. The source uses cluster analysis, Fisher exact comparisons for sign/resection associations, and random-effects prevalence meta-analysis.
sources.source_report_summary: Oane et al., “Ictal semiology in temporo-frontal epilepsy: A systematic review and meta-analysis” (Epileptic Disorders 2025;27:171–186), synthesizes 109 patients from 40 articles with temporo-frontal or fronto-temporal network involvement. It separates temporal-onset with frontal propagation from frontal-onset with temporal propagation, reports sign-category prevalence and cluster association coefficients, and supplies a random-effects prevalence forest plot. The source-native signs, network structures, phase relations, estimates, confidence intervals, weights, and heterogeneity statistics are retained atomically without forced hemisphere or Brodmann mappings.
