findings.claim: In the primary cohort, having at least three generalised convulsive seizures in the previous year was associated with increased SUDEP risk versus fewer than three: Table 1 reported 23/39 (59%) in the SUDEP-or-near-SUDEP group versus 722/2216 (33%) in the non-SUDEP group, the primary Cox model gave HR 3.10 (95% CI 1.64-5.87; p=0.0005), and the 5-year SUDEP risk was 4.3% (2.2-6.5) versus 1.4% (0.5-2.3); adjusted HRs across the reported models were 2.75 (1.10-6.88), 2.76 (1.10-6.94), and 2.84 (1.12-7.23), and exclusion of possible and near-SUDEP cases gave HR 3.54 (1.67-7.49).
findings.evidence_text: The primary analysis states that three or more generalised convulsive seizures in the previous year predicted increased SUDEP risk, with HR 3.10 (1.64-5.87), and Figure 2 uses the <3 versus >=3 comparison.
findings.laterality_localization: NOT_APPLICABLE
findings.limitations: The source also states that results were similar when one or more versus none was used as the cutoff; exact missing-data handling and subgroup denominators beyond the reported values are not expanded in the main text.

findings.claim: Postictal central apnoea was present in 13/30 (43%) of SUDEP-or-near-SUDEP participants with available data versus 198/1001 (20%) of non-SUDEP participants, and median duration was 21 seconds (IQR 14-50) versus 13 seconds (9-24); each 10-second increase was associated with higher SUDEP risk in the primary Cox model, HR 1.32 (95% CI 1.14-1.54; p=0.0002), while the 5-year risk was 13.4% (0-24.9) for median duration >14 seconds versus 3.6% (1.8-5.3) for <=14 seconds. The association did not reach significance in the adjusted multivariable model or after excluding possible and near-SUDEP cases, when the reported HR was 1.25 (1.00-1.56).
findings.evidence_text: The report links longer postictal central-apnoea duration to increased SUDEP risk in the primary analysis and gives the >14-second Kaplan-Meier comparison.
findings.laterality_localization: NOT_APPLICABLE
findings.limitations: The abstract and Figure 2 use >14 seconds, whereas the Discussion describes prolonged postictal central apnoea as >=15 seconds; these are study-specific, unvalidated risk-stratification cutoffs, not source-defined semiologic thresholds. The operational definition is referred to the unavailable appendix.

findings.claim: Ictal central apnoea was present in 9/25 (36%) of SUDEP-or-near-SUDEP participants with available data versus 344/799 (43%) of non-SUDEP participants, but median duration was longer at 44 seconds (IQR 28-49) versus 17 seconds (10-27); each 10-second increase was associated with higher SUDEP risk in the primary Cox model, HR 1.11 (95% CI 1.05-1.18; p<0.0001), while the 5-year risk was 7.4% (1.3-13.1) for median duration >17 seconds versus 3.7% (1.3-6.1) for <=17 seconds, a threshold comparison with p=0.11. The adjusted association was not significant after clinical covariate adjustment, and exclusion of possible and near-SUDEP cases gave HR 1.06 (0.82-1.37).
findings.evidence_text: The primary analysis reports higher SUDEP risk with longer ictal central-apnoea duration, while the Figure 2 >17-second comparison is not statistically significant.
findings.laterality_localization: NOT_APPLICABLE
findings.limitations: The >17-second cutoff is a study-specific median cutoff and the authors state that prolonged ictal central apnoea requires further prospective validation. The operational definition is referred to the unavailable appendix.

findings.claim: Any peri-ictal arrhythmia was present in 27/31 (87%) of SUDEP-or-near-SUDEP participants versus 734/1382 (53%) of non-SUDEP participants; the primary Cox model estimated HR 4.96 (95% CI 1.74-14.2; uncorrected p=0.0028), an association the authors state did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction. After excluding possible and near-SUDEP cases, the reported HR was 4.93 (1.46-16.59).
findings.evidence_text: Any arrhythmia was more prevalent in the SUDEP-or-near-SUDEP group and had an uncorrected HR of 4.96, but the authors state that the association did not retain significance after Bonferroni correction.
findings.laterality_localization: NOT_APPLICABLE
findings.limitations: The source says its peri-ictal-arrhythmia definition was broad and could count one or two postictal bradycardic beats; the exact operational definition is referred to the unavailable appendix.

findings.claim: Postictal generalised EEG suppression was present in 16/20 (80%) of SUDEP-or-near-SUDEP participants versus 400/540 (74%) of non-SUDEP participants with available data, and median duration was 49 seconds (IQR 44-64) versus 37 seconds (27-46); each 10-second increase had HR 1.12 (95% CI 1.03-1.22; uncorrected p=0.0071) in the primary Cox model, but the association did not remain significant after Bonferroni correction. findings.evidence_text: The source reports longer postictal generalised EEG suppression in the SUDEP-or-near-SUDEP group and an uncorrected association that did not survive Bonferroni correction.

sources.source_report_limitations: All 11 native pages were readable in both the packaged text and page renderings; no page is blocked. The verified package contains the main 11-page article only, while the article repeatedly refers to an online appendix for operational definitions, additional subgroup results, and additional quantitative details. The appendix was not present and was not consulted, so no appendix-specific definition, denominator, or result has been inferred. The primary cohort reports no seizure-side or hemisphere-specific result, and the primary findings therefore do not establish lateralization. Cited-study restatements and mechanistic interpretations are retained as such and were not verified against their cited sources.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The study enrolled 2632 children and adults with epilepsy at nine epilepsy-monitoring centres in the USA and UK between 2011 and 2021; 164 were lost to follow-up and 2468 participants were included in the primary follow-up analyses. There were 38 SUDEP outcomes and two near-SUDEP events. During admission, 1660 participants had seizures captured, 1432 had analysable seizures, and the report describes 1091 analysable generalised convulsive seizures and 2117 non-convulsive seizures. The primary endpoint was time to SUDEP or censoring due to other causes. Cox proportional hazards models assessed clinical and electroclinical predictors; repeated seizure predictors were aggregated to the most severe feature per patient, using the maximum for continuous features or presence for categorical features. Analyses used prolonged video-EEG, ECG, pulse oximetry, and chest/abdominal inductance plethysmography. Statistical significance in primary analyses required two-sided p<0.05 after Bonferroni correction; the report states that secondary-analysis confidence intervals were not intended for hypothesis testing. Main-text results include varying denominators and missing data, which are retained below.
sources.source_report_summary: Ochoa-Urrea et al., “Risk markers for sudden unexpected death in epilepsy: an observational, prospective, multicentre cohort study,” is an original prospective observational cohort report. Its in-scope contribution is prospective comparison of seizure manifestations and peri-ictal respiratory, cardiac, EEG, and motor signs in relation to SUDEP risk. The primary study does not report seizure-side or other direct lateralization results; localization content is limited to explicitly attributed prior claims discussed by the authors.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a small, retrospective, uncontrolled case series with history-based identification. EEG was absent at the time of palinacousis in cases 5 and 6, uncertain in case 4, and negative for electrographic seizures during case 7; extracranial EEG could not localize an exact generator in cases 2 and 3. The source reports an internal duration discrepancy for case 5 and refers to Supplemental Table E1 without including it in the locked four-page package. Literature counts, prior-study descriptions, and novelty statements are current-document syntheses or cited restatements rather than independently verified source results. Silence or absent EEG was not treated as evidence that an episode was non-ictal.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This retrospective case series included seven patients seen at The Mount Sinai Hospital epilepsy clinic or EMU between July 2009 and May 2016 who experienced palinacousis. All patients had epilepsy; EEG and MRI were performed at some point during their clinical course, and the authors reviewed those records after identifying the phenomenon by history. No comparator, uniform event-time reference standard, or inferential statistical analysis was reported.
sources.source_report_summary: Fields et al., Journal of Clinical Neurophysiology 2018;35:173-176, is a case report and case series describing seven epilepsy patients with palinacousis seen at an epilepsy clinic or epilepsy monitoring unit. It contributes case-level evidence about auditory perseveration during direct cortical stimulation, electrographic seizures, and peri- or post-ictal states, together with a narrative localization review.

findings.citation: Montavont A, Mauguiere F, Mazzola L, et al. On the origin of painful somatosensory seizures. Neurology 2015;84:594–601.
findings.claim: In the Case 2 discussion, the source states that somatosensory auras are usually localized to primary sensory cortex, secondary somatosensory cortex in the parietal operculum, or the posterior third of the insular cortex; painful seizures likely arise in the same regions, although supplementary motor, inferior parietal, and cingulate localizations have been proposed, and somatosensory auras are usually contralateral to the epileptic focus even when the insula is involved.

findings.limitations: Chapter synthesis of cited literature applied to an illustrative case; no denominator or diagnostic performance estimate

findings.claim: In Case 2, unilateral left interictal abnormalities, centro-temporal seizure onset, right-sided sensory pain and auditory auras, and late hypermotor manifestations were interpreted as favoring a left posterior or midposterior insular and temporo-parietal opercular origin with frontal propagation rather than primary frontal onset; invasive recordings showed preictal spikes over parietal-opercular and posterior-insular contacts followed by low-voltage fast activity in the same contacts, and the patient remained seizure-free 1.5 years after left posterior insulectomy and partial parietal opercular resection.

findings.laterality_localization: Left posterior/midposterior insula and temporo-parietal/parietal operculum; later hypermotor activity interpreted as frontal propagation; left hemisphere
findings.limitations: Single illustrative case; invasive concordance and seizure freedom do not establish a general localization or treatment effect

sources.source_report_limitations: This chapter is an educational narrative synthesis rather than a systematic review or primary cohort, and its cited-study restatements were not independently checked against the cited sources. Many cited populations, subgroup sizes, numerators, denominators, and analysis units are unavailable or not re-specified; silence is not treated as a negative finding. The two cases are illustrative and have no population-level generalizability. Figure captions and implantation maps were inspected as context; no stable sign identifier or cross-document mapping was assigned.
sources.source_report_methods_population: No formal search strategy, eligibility criteria, pooled analysis, common comparator, or uniform reference standard is reported. The chapter includes two individual case observations: Case 1 is a 27-year-old right-handed woman with seizure onset at age 9, and Case 2 is a 46-year-old right-handed man with seizures since age 16. Other populations are cited literature populations as reported in individual findings, including a review of 153 patients and a 22-patient nonlesional operculo-insular series; these are not an original chapter cohort.
sources.source_report_summary: This is an educational textbook chapter and narrative review, Chapter 17, Operculo-Insular Epilepsy, by Raluca Pana and Dang Khoa Nguyen in A Practical Approach to Stereo EEG. It synthesizes cited literature on ictal semiology and localization and presents two illustrative cases; it is not a primary cohort study. The source contributes source-native semiology/localization relationships, cited-study restatements, and case-specific EEG, stimulation, and invasive findings.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a left-hemisphere post-stroke aphasia study, not an epilepsy cohort. It contains no ictal or postictal observations, seizure-onset reference standard, EEG localization, seizure count, or seizure-lateralization endpoint. All primary localization results are associations between performance and diffusion-derived QA, not causal lesion or seizure-onset claims. The connected-singing analysis lost two recordings; the less/more severe subgroup analyses used n=22 and n=21, and the post hoc analysis used n=5 versus n=6. The authors caution that the subgroup right-sided and negative associations may be false positives, did not directly quantitatively compare the nonidentical speech and singing production tasks, and did not include right-hemisphere lesion or age-matched healthy control groups. The main connected-singing tract list includes a right middle cerebellar peduncle, while the Discussion says no clear right-hemisphere association was detected and emphasizes additional right-sided effects in the less-severe subgroup; both source statements are retained without reconciliation. Cited-study rows are restatements as reported by the current document and retain the current document's missing cohort and denominator information.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Forty-five adults with chronic aphasia more than 6 months after a clinically confirmed left-hemisphere stroke were recruited in Helsinki and Turku in 2017-2019; all were Finnish native speakers, over 18 years, and had no hearing deficit, severe cognitive impairment, substance abuse, or neurological/psychiatric comorbidity. Connected spoken-language production was mean correct information units per minute across three discourse tasks; connected singing was correct words per minute while singing the familiar song Jaakko-kulta; two connected-singing recordings were lost, leaving n=43 for that analysis. Repetition used 16 identical 1-5-word phrases in spoken and melodically intoned formats, with the first attempt scored and correct words per minute calculated. Six participant-level local-connectome regression models used age and lesion volume as covariates; tract tracking used a T-score threshold of 3, 2,000 permutations, and FDR <0.0083 after Bonferroni correction.
sources.source_report_summary: Original empirical Communications Biology study using whole-brain multi-shell diffusion MRI and quantitative-anisotropy connectometry to relate white-matter pathways to spoken-language production, singing, and repetition performance in adults with chronic post-stroke aphasia. It provides indirect neuroanatomical localization/lateralization evidence for language and sung-word production, not seizure-semiology evidence.

sources.source_report_limitations:
The included sample is small (12 patients, 17 symptom-evoking cingulate stimulations) and the cingulate and other implanted structures were sampled for clinical presurgical purposes with variable spatial coverage. The authors report no clear control over subjective clinical effects, no specific quantitative assessment such as visual-analog scales, and no independent reference standard for the complex body-perception reports. The stimulation effects were rare and not equivalent to spontaneous seizure semiology; the source explicitly reports that usual seizure semiology did not contain similar signs in the included patients. The connectivity analysis used a 5-s POSTSTIM signal epoch rather than activity during HFS because of stimulation artifact, limiting temporal resolution, and its network graphs are affected by variable sampling across patients and structures.

The source contains unresolved internal reporting inconsistencies relevant to exact attribution: Section 3.1 names Patient 13 for upper-limb pain associated with a heaviness effect and Patients 11 and 14 for movement observations, whereas Table 1 contains 12 patients and Table 2 assigns the corresponding rows to Patients 11, 9, and 12; Section 3.1 describes Patient 4 pressure as upper-extremity pressure whereas Table 2 lists head/top-of-head pressure; and the prose calls the right PCC movement relationship contralateral while Table 2 labels S17 ipsilateral. These source discrepancies are retained in the affected findings rather than resolved by inference. Page 14 points to online Supporting Information, but no supplemental object is present in the locked 14-page package and no claim from it is reviewed here.
sources.source_report_methods_population:
Patients underwent phase-two invasive presurgical evaluation at the University Emergency Hospital Bucharest or Strasbourg University Hospital between 2000 and 2017. The source reviewed 110 patients whose cingulate cortex was sampled and functionally mapped and included 12 right-handed patients with body-perception changes: 8 from Bucharest and 4 from Strasbourg. All had focal drug-resistant epilepsy; the epileptogenic zone was frontal in 9 patients, temporo-basal in 1, insular-opercular in 1, and insular in 1. Patients were selected when at least one electrode sampled cingulate cortex outside the epileptogenic zone; cognitive or psychiatric comorbidity judged likely to interfere with reliable interaction was excluded. Structures and stimulation sites were selected for clinical presurgical purposes, not for this study. The source reports no visible MRI lesion in the included patients and states that the stimulated locations did not overlap the delineated epileptogenic zone in the two patients who did not undergo surgery.

Functional mapping used bipolar high-frequency stimulation at 50 Hz for 5 s through adjacent contacts with biphasic 1 ms pulses; current was gradually increased from 0.1 to 3 mA until a clinical or electrical response. Patients reported psychological or physical changes during or after stimulation. Body-representation changes were analyzed at the lowest intensity that evoked a symptom (SYM target group) and compared with typically half-intensity stimulations without a symptom (NS control group); after-discharges, auras, and seizures were excluded. Repeated trials, including 0 mA sham trials, were used for response consistency and psychogenic-event control. The separate connectivity analysis used h2 values from nonstimulated contacts in 10-s PRESTIM and 5-s POSTSTIM epochs; those network measurements are kept distinct from the semiologic findings below. No independent reference standard was reported for the subjective stimulation responses.
sources.source_report_summary: Popa et al., “Illusory own body perceptions mapped in the cingulate cortex—An intracranial stimulation study,” is an original retrospective empirical study of stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG)-guided high-frequency direct electrical stimulation in people with focal drug-resistant epilepsy. The paper reports body-perception phenomena evoked by stimulation of cingulate cortex contacts outside the epileptogenic zone, with cingulate subregion and body-side relationships, and separately reports an h2-based functional-connectivity analysis. The semiologic observations in this report are stimulation-evoked; the paper separately addresses usual seizure semiology and does not establish that the evoked phenomena are spontaneous seizure signs.

sources.source_report_limitations: The PDF is a scan with no text layer; all eight pages were represented by verified page renderings and reviewed visually, and no page was blocked. The study is a small surgical unilateral-TLE cohort with repeated seizure observations per patient. Table 1 percentages are relative to all 116 seizures, while parenthetical values are patient counts; behavior-specific denominators and confidence intervals are generally not reported. The language table likewise uses total-seizure percentages while comparing NHS and DHS groups. The source reports an internal wording/table discrepancy for unilateral automatism and uses both ictal-language and postictal-dysphasia phrasing in different sections; neither discrepancy was resolved by inference. Pages 7-8 contain the discussion tail and references; bibliography entries were not treated as findings.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The study included 19 patients with unilateral TLE who underwent anterior temporal lobectomy with amygdalohippocampectomy. Long-term video/EEG monitoring used scalp and sphenoidal electrodes; hippocampal depth electrodes were used in five patients. The epileptogenic zone was determined from ictal EEG, MRI findings including mesial temporal sclerosis, ictal SPECT, regional temporal PET, and surgical outcome; Wada-test results were used for dominant versus nondominant hemisphere classification. Two to ten seizures per patient were reviewed (mean 6.1); the cohort included 10 females and 9 males, mean age 28.7 years (range 12-43). Sixty-five seizures were classified as nondominant-hemisphere onset and 51 as dominant-hemisphere onset; 85 seizures arose from the right temporal lobe and 31 from the left. Chi-square testing was used for statistical analysis.
sources.source_report_summary: Roh, Hong, and Seo (1996) is an original empirical study of the lateralizing value of ictal behaviors in surgically treated unilateral temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). The investigators reviewed 116 seizures in 19 patients using video/EEG and classified unilateral motor signs, ictal language, and other automatisms by their relation to EEG seizure focus, dominant or nondominant hemisphere onset, or right versus left TLE.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a long, historically heterogeneous surgical series with changing EEG, imaging, electrocorticography, stimulation, and follow-up practices across 1930-1991. Surface EEG, ictal EEG, depth recordings, ECoG, imaging, field examination, stimulation, and clinical signs use different denominators and are not interchangeable localization tests. Several results are cited restatements rather than primary data from the 42-patient cohort. Table 1 contains direct semiology but also extensive demographics, etiology, imaging, surgery, pathology, and outcome cells. Standalone demographics, methods, surgery, pathology, and outcome counts were retained as compact context only and were not promoted to atlas findings. The source reports 12 patients (29%) with ictal blindness in Results and 28% with ictal blindness as an initial manifestation in the Discussion. It also reports bitemporal independent discharges as 9/39 (24%) in Table 2 and 23% in the Discussion. These values remain separate rather than being silently reconciled. No accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, or predictive-value analysis is supplied for the semiologic or localization observations. No Brodmann-area or Lüders/ILAE classification is source-explicit, so no such mapping is assigned.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The source reports 42 medically refractory patients with clinically and electrographically supported occipital lobe epilepsy who underwent surgery during 1930-1991. Clinical history, serial scalp EEG, imaging when available, pre- and post-excision electrocorticography, depth recordings in selected patients, and intra-operative cortical stimulation were used. The EEG and electrocorticography denominators vary by available study and are preserved per result. The source’s operational occipital localization and its historical terminology are retained without adding a Brodmann-area mapping or a Lüders/ILAE classification not stated by the source.
sources.source_report_summary: This 1992 primary surgical series describes electroclinical manifestations, EEG and electrocorticographic localization, cortical-stimulation responses, and spread patterns in 42 medically refractory patients treated for source-defined occipital lobe epilepsy at the Montreal Neurological Institute between 1930 and 1991. Findings retained here are limited to source-native seizure signs, visual and ocular phenomena, seizure evolution, seizure-onset or interictal localization, hemispheric lateralization, stimulation responses, and statistics directly attached to those phenomena or localization results. Table 1 demographic, etiologic, surgery, pathology, and outcome cells are not individually promoted to findings. Direct semiology in the table is retained through the source terminology and the source’s aggregate results, with specific illustrated or localization-linked cases retained separately.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a historically heterogeneous surgical series spanning 1929-1988 with changing imaging, EEG, ECoG, stimulation, and surgical practices. Surface EEG was often lateralizing rather than localizing, and modality denominators differ. The source presents both table aura-entry counts and narrative patient counts. For somatosensory, body-image, visual-illusion, vertiginous, aphasic, and inability-to-move categories, these units are preserved separately because the Table 1 footnote states that aura entries can exceed patient counts. Appendix rows contain direct semiology but also standalone demographics, neurological examination context, imaging, surgery, pathology, and outcome cells. Only direct seizure signs, evolution, localization/lateralization, or statistics attached to them are promoted to Findings. No sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, or formal accuracy analysis is reported. The source’s composite localization statement for automatism patients does not provide separate counts for inferior parietal, parietal opercular, and superior-posterior temporal extension. No Brodmann, Lüders, or ILAE classification is assigned.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The source studied 82 medically refractory patients whose seizure foci largely involved the parietal association area. Patients with large resections extending into anterior occipital, posterior temporal, or precentral regions and patients with parietal tumours were excluded. Surface EEG was available in 66 patients, seizures were recorded in 36, pre-resection ECoG was performed in 63, and intra-operative cortical stimulation was performed in 80. Denominators remain specific to each modality and subgroup. The source’s “parietal association area,” epileptogenic-zone definition, functional anatomy, and source-native terms are preserved without a forced Brodmann, Lüders, or ILAE mapping.
sources.source_report_summary: This 1995 primary surgical series reports clinical manifestations, surface EEG, pre-resection electrocorticography, cortical-stimulation responses, and outcome in 82 patients with nontumoural parietal lobe epilepsy treated at the Montreal Neurological Institute between 1929 and 1988. Findings retained here bear directly on aurae, somatosensory and visual phenomena, seizure evolution, motor and post-ictal signs, seizure-onset localization, hemispheric lateralization, and stimulation- or ECoG-linked localization. Appendix demographics, etiology, surgery, pathology, and outcome cells are retained only as compact context. Direct semiology from the appendix is represented through source terminology and the illustrated case observations rather than by promoting every patient-row cell to a finding.

sources.source_report_limitations: The evidence base is small and heterogeneous, with temporal-polar estimates drawn from a limited number of publications and medio-lateral evidence from only two publications. The source cautions that propagation topography can produce the observed semiology and that electrode trajectories or lack of selective polar resection may miss or fail to distinguish the relevant onset or propagation pattern. Table 3 and Table 6 values are retained as printed, with point estimates, ranges, study counts, and cited-study percentages kept in separate records. The abstract prints 51/120 for mesio-lateral cases while also reporting 129 patients overall; this denominator relationship is not reconciled by the source and remains a genuine owner question. No standalone surgery, outcome, search, or review-process counts are treated as findings.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The source is a systematic review of temporal-polar and medio-lateral temporal seizure semiology. It reports 129 patients overall; the abstract prints 78/129 temporal-pole cases and 51/120 mesio-lateral cases. The temporal-polar section describes 11 publications with a maximum of 23 patients, and the medio-lateral section describes two publications. The printed 51/120 denominator is preserved as source context and is flagged as an internal denominator question below. Search-flow counts, reviewer counts, generic eligibility or risk-of-bias details, and standalone Table 1/2 demographic, imaging, surgery, and outcome cells are not findings.
sources.source_report_summary: Schulze-Bonhage and San Antonio-Arce, “Semiology of seizures with temporo-polar or ‘medio-lateral’ temporal origin: A systematic review” (2025), reviews temporal-polar and rapid temporo-lateral/temporo-mesial seizure patterns. The source emphasizes that observed semiology reflects propagation topography and that no sign is sufficiently specific and frequent to localize the temporal pole. Source-native anatomy, semiology, propagation terms, definitions, limitations, and directly attached statistics are retained without forced hemisphere, Brodmann, Lüders 5D, or ILAE 2025 mappings.

sources.source_report_limitations: The primary localization reference was the operated temporal side, supported by post-operative outcome rather than an independent seizure-onset standard. Group A was presumed more accurately localized because patients became seizure-free or almost so; Group B remained less valid because continuing attacks could reflect bilateral or other seizure sites. Speech dominance was presumed from left-sided resection in right-handed patients, with all but three patients right-handed, without intracarotid sodium amytal testing in doubtful cases. Tables distinguish cases from patients and speech types can overlap; the Table I overlap count conflicts with the Summary as described in F001. Several qualitative claims, including grand-mal and radiological associations, lack exact numerators and denominators. Speech arrest and vocalization were excluded by the authors. Cited-study results are retained as restatements of the current document and were not independently reviewed.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The first 100 consecutive patients with temporal lobe epilepsy operated on by anterior temporal lobectomy were studied; pre-operative documentation recorded the presence or absence and nature of speech disturbance connected with fits, and follow-up was mostly by personal interview for 2-10 years. The operated side was used as an imperfect reference for the presumed primary epileptogenic site: Group A comprised 53 patients who became seizure-free or almost so and were presumed correctly diagnosed, while Group B comprised 47 patients with continuing attacks and lower localization validity, including 30 improved patients and 17 slightly benefited or unchanged patients. Table I reports 56 left-sided and 44 right-sided resections. All patients had pre-operative psychomotor seizures and many also had grand mal attacks. All but three patients were right-handed for ordinary tasks; cerebral speech dominance was presumed from left-sided resection in right-handed persons because intracarotid sodium amytal testing had not yet been used in doubtful cases.
sources.source_report_summary: Original empirical surgical series by E. A. Serafetinides and M. A. Falconer, “Speech Disturbances in Temporal Lobe Seizures: A Study in 100 Epileptic Patients Submitted to Anterior Temporal Lobectomy” (1963). The report describes pre-operative paroxysmal dysphasia and speech automatisms, their source-native definitions and subtypes, frequency, laterality, pre-operative interictal EEG associations, and post-operative course in temporal lobe epilepsy.

findings.evidence_text: The source defines the dorsal anterior field by ICMS-evoked chewing, mouthing, and swallowing and the inferior anterior field by lip-lifting, nose-wrinkling, gag-related, mouth-gaping, spitting, and retching responses.

findings.limitations: These were high-intensity, short-train ICMS responses in macaques and cannot be treated as spontaneous seizure semiology; the paper reports no ictal observations or clinical localization validation.

The discussion reports lip-smacking during direct eye contact with a specific experimenter and notes that the behavior can also occur during anxiety or fear.

findings.claim: In macaques, ICMS of the caudalmost insular region produced simple limb-muscle reactions, axial movements, and bodily tremors: proximal movements clustered in the dorsal posterior sector, axial movements occupied the ventral posterior sector, and tremors occurred across both sectors. The source also describes posterior-insula responses including tremors coupled with limb or axial movements, postural adjustments, and ventral-sector trunk rotation toward contralateral space with a gaze shift in the same direction.
findings.evidence_text: The source places proximal responses dorsally, axial responses ventrally, and tremors in both dorsal and ventral caudal insular sectors, with a ventral response described as trunk rotation toward contralateral space and gaze shift.

findings.limitations: These are electrically evoked macaque responses and may reflect recruitment of distributed networks; they do not establish spontaneous seizure semiology, seizure laterality, or clinical localization.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a macaque anatomo-functional connectivity study, not a seizure study. The behavioral observations derive from ICMS maps, including maps from prior work, and the stimulation used a 4 mA, 50 Hz, 3-second train after a quiet baseline; the authors note that insular responses may recruit large-scale networks beyond the stimulated site. The paper contains no patients with insular seizures, no spontaneous ictal or postictal observations, no seizure-onset reference standard, and no patient or seizure denominators for the stimulation-evoked behaviors. Resting-state fMRI was acquired in sedated macaques, and tract-tracing and connectivity results provide network context rather than direct evidence of seizure expression. Bibliographic citations to human insular stimulation or seizure studies do not convert this source into a seizure study.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The paper summarizes prior macaque ICMS mapping performed with 200-microsecond biphasic pulses at 50 Hz, 4 mA, for 3 seconds; a behavior entered the dataset when two observers recognized it and it was evoked in more than 50% of trials. The present analyses used ICMS maps and insular tracer injections in two male rhesus macaques (Mk1 and Mk2), indirect tracer data from 22 additional animals, and resting-state fMRI from 12 male macaques aged 4-8 years. The authors warped the ICMS maps and injection sites onto the INIA19 macaque template and delineated six insular fields. No seizure cohort, ictal or postictal observations, or clinical localization reference standard was studied.
sources.source_report_summary: Simone et al., Progress in Neurobiology 247 (2025) 102748, is an original experimental nonhuman-primate study combining macaque intracortical microstimulation (ICMS)-defined insular field maps, tract tracing, and resting-state fMRI to characterize insular anatomo-functional networks. The functional-localization observations below are stimulation-evoked macaque behaviors; this source is not a seizure study.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review with heterogeneous cited populations and no single source cohort, unified ascertainment method, quantitative evidence table, or source-verified cited-study dataset. The review mentions that FCD may have “particular ictal changes” on EEG and that lissencephaly may have a characteristic interictal EEG appearance, but it does not name or describe those patterns; they are therefore not represented as sign-level findings. The bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria phenotype, congenital hemiparesis, developmental delay, pseudobulbar palsy, and spastic quadruparesis are non-ictal developmental or neurological features and are not converted into seizure-atlas findings. No claim in this report establishes a body-side or hemisphere direction.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The article is a narrative review rather than a single primary cohort. The review states that it identified material through MEDLINE and Current Contents searches using MCD, malformation, epilepsy, named-gene, and related terms, supplemented by relevant articles and the author's files; only papers published in English were reviewed. The populations and designs vary across the cited reports and are often not specified in the review text. Cohort descriptors, prevalence estimates, surgery outcomes, treatment response, mortality, and developmental context are retained only as background when needed to interpret an in-scope claim, not as independent atlas findings.
sources.source_report_summary: This is a narrative clinical review by Sanjay M Sisodiya, published as Malformations of cortical development: burdens and insights from important causes of human epilepsy (Lancet Neurol 2004;3:29-38). It surveys focal cortical dysplasia, periventricular heterotopia, polymicrogyria, subcortical band heterotopia and lissencephaly, dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumours, and microdysgenesis. This report retains only source-reported seizure manifestations or statements that bear directly on epileptogenic localization; malformation taxonomy, genetics, imaging descriptors, treatment, outcomes, and general burden are not represented as findings.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a single case report with no comparator, reference standard, cohort-level denominator, statistical analysis, or uncertainty estimates. Initial ictal scalp EEG was nonlocalizable, while MRI and FDG-PET did not identify a focal abnormality. The authors note that the first resection could have affected the brain network and that more cases are needed; cited-study statements above were not independently reviewed.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Single case report: an 18-year-old right-handed girl with medically refractory reflex and spontaneous seizures since age 12. The evaluation included MRI, FDG-PET, scalp and long-term video EEG, two MEG analyses, two chronic subdural-electrode evaluations with functional mapping, ictal SPECT during provocation, resections, histopathology, and postoperative follow-up. No comparator or reference standard was reported.
sources.source_report_summary: Suzuki et al., “The Involvement of Sensory-motor Networks in Reflex Seizure,” NMC Case Report Journal 2017;4:127–130, is a single-patient case report describing stimulus-triggered reflex seizures, multimodal presurgical localization, two invasive evaluations and resections, ictal SPECT, and follow-up. The source is relevant to seizure semiology and case-specific left-sided and bilateral sensory-motor network localization.

sources.source_report_limitations: All 25 native pages were represented and reviewed; no page was blocked. This is an educational chapter combining review synthesis, cited-study restatements, a selected representative table, and one clinical case rather than one defined cohort. Many cited results lack denominators, response counts, effect sizes, or uncertainty estimates in the chapter, and cited sources were not independently reviewed. The source itself notes variability of stimulation responses, possible distant or systemic effects, incomplete understanding of functional networks, and difficulty interpreting memory mapping at the individual level. Table 10.1 is explicitly a selected sample; its final executive-function cell is visibly truncated to “No dis” in the rendered source and was not used for an in-scope finding. The chapter does not establish spontaneous-seizure semiology frequencies, diagnostic accuracy, or equivalence between stimulation-induced responses and spontaneous seizures.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The source describes clinical SEEG functional mapping using stimulation of sampled contacts during patient-specific tasks and summarizes cited studies involving patients with epilepsy, plus selected non-SEEG and awake-mapping studies in Table 10.1. Cited-study populations, sampling frames, analysis units, and denominators are frequently not reported in this chapter. One source-described clinical example is a 17-year-old patient with left temporo-perisylvian epilepsy and MRI-negative imaging (Fig. 10.4). The source distinguishes stimulation-induced clinical/electrophysiological responses from spontaneous seizures and treats afterdischarges as interpretation context.
sources.source_report_summary: Educational Chapter 10, “Electrical Stimulation for Functional Mapping During SEEG Exploration,” by Agnès Trébuchon and Daniel L. Drane in The Fundamentals of Stereoelectroencephalography (2025). The chapter reviews SEEG stimulation mapping and selected representative stimulation studies, with emphasis on how induced functional effects can localize functional sub-units and how they should be interpreted alongside seizure electro-clinical data. It is not a single spontaneous-seizure cohort.

findings.claim: The review states that seizure semiology localizes the symptomatogenic zone, which either overlaps or is close to the epileptogenic zone, and that later symptoms are more likely to reflect ictal spread and may have lateralizing rather than localizing value.
findings.evidence_text: “Seizure semiology is a simple and cost effective tool that allows localization of the symptomatogenic zone which either overlaps or is in close proximity of the epileptogenic zone.”
findings.laterality_localization: Symptomatogenic-zone localization is related to, but is not stated to be identical with, epileptogenic-zone localization; later spread-related signs may lateralize side without localizing origin
findings.limitations: NONE
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract; PDF p.1, Introduction
findings.population: Medically refractory focal epilepsy and epilepsy-surgery context; no single cohort reported

findings.evidence_text: “Ideally the signs used for localization should fulfill these criteria” followed by early timing, reliability, defined symptomatogenic zone, and stimulation-reproducibility criteria.

findings.limitations: NONE

findings.citation: References 2 and 3: Pugnaghi M, Meletti S, Castana L, Francione S, Nobili L, Mai R, et al. Features of somatosensory manifestations induced by intracranial electrical stimulations of the human insula. Clin Neurophysiol 2011;122:2049-2058; Stephani C, Fernandez-Baca Vaca G, Maciunas R, Koubeissi M, Luders HO. Functional neuroanatomy of the insular lobe. Brain Struct Funct 2011;216:137-149.
findings.claim: The review states that unilateral distal somatosensory auras confined to a clearly defined body region usually correspond to the contralateral primary sensory cortex, whereas bilateral or widespread sensations can arise from the supplementary sensorimotor area or S2; S2 stimulation can produce heat or pain, and poorly localized or lateralized “all body sensations” have no localizing or lateralizing value. Low-intensity motor-area stimulation may be perceived as a somatosensory aura when contractions do not produce actual movement.
findings.evidence_text: “The contralateral primary sensory cortex is usually the symptomatogenic zone” for unilateral distal auras; “Bilateral and more widespread” sensations can be produced from SSMA or S2; “all body sensations” have no localizing or lateralizing value.
findings.laterality_localization: Unilateral distal distribution points to contralateral primary sensory cortex; bilateral/widespread distribution can involve SSMA or S2; all-body sensations are explicitly nonlocalizing and nonlateralizing
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited stimulation literature; cited sources were not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.1, Somatosensory auras; PDF p.2, Somatosensory auras (continued)
findings.population: Patients with unilateral/distal, bilateral/widespread, or poorly localized somatosensory auras; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 4: Kuzniecky R. Symptomatic occipital lobe epilepsy. Epilepsia 1998;39 Suppl 4:S24-S31.
findings.claim: The review states that visual auras are often perceived in front of both eyes without clear lateralization, but may occasionally be lateralized to one visual field contralateral to the symptomatogenic zone and may be localized to an upper or lower field; simple visual hallucinations are assigned to Brodmann areas 17 and 18, while complex hallucinations or illusions more likely involve parieto-temporal association cortex or adjacent lobes. During or after amaurosis, flashing lights may appear over the blind field.
findings.evidence_text: Visual hallucinations are “frequently” reported in front of both eyes without clear lateralization; an aura may be lateralized to a visual field “contralateral to the symptomatogenic zone”; the symptomatogenic zone for visual hallucinations is Brodmann areas 17 and 18.
findings.laterality_localization: Bilateral visual reports are usually nonlateralizing; a unilateral visual field is contralateral to the symptomatogenic zone; simple versus complex visual phenomena are associated with primary versus association visual regions
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with one cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.phase: Aura; amaurosis may occur during or after the epileptic seizure
findings.population: Patients with visual auras; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 5: Florindo I, Bisulli F, Pittau F, Naldi I, Striano P, Striano S, et al. Lateralizing value of the auditory aura in partial seizures. Epilepsia 2006;47 Suppl 5:68-72.
findings.claim: The review describes simple auditory auras such as a buzz or noise as arising from Heschl's gyrus in the superior temporal gyrus and states that perceived sound laterality is not reliable for lateralizing the epilepsy, even when the patient perceives the sound on one side.
findings.evidence_text: “Even when the sound is perceived as lateralized to one side it is not a reliable sign to lateralize the epilepsy.”
findings.laterality_localization: Heschl's gyrus/superior temporal gyrus is the stated symptomatogenic zone; perceived sound side is not a reliable epilepsy-lateralizing direction
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.population: Patients with simple auditory auras; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 6: Acharya V, Acharya J, Lüders H. Olfactory epileptic auras. Neurology 1998;51:56-61.
findings.claim: The review states that olfactory auras are usually unpleasant smells, have no lateralizing value, and are most frequently seen in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy; it also reports that a relatively high percentage of these patients have neoplasms involving the amygdala.
findings.evidence_text: “They have no lateralizing value but are most frequently seen in patients with mesial temporal lobe epilepsy”; a “relatively high percentage” have neoplasms involving the amygdala.
findings.laterality_localization: No lateralizing value; association with mesial temporal lobe and, in the review's cited statement, amygdala-involving neoplasms
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with an unquantified cited restatement
findings.population: Patients with olfactory auras, particularly mesial temporal lobe epilepsy; percentage and cohort denominator not reported

findings.citation: Reference 3: Stephani C, Fernandez-Baca Vaca G, Maciunas R, Koubeissi M, Luders HO. Functional neuroanatomy of the insular lobe. Brain Struct Funct 2011;216:137-149.
findings.claim: The review describes gustatory auras as unpleasant tastes, states that cortical stimulation studies identify the insula as a symptomatogenic zone, and states that these auras have no lateralizing value.
findings.evidence_text: “Cortical stimulation studies have found the insula to be a symptomatogenic zone for this aura”; “These auras have no lateralizing value.”

findings.claim: The review distinguishes subjective autonomic auras from “autonomic seizures,” which it says should be diagnosed when an autonomic alteration is objectively documented, such as tachycardia on ECG; the symptomatogenic zone of most autonomic auras is stated to be most likely the insular cortex.
findings.evidence_text: Autonomic seizures are described as having an autonomic alteration “that can be documented objectively”; the symptomatogenic zone of most autonomic auras is “most likely the insular cortex.”
findings.laterality_localization: Most autonomic auras are assigned most likely to the insular cortex; no laterality direction stated

findings.citation: Reference 8: Van Buren JM. The abdominal aura. A study of abdominal sensations occurring in epilepsy and produced by depth stimulation. Electroencephalogr Clin Neurophysiol 1963;15:1-19.
findings.claim: The review states that abdominal auras are frequent and usually secondary to temporal lobe epilepsy, but can occasionally be triggered by extratemporal epilepsy, mainly frontal or insular. The sensation usually begins in the epigastrium or midline stomach and may rise to the chest, throat, head, or face; when it rises to the neck or face, loss of consciousness is described as almost invariable. The review also reports that Van Buren's balloon studies found no gastromotor effect except rare gastric inhibition, and that stimulation has elicited similar sensations from the insula and other structures, with spread-related afterdischarges not excluded.
findings.evidence_text: “Abdominal auras are frequent and are usually secondary to temporal lobe epilepsies”; the sensation “begins usually in the epigastrium or stomach in the midline” and may rise to the neck or face, when the patient “loses consciousness.”
findings.laterality_localization: Usual temporal association with occasional frontal/insular extratemporal association; epigastric sensations can be elicited from insula, mesial temporal structures, basal ganglia, SSMA, pallidum, and centrum medianum of thalamus
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited stimulation findings and an explicit afterdischarge-spread qualification
findings.phase: Aura; upward spread of the aura may precede loss of consciousness
findings.population: Patients with abdominal auras; cited spontaneous, induced, and stimulation observations, with no common cohort size reported

findings.citation: References 9 and 10: Devinsky O, Feldmann E, Burrowes K, Bromfield E. Autoscopic phenomena with seizures. Arch Neurol 1989;46:1080-1088; Bancaud J, Brunet-Bourgin F, Chauvel P, Halgren E. Anatomical origin of deja vu and vivid ‘memories’ in human temporal lobe epilepsy. Brain 1994;117:71-90.
findings.claim: The review states that psychic auras include complex hallucinations or illusions such as autoscopy, fear, elation, déjà vu, and jamais vu. The temporal lobe is usually involved in autoscopic phenomena, but they have no lateralizing value; stimulation has elicited related sensations from the temporal convexity or posterior temporal-occipital/parietal junction, with mesial temporal structures concurrently involved in most cited cases.
findings.evidence_text: “The temporal lobe is usually involved with these phenomena but they have no lateralizing value”; mesial temporal structures were “concurrently involved in most cases.”
findings.laterality_localization: Temporal and often mesial temporal involvement; no lateralizing value stated for autoscopic phenomena
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited stimulation and clinical reports; cited sources were not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Psychic auras; PDF p.3, Psychic auras (continued)
findings.population: Patients with psychic or autoscopic auras; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 7: Baumgartner C, Lurger S, Leutmezer F. Autonomic symptoms during epileptic seizures. Epileptic Disord 2001;3:103-116.
findings.claim: The review states that pilomotor seizures have a somatotopic distribution and may spread in a Jacksonian-march-like pattern; they tend to be ipsilateral to the seizure-onset zone, but their localization value is poor.

findings.claim: The review states that ictal vomiting and retching are observed mainly in adult temporal lobe seizures, have no definite lateralizing value, and have some evidence supporting a role for the insula as visceral sensory cortex.

findings.claim: The review describes ictal spitting as a rare sign that also occurs in temporal lobe epilepsy and has no lateralizing value.
findings.evidence_text: “Ictal spitting is a rare sign that also occurs in temporal lobe epilepsy but has no lateralizing value.”

findings.claim: The review states that ictal hypersalivation is an uncommon sign found more frequently in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, particularly in the non-dominant hemisphere.
findings.evidence_text: “Ictal hypersalivation is another uncommon sign found more frequently in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy particularly in the non-dominant hemisphere.”

findings.citation: Reference 13: Wyllie E, Lüders H, Morris HH, Lesser RP, Dinner DS. The lateralizing significance of versive head and eye movements during epileptic seizures. Neurology 1986;36:606-611.
findings.claim: The review states that the epileptogenic zone in dialeptic seizures tends to be distant from primary or supplementary motor areas, whereas seizures originating at or near those areas tend to be predominantly motor and may have preserved consciousness; dialeptic seizures from mesial temporal structures are longer than those arising from the frontal lobe.
findings.evidence_text: “The duration ... has a localizing value with seizures originating from the mesial temporal structures being of longer duration than the ones arising from the frontal lobe.”
findings.laterality_localization: Dialeptic semiology is associated with distance from primary/SSMA motor areas; longer duration is associated with mesial temporal versus frontal origin
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.phase: Ictal consciousness alteration and seizure duration
findings.population: Patients with dialeptic seizures compared with seizures originating at or near primary or supplementary motor areas; no cohort reported

findings.citation: References 15 and 16: Bagla R, Skidmore CT. Frontal lobe seizures. Neurologist 2011;17:125-135; Werhahn KJ, Noachtar S, Arnold S, Pfänder M, Henkel A, Winkler PA, et al. Tonic seizures: their significance for lateralization and frequency in different focal epileptic syndromes. Epilepsia 2000;41:1153-1161.
findings.claim: The review states that focal tonic seizures preferentially affect proximal muscle groups, may be unilateral or bilateral, and tend to be asymmetric; consciousness is often preserved at onset. Preserved consciousness during bilateral motor activity can localize a focus to the supplementary motor area. Tonic seizures are reported in 62.2% of frontal-lobe epilepsy and 1.7% of temporal-lobe epilepsy; temporal-lobe tonic seizures were unilateral, whereas 32% of frontal-lobe tonic seizures were bilateral. A clearly unilateral tonic seizure has high lateralizing significance toward the contralateral seizure onset.
findings.evidence_text: “Tonic seizures occur most commonly in frontal lobe epilepsy (62.2%) and very rarely in temporal lobe epilepsy (1.7%).”
findings.laterality_localization: Bilateral motor activity with preserved consciousness can point to SSMA; clearly unilateral tonic activity points to contralateral seizure onset; temporal and frontal distributions differ as stated
findings.limitations: Review-reported comparative percentages; cited sources were not separately reviewed here

findings.claim: The review describes a sequence beginning with version and tonic pulling of the face to the contralateral side, followed by the M2e fencing position and then asymmetric tonic limb posturing called the “sign of four.” It states that confidence in lateralizing the epileptogenic zone increases when at least two of the four signs are observed; the tonic face and versive signs point contralaterally, M2e points to the hemisphere contralateral to the raised arm, and the sign of four to the hemisphere contralateral to the extended arm. These signs lateralize but do not localize seizure origin.

findings.laterality_localization: Face tonic seizure and version contralateral; M2e contralateral to raised arm; sign of four contralateral to extended arm; signs lateralize but do not localize origin
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited sources; the review does not provide the underlying denominators or independent validation of the combination rule

findings.claim: The review describes epileptic spasms as relatively symmetric tonic or myoclonic contractions affecting proximal axial muscles, usually with trunk flexion and arm extension/abduction in a “salaam position”; they commonly occur in clusters as the patient goes to sleep and have predominantly generalized EEG patterns. They are usually seen with generalized epilepsies, but well-documented focal cases, particularly parieto-occipital, have undergone successful resective surgery; the mechanism is not clearly determined.

In temporal lobe epilepsy, the face, frontal eye field, and hand areas tend to be affected earlier than the legs; when clonus without altered consciousness is the first seizure sign, the epileptogenic zone is usually at or near the primary motor strip. Unilateral clonic seizures have high lateralizing value toward the contralateral hemisphere.

findings.claim: The review states that automotor seizures consist mainly of distal hand, foot, mouth, and tongue automatisms and are typical of temporal-lobe epilepsy, although they can occur in frontal-lobe seizures; frontal automotor seizures tend to be shorter. Unilateral automatisms are more frequently associated with an ipsilateral epileptogenic zone, possibly because contralateral limb dystonia interrupts distal automatisms. Altered consciousness accompanies 95% of automotor seizures, while preserved consciousness is observed almost exclusively in non-dominant mesial temporal epilepsy.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source is a narrative review whose stated basis is a literature review plus results consistent with the authors' experience; it does not provide a reproducible search, eligibility process, unified cohort, common reference standard, or pooled estimate. Many cited results are restatements of other publications and are not primary findings of this document. Quantitative statements such as 62.2%, 1.7%, 32%, 95%, approximately 50%, and 46% are reported without the underlying numerators, denominators, uncertainty intervals, or, where applicable, explicit analysis units. The review itself emphasizes substantial inter-rater variability, including different definitions across epilepsy centers and possible confusion between versive and non-versive head turning. It also cautions that semiology may reflect ictal spread: different epileptogenic zones can activate the same symptomatogenic zone, and the same epileptogenic zone can activate different symptomatogenic zones. Finally, focal-appearing semiology can occur in generalized epilepsy, and the review reports conflicting signs within a single seizure; its proposed safeguards are standardization, unambiguous signs, observer consensus, sequence, and specificity.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The document is a narrative literature review organized by a semiological classification of paroxysmal events, auras, autonomic, dialeptic, motor, special, and additional lateralizing signs. It does not report a systematic search method, eligibility criteria, aggregate review population, cohort size, comparator, or common reference standard. Individual findings retain the population, phase, comparator, and cited-study attribution stated in the review.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2012 J Clin Neurol narrative review by Krikor Tufenkjian and Hans O. Lüders summarizes seizure-semiology findings considered useful for localizing the epileptogenic zone, with emphasis on prominent and consistent signs and on lateralizing signs. The review states that its information is based on literature review and results consistent with the authors' experience; it is not a report of one newly enrolled cohort.

sources.source_report_limitations: The article is a narrative critical appraisal rather than a single cohort or quantitative synthesis; most table entries are citation groupings without category counts, denominators, uncertainty intervals, or standardized analysis units. The source explicitly notes that impaired consciousness, short ictal duration, accompanying or evolving seizure types, and difficult ictal/postictal differentiation limit precise classification. The illustrated EEG panels are single case observations and do not establish cohort frequencies. Cited-study restatements above remain unverified against their cited targets because only this PDF and its fresh source package were in the evidence boundary. The body attributes one result to “Privitera and Kim [73]” and another to “Lösch et al. [74]”; this report preserves those source-native attributions without reconciling internal citation numbering against the bibliography. No sign identity is assigned.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors report an extensive literature search on the term “epileptic aphasia,” analysis of semiology and terminology indicating language-associated seizure symptoms, and an overview of EEG, etiology, brain imaging, and ictal language disorders. The document is not a single-cohort study; its evidence base includes cited case reports, case series, and studies involving ictal aphasia, aphasic status epilepticus (ASE), temporal/frontal/other focal epilepsies, and postictal language dysfunction. The review does not report one pooled analysis population or common denominator.
sources.source_report_summary: Unterberger et al. (Epilepsy & Behavior, 2021) is a narrative critical appraisal of epileptic aphasia and other ictal/postictal language disturbances. It reviews source terminology and semiology and summarizes EEG, etiology, brain imaging, and seizure-associated language lateralization/localization evidence. The article is relevant to language-associated seizure semiology, dominant-hemisphere lateralization, and the limits of finer localization.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a retrospective, selected 22-patient series from a presurgical SEEG population; inclusion required complete presurgical evaluation and clear seizure-semiology video, and the cohort mixed pediatric and adult patients. Scalp-EEG interpretation used representative or predominant patterns, and at least two habitual seizures per patient were reviewed rather than every recorded seizure. The voxel-based PET comparison excluded five patients and used a left-transposed representation for right-sided epileptogenic foci; PET hypometabolism may extend beyond the seizure-onset or propagation cortex, as the authors note. Aggregate laterality is incomplete: several “ipsilateral” or “contralateral” descriptors do not restate their reference side, and many aggregate results do not provide side-specific counts. The online supporting information named on page 13 (Table S1 and Figure S1) is not included in the locked 13-page source package and was not reviewed.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The study retrospectively identified 22 consecutive medication-resistant patients evaluated between January 2015 and March 2018; 12 were adults and 10 were pediatric patients. Insulo-opercular seizure origin was defined by SEEG, and patients without complete presurgical evaluation or clear seizure-semiology video were excluded. At least two habitual seizures were reviewed per patient for scalp video-EEG (53 seizures total), and EI was computed for two habitual seizures per patient. PET visual/MRI-coregistration analyses involved the patient group; the voxel-based PET comparison used 17 patients after excluding three with previous epilepsy surgery and two younger than 7 years, compared with 18 healthy subjects.
sources.source_report_summary: Wang et al., “Electroclinical features of insulo-opercular epilepsy: an SEEG and PET study,” Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology 2019;6:1165-1177, is an original retrospective empirical study of presurgical electroclinical features, interictal PET, and ictal SEEG in patients with SEEG-defined insulo-opercular epilepsy. Its in-scope contribution is a source-reported characterization of seizure semiology, scalp-EEG distribution, PET abnormalities, and EI-based localization.

sources.source_report_limitations:
This is a small, single-center cohort of eight patients selected through epilepsy surgery and temporal-pole lesion review. The source contains detailed observations for a few recorded seizures and two invasive cases, so patient-level and seizure-level denominators are not interchangeable. Table 1 is retained only for direct semiology and localization/lateralization; age, sex, pathology totals, surgery, and outcome cells are not individual findings. The temporal-pole-to-frontal spread statement is explicitly an author hypothesis, and no independent causal or diagnostic-performance estimate is available.

Owner question: Should the source authors’ inferred temporal-pole onset in the two subdural-grid cases be integrated as localization evidence separately from the orbitofrontal propagation findings, given the limited invasive sample?
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors retrospectively reviewed consecutive epilepsy-surgery patients with MRI and pathology evidence of temporal pole lesions. Eight patients with intractable complex partial seizures were identified; long-term scalp-sphenoidal video-EEG was obtained, and two patients also underwent subdural-grid monitoring. MRI was performed in all patients; FDG PET was available for seven and ictal SPECT for three. The study classified recorded seizures as hypermotor or typical psychomotor under the source-described semiologic scheme.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2008 primary study examines hypermotor seizure semiology in eight patients with lesions involving the temporal pole. Directly retained evidence includes source definitions of “hypermotor” and “hyperkinetic,” hypermotor and psychomotor signs, patient-level aura and lesion-side terms, temporal-pole MRI/PET/SPECT localization, temporal and orbitofrontal EEG onset/spread, and seizure-evolution timing. Generic demographics, operative-procedure counts, pathology totals, and postoperative outcomes remain context only.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a single-center retrospective cohort of 19 patients with hypothesis-driven SEEG sampling. Pattern and phenotype assignments reflect predominant early electroclinical trajectories, not exclusive anatomical routes; cross-stream propagation and incomplete sampling can affect the apparent correspondence. Several qualitative statements lack denominators, and Table 2 case sequences are not a population frequency table. Table 1 demographic, imaging-cell, electrode, treatment, pathology, follow-up, and Engel-outcome details were not promoted to individual findings unless directly tied to a seizure-localization or semiology claim. The authors identify ASM tapering, subjective-aura underreporting, sampling bias, and absent gold-standard classification validation as limitations. No Lüders or ILAE classification, anatomy synonym, or Brodmann mapping is inferred.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This single-center retrospective case series included 19 patients with SEEG-confirmed occipital lobe seizure onset. The authors reviewed video-EEG/clinical descriptions and SEEG-anchored temporal evolution, used MRI/CT-fused electrode localization, and assigned a predominant propagation pattern through electroclinical concordance. The source’s occipital parcellation and phenotype labels are preserved without imposing a Lüders or ILAE crosswalk.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2026 primary retrospective SEEG case series studied 19 patients with occipital lobe epilepsy and proposed five clinical phenotypes linked to four predominant SEEG propagation patterns. Findings retained here are limited to source-native seizure signs, semiologic evolution, seizure-onset localization, hemispheric lateralization, propagation, and directly linked quantitative results. Table 1 demographics, generic sampling and treatment cells, pathology, follow-up, and Engel outcomes are retained only as context and are not individual findings. Direct clinical and SEEG information from Table 2 and the illustrated electroclinical cases is retained.

findings.claim: The ictal EEG pattern remained clearly lateralized into onset of the contraversive movement in 54 seizures from 24 patients; 3 previously lateralized seizures were obscured by EMG artifact, and 4 remaining seizures included 3 with nonlateralized EEG onset and 1 with temporal onset spreading equally to both temporal lobes before contraversion.
findings.evidence_text: The EEG seizure pattern remained clearly lateralized into the onset of the contraversive movement during 54 seizures from 24 patients.
findings.laterality_localization: In an illustrative seizure, ictal EEG began in the right mesial temporal lobe for 79 seconds, spread to both temporal lobes equally for 75 seconds, and was followed by leftward contraversion with left arm and face clonic activity; the movement remained contralateral to the initial onset hemisphere
findings.limitations: Three seizures with generalized EEG onset were interpreted using interictal focus in the methods, and EMG artifact obscured three previously lateralized patterns.

findings.claim: Thirty-five of 61 versive seizures (57%) began with the versive movement; these were predominantly frontal-onset (91%) and none was temporal-onset, whereas the other versive seizures were preceded by quiet staring or staring with automatisms as detailed in Table 2.
findings.evidence_text: Thirty-five (57%) of the 61 versive seizures began with the versive movement.
findings.laterality_localization: Contraversive movement was related to the EEG-defined seizure-onset region; onset region was frontal, temporal, parietal, or occipital
findings.limitations: Quiet staring without automatisms occurred in both temporal and extratemporal onset seizures and was not assigned a specific mechanism.

findings.population: 27 patients; 61 versive seizures categorized by frontal, temporal, parietal, or occipital onset

findings.claim: Quiet staring preceded contraversion for 8 versive seizures for 2-31 seconds (mean 17), while staring with automatisms preceded contraversion for 18 seizures for 4-227 seconds (mean 34); all seizures with automatisms before contraversion originated in temporal lobes, whereas the quiet-staring subgroup arose from temporal (25%) and extratemporal (75%) locations.
findings.evidence_text: All seizures with contraversion preceded by automatisms originated in temporal lobes.
findings.laterality_localization: Contraversion followed a period of temporal localization when preceded by staring with automatisms; quiet-staring onset was temporal or extratemporal
findings.limitations: The paper did not report numerators for the 25% and 75% onset-region proportions in the quiet-staring subgroup.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Table 2; PDF p.3, paragraphs reporting quiet-staring and automatisms durations and onset regions; PDF p.4, discussion of temporal localization before contraversion

findings.claim: During contraversion, arm and face motor activity occurred on the side toward which contraversion was directed: arm clonic movement or tonic posturing occurred in 32 of 61 versive seizures (52%), face tonic or clonic contraction in 26 of 55 seizures with continuously visible faces (47%), and arm and face involvement occurred with equal frequency in temporal and extratemporal onset seizures.

findings.limitations: Facial analysis excluded 6 seizures without continuous full facial visibility.

findings.claim: In 23 versive seizures from 14 patients, arm posturing included the “fencing position” with elbow flexion followed by approximately 90-degree shoulder abduction; the authors state that M2e posturing was common in temporal and extratemporal onset versive seizures without ictal activity localized to the supplementary motor areas and probably reflected widespread ictal involvement of precentral contraversive and arm/face motor areas rather than localized supplementary motor activation.
findings.evidence_text: In 23 versive seizures from 14 patients, this posturing involved assumption of the “fencing position.”
findings.laterality_localization: Fencing posture involved the arm on the side of contraversion; the proposed localization was widespread precentral contraversive and motor arm/face involvement, not a localized supplementary motor area
findings.limitations: The paper does not provide a separate denominator or statistical comparison for the M2e subgroup.

findings.claim: None of 13 complex partial seizures without contraversion generalized; among versive seizures, 27 (44%) secondarily generalized 2-34 seconds (mean 15) after contraversive movement, with generalized tonic-clonic activity lasting 27-82 seconds (mean 54), and generalization frequency and duration did not differ by focal arm/face involvement or temporal versus extratemporal onset.
findings.evidence_text: Of the 13 complex partial seizures without contraversion, none generalized.
findings.laterality_localization: Secondary generalization was evaluated after contraversive head and eye movement; focal arm/face activity was on the side of contraversion
findings.limitations: The paper reports no p values or separate effect estimates for the stated null comparisons.

sources.source_report_limitations: The cohort was selected for lateral head and eye movement and therefore does not represent all seizures. Two of 39 selected patients were excluded because EMG artifact obscured seizure onset. Three seizures had generalized ictal EEG onset and were assigned to an interictal focus; three other previously lateralized patterns were obscured by EMG artifact at contraversion. The distinction between versive and nonversive movement depended on high-quality video and consistent interpretation, and the authors note that lower-resolution or time-lapse recordings can mix subtle nonversive and forced movements. Ictal consciousness was difficult to assess because edited videotapes often lacked routine postictal interviews, so the authors could not reliably apply the contemporary partial-seizure consciousness distinction. Occipital-onset evidence comprised two seizures from one patient and was insufficient to evaluate mechanism. Background comparisons with cited studies are restatements from this paper and were not independently verified here. Page 6 is primarily references and page 7 is publisher information; no additional scientific findings were present in those pages.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Thirty-nine patients aged 1-48 years (mean 22) were selected for lateral head and eye movement during seizures; 2 were excluded because electromyographic artifact obscured electroencephalographic seizure onset. The analyzed sample was 37 patients with 74 spontaneous seizures: 20 patients were studied for complex partial seizures with or without secondary generalization and 17 for partial motor seizures with or without altered consciousness or secondary generalization. All seizures occurred spontaneously in the EEG laboratory, were recorded from onset, and had high-quality synchronized audio-video and EEG recordings; scalp, nasopharyngeal or sphenoidal electrodes were used, and 8 patients also had chronic subdural electrode arrays. Video and EEG were analyzed independently, and movement classification was performed without knowledge of EEG or clinical data. Ictal EEG seizure-onset location was used for all seizures except 3 with generalized ictal EEG onset, which were assigned to the location of the interictal focus because of other lateralizing EEG data. Table 1 onset totals were frontal 39 (12 patients), temporal 31 (22), parietal 2 (2), and occipital 2 (1); table values are seizures with patient counts in parentheses.
sources.source_report_summary: Original empirical observational study by Wyllie, Luders, Morris, Lesser, and Dinner, published in Neurology in 1986, evaluating whether forced lateral head and eye turning during spontaneous epileptic seizures lateralizes seizure onset. Independent blinded video and EEG review was used to compare versive and nonversive movements, onset region, preceding ictal behavior, associated motor signs, and secondary generalization.

findings.claim: Across the Case-1 SEEG recordings, the source reports initial ictal discharges or polyspikes followed by high-frequency oscillations in the inferioposterior temporal region; the second recording’s initial discharge originated in posterior inferior temporal gyrus, with propagation to the posterior inferior temporal sulcus, anterior and posterior banks of AOS, lateral occipital sulcus, and the frontal eye-field region within 400 ms, while the first recording showed wider propagation including temporo-occipital, supramarginal, angular, and intraparietal regions within 600 ms.

findings.claim: Across the two reported cases, the source reports forced ipsilateral eye deviation as the initial clinical sign and ictal SEEG localization of the epileptogenic zones to the inferioposterior temporal region; the authors further report overlap between the epileptogenic zones and the human MT/MST complex, especially human MST on the anterior/dorsal bank of AOS.

findings.limitations: The combined statement is a case-series observation and cannot support a general rule for all temporal or temporo-occipital seizures.
